A line joining two points $P_1,P_2$ has direction $\vec{P_1P_2}$; it is the normal of every plane perpendicular to it, e.g. the perpendicular bisector plane.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the image of the point $P(2,-1,3)$ in the plane $x+2y-z=0$ be $Q$. Then the distance of the plane $3x+2y+z+29=0$ from the point $Q$ is:
questions.key_idea: The image is $P$ moved along the normal by twice its signed distance, so $Q=P-2\frac{f(P)}{|n|^2}\vec n$.
solution: The line $PQ$ is perpendicular to the plane, so $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-3}{-1}=\frac{-2(2-2-3)}{1^2+2^2+(-1)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Here $|\vec n|^2=6$ and $f(P)=-3$, so $Q=P+\vec n$; then the second plane's expression changes by $\vec n_2\cdot\vec n_1$.
solution: Let $f_2=3x+2y+z+29$ with $\vec n_2=(3,2,1)$. Since $f_2$ is linear, $f_2(Q)=f_2(P)+\vec n_2\cdot(Q-P)=f_2(P)+\vec n_2\cdot\vec n_1$.

useful_results: Image of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ in $ax+by+cz+d=0$: $\frac{x-x_0}{a}=\frac{y-y_0}{b}=\frac{z-z_0}{c}=-\frac{2(ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$; the foot of the perpendicular has factor $-\frac{(\cdots)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$ (half of it).
If $f(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz+d$, the image is $Q=P-\frac{2f(P)}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$ and $f(Q)=-f(P)$, so $P$ and $Q$ are equidistant from the plane on opposite sides.
For a linear function $g(Q)=g(P)+\vec n_g\cdot(Q-P)$: the value of another plane's expression at a displaced point needs only a dot product.
Check on this question: $f(P)=2-2-3=-3$ and, for $Q=(3,1,2)$, $f(Q)=3+2-2=3=-f(P)$, as expected.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-4}{-3}$ and $\frac{x+3}{1}=\frac{y+5}{4}=\frac{z-1}{-5}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance between skew lines is the projection of the join of two points on $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$.
solution: For lines through $(x_1,y_1,z_1),(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ with direction ratios $(a_1,a_2,a_3),(b_1,b_2,b_3)$: $SD=\frac{\left|\begin{matrix}x_1-x_2&y_1-y_2&z_1-z_2\\a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\end{matrix}\right|}{\sqrt{(a_2b_3-a_3b_2)^2+(a_3b_1-a_1b_3)^2+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)^2}}$.
questions.correction_note: Only a notational slip: the PDF writes the first component of $\vec a\times\vec b$ as $a_1b_3-a_3b_2$; it should be $a_2b_3-a_3b_2$. The numbers it substitutes ($-10+12$, $-5+3$, $4-2$) are correct, so the answer $6\sqrt3$ is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take general points on the two lines and impose that the joining segment is perpendicular to both directions.
solution: Let $P(5+s,\,2+2s,\,4-3s)$ on the first line and $Q(-3+t,\,-5+4t,\,1-5t)$ on the second.

useful_results: Shortest distance between $\vec r=\vec a_1+s\vec b_1$ and $\vec r=\vec a_2+t\vec b_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$ when $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\neq\vec 0$.
The lines intersect (or are coplanar) iff the triple product $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=0$, i.e. the SD determinant is zero.
For parallel lines use $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\times\vec b|}{|\vec b|}$ instead, since $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\vec0$.
The common perpendicular is parallel to $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$; here the join $(6,6,6)$ is parallel to $(2,2,2)$, a quick check of the answer.

concepts: Plane through the intersection of two planes, perpendicular planes and distance from a point
questions.question: Let the plane $P$ pass through the intersection of the planes $2x+3y-z=2$ and $x+2y+3z=6$, and be perpendicular to the plane $2x+y-z+1=0$. If $d$ is the distance of $P$ from the point $(-7,1,1)$, then $d^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A plane through the intersection of two planes is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; perpendicularity fixes $\lambda$ via the normals' dot product.
solution: Any plane through the intersection of the two given planes: $2x+3y-z-2+\lambda(x+2y+3z-6)=0$.
It is perpendicular to $2x+y-z+1=0$, so the normals have zero dot product: $2(2+\lambda)+1(3+2\lambda)+(-1)(3\lambda-1)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The normal of $P$ is perpendicular both to the intersection line and to the given plane's normal, so it is their cross product.
solution: The line of intersection has direction $\vec d=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=(2,3,-1)\times(1,2,3)=(11,-7,1)$.
$P$ contains this line and is perpendicular to the plane with normal $(2,1,-1)$, so its normal is $\vec d\times(2,1,-1)=(6,13,25)$.
A point on the line: put $z=0$: $2x+3y=2$, $x+2y=6$ give $x=-14,\ y=10$, so $(-14,10,0)$.

useful_results: The plane $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ represents every plane through the line $P_1=P_2=0$ except $P_2=0$ itself.
The line of intersection of $\vec n_1\cdot\vec r=k_1$ and $\vec n_2\cdot\vec r=k_2$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Plane $\perp$ plane $\iff$ normals are perpendicular; plane $\parallel$ line $\iff$ normal $\perp$ direction.
A plane containing a line with direction $\vec d$ and perpendicular to a plane with normal $\vec m$ has normal $\vec d\times\vec m$ (here $(11,-7,1)\times(2,1,-1)=(6,13,25)$).

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-6}{2}$ and $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{1-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{0}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Rewrite $\frac{1-y}{2}$ as $\frac{y-1}{-2}$ so the second direction is $(3,-2,0)$, then use the triple-product formula.
solution: Rewrite the second line as $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z+8}{0}$: it passes through $(6,1,-8)$ with direction $\vec b=(3,-2,0)$.
The first line passes through $(2,-1,6)$ with direction $\vec a=(3,2,2)$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&2&2\\3&-2&0\end{matrix}\right|=4\hat i+6\hat j-12\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: Sign slip in the PDF: it prints $\vec a\times\vec b=-4\hat i+6\hat j-12\hat k$, but the correct value is $4\hat i+6\hat j-12\hat k$. The magnitude (14) and the triple product (196) used afterwards are correct, so the answer 14 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take general points on the lines and make the joining segment perpendicular to both directions.
solution: Let $P(2+3s,\,-1+2s,\,6+2s)$ and $Q(6+3t,\,1-2t,\,-8)$ be points on the two lines.

useful_results: Skew-line distance $=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$; the numerator is $\pm$ the volume of the parallelepiped on $\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\vec b_1,\vec b_2$.
Normalise the symmetric form first: $\frac{1-y}{2}$ means direction ratio $-2$ for $y$, a frequent trap.
A zero direction ratio ($\frac{z+8}{0}$) means the line stays in the plane $z=-8$; it is perpendicular to the $z$-axis.
Check: the join of the closest points is parallel to $\vec a\times\vec b$; here both equal $(4,6,-12)$.

concepts: Plane through a line and parallel to another line (family of planes)
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the equation of the plane passing through the line $x-2y-z-5=0=x+y+3z-5$ and parallel to the line $x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$ be $ax+by+cz=65$. Then the distance of the point $(a,b,c)$ from the plane $2x+2y-z+16=0$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: The plane is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, and parallelism with the second line means its normal is perpendicular to that line's direction.
solution: The plane through the first line is $(x-2y-z-5)+\lambda(x+y+3z-5)=0$, i.e. $(1+\lambda)x+(\lambda-2)y+(3\lambda-1)z-5-5\lambda=0$. (1)
Parallel to the line means normal $\perp$ direction: $-5(1+\lambda)+3(\lambda-2)+1(3\lambda-1)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The plane contains one line and is parallel to another, so its normal is the cross product of the two line directions.
solution: A point on the first line: put $z=0$: $x-2y=5$ and $x+y=5$ give $(5,0,0)$.

useful_results: Plane through the line $P_1=P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; one extra condition (parallel to a line, passing through a point, perpendicular to a plane) fixes $\lambda$.
Plane containing a line of direction $\vec d_1$ and parallel to another of direction $\vec d_2$ has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ (valid when $\vec d_1\not\parallel\vec d_2$).
Line $\frac{\vec n_1\cdot\vec r=k_1}{\vec n_2\cdot\vec r=k_2}$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$; here $(1,1,2)\times(2,3,1)=(-5,3,1)$.
A line is parallel to the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ iff $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+\sqrt6}{2}=\frac{y-\sqrt6}{3}=\frac{z-\sqrt6}{4}$ and $\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2\sqrt6}{4}=\frac{z+2\sqrt6}{5}$ is $6$, then the square of the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: The shortest distance involves an absolute value, so $4\sqrt6-\lambda=\pm6\sqrt6$ gives two values of $\lambda$.
solution: First line: through $\vec a_1=(-\sqrt6,\sqrt6,\sqrt6)$ with $\vec b_1=(2,3,4)$. Second: through $\vec a_2=(\lambda,2\sqrt6,-2\sqrt6)$ with $\vec b_2=(3,4,5)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The shortest distance is the distance between the two parallel planes containing the lines, i.e. a point-to-plane distance.
solution: Plane $\Pi_1$ through the first line containing both directions has normal $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=(-1,2,-1)$.
The second line is parallel to $\Pi_1$, so $SD$ is the distance of its point $(\lambda,2\sqrt6,-2\sqrt6)$ from $\Pi_1$.
Setting this equal to $6$ gives $\lambda=-2\sqrt6$ or $10\sqrt6$; the sum is $8\sqrt6$ and its square is $384$.

useful_results: Two skew lines lie in parallel planes with common normal $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$; $SD$ is the gap between these planes.
$|\vec u|=d$ gives two values of a parameter that enters linearly: $\vec u\cdot(\ldots)=\pm d|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|$ (here $4\sqrt6-\lambda=\pm6\sqrt6$).
If $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ are the two roots of $|c-\lambda|=k$, their sum is $2c$, the midpoint twice (here $c=4\sqrt6$, sum $=8\sqrt6$).
Cross product check: $(2,3,4)\times(3,4,5)=(-1,2,-1)$, which is orthogonal to both directions: $-2+6-4=0$ and $-3+8-5=0$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the line joining the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,3,4)$, and the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-2}{0}$ is $\alpha$, then $28\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The first line has direction $(1,1,1)$; then the skew-line triple product gives $\alpha=\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}$.
solution: The line through $A(1,2,3)$ and $(2,3,4)$ has direction $\vec p=(1,1,1)$.
The second line passes through $B(1,-1,2)$ with direction $\vec q=(2,-1,0)$.
questions.correction_note: The working printed in the PDF under Q50 does not belong to this question: it uses other lines ($\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y}{1/2}=\ldots$) and ends with $SD=2$, not matching the key 18. Written afresh; the key 18 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put a plane through the second line parallel to the first line, then measure the distance of a point of the first line from it.
solution: Plane through $B(1,-1,2)$ containing direction $\vec q=(2,-1,0)$ and parallel to $\vec p=(1,1,1)$ has normal $\vec p\times\vec q=(1,2,-3)$.
The first line is parallel to this plane, so $\alpha$ is the distance of $A(1,2,3)$ from it.

useful_results: A line through points $P_1,P_2$ has direction $\vec{P_1P_2}$; many 3D problems are disguised this way.
$SD=\frac{|\vec{AB}\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)|}{|\vec p\times\vec q|}$ for skew lines through $A,B$ with directions $\vec p,\vec q$; if the numerator is 0 the lines are coplanar.
Distance squared keeps a rational answer: $\alpha^2=\frac{(\vec{AB}\cdot\vec n)^2}{|\vec n|^2}=\frac{9}{14}$ here.

The lines are skew iff $\vec p	imes\vec q
eq\vec 0$ and $\vec{AB}\cdot(\vec p	imes\vec q)
eq0$ (here $-3
eq0$).

concepts: Plane containing a line
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the equation of the plane $P$ containing the line $x+10=\frac{8-y}{2}=z$ be $ax+by+3z=2(a+b)$ and the distance of the plane $P$ from the point $(1,27,7)$ be $c$. Then $a^2+b^2+c^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The plane contains a point of the line and its normal is perpendicular to the line's direction, giving two linear equations in $a,b$.
solution: The line is $\frac{x+10}{1}=\frac{y-8}{-2}=\frac{z}{1}$: it passes through $(-10,8,0)$ with direction $(1,-2,1)$.
The plane contains the point $(-10,8,0)$: $-10a+8b=2a+2b$, so $b=2a$. (3)
The normal $(a,b,3)$ is perpendicular to the direction $(1,-2,1)$: $a-2b+3=0$. (4)

alternate_solutions.idea: Use two points of the line instead of its direction: both must satisfy the plane equation.
solution: Two points of the line: $t=0$ gives $(-10,8,0)$ and $t=1$ gives $(-9,6,1)$ (from $(t-10,\,8-2t,\,t)$).

useful_results: A plane contains a line iff it contains one point of the line and its normal is perpendicular to the line's direction, or iff it contains two points of the line.
Normalise symmetric forms: $\frac{8-y}{2}$ means the $y$-direction ratio is $-2$ and the $y$-value of the point is $8$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; square it to avoid surds ($c^2=\frac{4900}{14}=350$).
Statement note: the printed question lost the symbol $c$ for the distance; it is restored from the Hindi version.

concepts: Distance of a point from a line in 3D
Area of a triangle
questions.question: Let the co-ordinates of one vertex of $\triangle ABC$ be $A(0,2,\alpha)$ and the other two vertices lie on the line $\frac{x+\alpha}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3}$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}$, if the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $21$ sq. units and the line segment $BC$ has length $2\sqrt{21}$ units, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12\cdot BC\cdot h$ gives the height $h=\sqrt{21}$, which is the distance of $A$ from the line.
solution: The line passes through $P(-\alpha,1,-4)$ with direction $\vec d=(5,2,3)$, $|\vec d|=\sqrt{38}$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot BC\cdot h=21$ with $BC=2\sqrt{21}$ gives $h=\sqrt{21}$, the distance of $A$ from the line.
$\vec{PA}\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&1&\alpha+4\\5&2&3\end{matrix}\right|=(-2\alpha-5)\hat i+(2\alpha+20)\hat j+(2\alpha-5)\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The first equation in the PDF is misprinted (right side $21\sqrt{21}$ instead of the area 21); the correct equation is $\frac12\cdot2\sqrt{21}\cdot\frac{|\vec{PA}\times\vec d|}{\sqrt{38}}=21$, i.e. $|\vec{PA}\times\vec d|=\sqrt{21}\sqrt{38}$, which is what the next line of the PDF uses. All later steps and the answer 9 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Drop the perpendicular from $A$ to the line and use Pythagoras: $h^2=|\vec{PA}|^2-\left(\frac{\vec{PA}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}\right)^2$.
solution: The projection of $\vec{PA}$ on the line: $\vec{PA}\cdot\vec d=5\alpha+2+3\alpha+12=8\alpha+14$, so its square over $|\vec d|^2$ is $\frac{(8\alpha+14)^2}{38}=\frac{32\alpha^2+112\alpha+98}{19}$.

useful_results: Distance of a point $A$ from the line through $P$ with direction $\vec d$: $h=\frac{|\vec{PA}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$, equivalently $h^2=|\vec{PA}|^2-\frac{(\vec{PA}\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}$.
If two vertices of a triangle lie on a line, area $=\frac12\cdot$(base on the line)$\cdot$(distance of third vertex from the line).
Integrality or range conditions pick one root out of a quadratic: $3\alpha^2+20\alpha-87=0$ has roots $3$ and $-\frac{29}{3}$.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$, which links the two methods above.

concepts: Plane perpendicular to a line (line given as an intersection of planes)
questions.question: If the equation of the plane passing through the point $(1,1,2)$ and perpendicular to the line $x-3y+2z-1=0=4x-y+z$ is $Ax+By+Cz=1$, then $140(C-B+A)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The line's direction is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$, and this is the normal of the required plane.
solution: The line is the intersection of planes with normals $\vec n_1=(1,-3,2)$ and $\vec n_2=(4,-1,1)$.
Its direction is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-3&2\\4&-1&1\end{matrix}\right|=-\hat i+7\hat j+11\hat k$.
A plane perpendicular to the line has this as normal: direction ratios $(-1,7,11)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid the cross product: the required normal $(A,B,C)$ must be perpendicular to both given normals and satisfy the plane at the point.
solution: The plane's normal $(A,B,C)$ is parallel to the line, so it is perpendicular to $\vec n_1$ and $\vec n_2$.
The plane passes through $(1,1,2)$ and equals $Ax+By+Cz=1$: $A+B+2C=1$.
From the first two: eliminating $A$: $(4A-B+C)-4(A-3B+2C)=11B-7C=0$, so $B=\frac{7C}{11}$; then $A=3B-2C=\frac{21C-22C}{11}=-\frac{C}{11}$.

useful_results: Direction of the line $\vec n_1\cdot\vec r=k_1,\ \vec n_2\cdot\vec r=k_2$ is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$; no need to find a point on it.
Plane through $\vec a$ with normal $\vec n$ is $\vec n\cdot(\vec r-\vec a)=0$; to write it as $Ax+By+Cz=1$, divide by the constant ($28$ here).
If the constant on the right is $0$ (plane through the origin) the form $Ax+By+Cz=1$ is impossible.

concepts: Distance of a point from a line in 3D
Line of intersection of two planes
questions.question: Let a line $L$ pass through the point $P(2,3,1)$ and be parallel to the line $x+3y-2z-2=0=x-y+2z$. If the distance of the point $(5,3,8)$ from $L$ is $\alpha$, then $3\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Direction of $L$ is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$; then use the foot of the perpendicular or $\frac{|\vec{PQ}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
solution: Let $Q(5,3,8)$ and let $R$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ on $L$: $R=(k+2,\,-k+3,\,-k+1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the point-to-line distance formula $\alpha=\frac{|\vec{PQ}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ with no foot of the perpendicular.
solution: $\vec{PQ}\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&0&7\\1&-1&-1\end{matrix}\right|=(0+7)\hat i-(-3-7)\hat j+(-3-0)\hat k=7\hat i+10\hat j-3\hat k$.

useful_results: Distance of $Q$ from the line through $P$ with direction $\vec d$: $\alpha^2=\frac{|\vec{PQ}\times\vec d|^2}{|\vec d|^2}=|\vec{PQ}|^2-\frac{(\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}$.
Check on this question: $|\vec{PQ}|^2=58$, $(\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d)^2/3=(3-7)^2/3=\frac{16}{3}$, so $\alpha^2=58-\frac{16}{3}=\frac{158}{3}$.
Direction of the line of intersection of two planes is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$ (any parallel multiple will do).
A line parallel to a given line through $P$ has the same direction ratios, so the point $P$ on it is all that is needed besides the direction.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane, foot of the perpendicular on a line
Area of a triangle
questions.question: Let the line $L:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}$ intersect the plane $2x+y+3z=16$ at the point $P$. Let the point $Q$ be the foot of perpendicular from the point $R(1,-1,-3)$ on the line $L$. If $\alpha$ is the area of triangle $PQR$, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Find $P$ by substituting a general point of $L$ in the plane, and $Q$ by $\vec{QR}\perp L$, then area $=\frac12|\vec{QR}\times\vec{QP}|$.
solution: Put in the plane: $2(2\lambda+1)+(-\lambda-1)+3(\lambda+3)=16$, i.e. $6\lambda+10=16$, so $\lambda=1$ and $P=(3,-2,4)$.
For $Q$, direction ratios of $\vec{RQ}$ are $(2\lambda,\ -\lambda,\ \lambda+6)$; direction of $L$ is $(2,-1,1)$.
questions.correction_note: Typographical slip in the PDF: it prints $\vec{QR}\times\vec{QP}=-12\hat i66-24\hat j$; the correct value is $-12\hat i-24\hat j+0\hat k$. The magnitude $\sqrt{144+576}$ used next and the answer 180 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $PQR$ has a right angle at $Q$, so area $=\frac12\,PQ\cdot QR$.
solution: $P=(3,-2,4)$ and $Q=(-1,0,2)$ as found from the line-plane intersection and the foot of the perpendicular.
$QR\perp L$ and $P$ lies on $L$, so $QR\perp QP$: check $(2,-1,-5)\cdot(4,-2,2)=8+2-10=0$.

useful_results: If $Q$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to a line and $P$ is another point on that line, then $\triangle PQR$ is right-angled at $Q$ and area $=\frac12\,PQ\cdot RQ$.

Foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line through $A$ with direction $\vec d$: $Q=A+\frac{(\vec{AR}\cdot\vec d)}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$; here $\frac{(0,0,-6)\cdot(2,-1,1)}{6}=-1$, matching $\lambda=-1$.
Area of triangle $=\frac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$ in any dimension; $\alpha^2=\frac14|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|^2$ avoids square roots.
Line meets plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ at the parameter where $\vec n\cdot(\vec a+\lambda\vec d)=k$, valid if $\vec n\cdot\vec d\neq0$ (here $4-1+3=6$).

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral using the vector product of its diagonals
questions.question: $A(2,6,2)$, $B(-4,0,\lambda)$, $C(2,3,-1)$ and $D(4,5,0)$, $|\lambda|\le5$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral $ABCD$. If its area is $18$ square units, then $5-6\lambda$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The area of a quadrilateral is $\frac12|\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}|$, which gives a quadratic in $\lambda$ whose roots are filtered by $|\lambda|\le5$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's cross product $\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}$ has sign slips in the $\hat j$ and $\hat k$ components (it prints $(3\lambda+15)\hat i+24\hat j-24\hat k$; the correct value is $(3\lambda+15)\hat i-24\hat j+24\hat k$). The magnitude, the quadratic $\lambda^2+10\lambda+9=0$ and the answer 11 are unaffected. Also note the PDF applies $\frac12|\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}|$ without remarking it needs planarity; this holds at $\lambda=-1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the quadrilateral along $AC$ into triangles $ABC$ and $ACD$ and add their areas.
solution: So $3\lambda+12=\pm9$, giving $\lambda=-1$ or $-7$; the condition $|\lambda|\le5$ leaves $\lambda=-1$.
Check: for $\lambda=-1$ the four points are coplanar (so splitting along $AC$ is valid), and $5-6\lambda=11$.

useful_results: Area of a planar quadrilateral with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$; for a skew quadrilateral this is only the magnitude of its vector area, not the sum of the two triangle areas.

In this question the four points are coplanar only for $\lambda=-1$ (determinant of $\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}$ vanishes), so the planar-area formulas apply exactly there; $\lambda=-9$ is excluded anyway by $|\lambda|\le5$.
A quadratic obtained by squaring a magnitude can give extraneous roots; check them against the given range.
Area of a parallelogram on $\vec u,\vec v$ is $|\vec u\times\vec v|$ and of a triangle is half of it.

concepts: Line-plane intersection and perpendicular from a point to a line in 3D
questions.question: The point $C$ of intersection of the plane $8x+y+2z=0$ and the line joining the points $A(-3,-6,1)$ and $B(2,4,-3)$ divides the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $k:1$. If $a,b,c$ ($|a|,|b|,|c|$ are coprime) are the direction ratios of the perpendicular from the point $C$ on the line $\frac{1-x}{1}=\frac{y+4}{2}=\frac{z+2}{3}$, then $|a+b+c|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The line lies in the given plane, so the perpendicular from $C$ lies in it too and is $\perp$ to both $\vec n$ and the line.
solution: The line is $\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y+4}{2}=\frac{z+2}{3}$ (direction $(-1,2,3)$). A point on it is $D(1-\lambda,\,-4+2\lambda,\,-2+3\lambda)$.
Substituting, direction ratios of $CD$ are $\frac{2-\frac{33}{14}}{3},\frac{-14+\frac{66}{14}}{3},\frac{-1+\frac{99}{14}}{3}$, i.e. $\frac{-5}{14},\frac{-130}{14},\frac{85}{14}$ (each divided by 3).
Proportional to $-5,-130,85$, i.e. to $-1,-26,17$, which are coprime: $a=-1,\,b=-26,\,c=17$.
questions.correction_note: Typo in the PDF working: it writes the given line as (x-1)/(-1)=(y+4)/2=(z+2)/2; the z-denominator should be 3 (direction (-1,2,3)), as in the question and as used in the rest of the PDF working. All values (k=2, C=(1/3,2/3,-5/3), lambda=11/14, drs -1,-26,17, answer 10) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: The line lies in the plane (its point and direction both satisfy it), so the perpendicular $CD$ is $\perp$ to the normal $\vec n$ and to the line direction: $CD\parallel\vec n\times\vec d$.
solution: As in the main solution, $k=2$ and $C=\left(\frac13,\frac23,-\frac53\right)$ lies on the plane $8x+y+2z=0$.
The line passes through $(1,-4,-2)$ with direction $\vec d=(-1,2,3)$. Check: $8-4-4=0$ and $-8+2+6=0$, so the whole line lies in the plane.
Hence $C$ and the foot $D$ both lie in the plane, so $\vec{CD}\perp\vec n=(8,1,2)$. Also $\vec{CD}\perp\vec d$.
Therefore $\vec{CD}\parallel\vec n\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\8&1&2\\-1&2&3\end{matrix}\right|=(3-4)\hat i-(24+2)\hat j+(16+1)\hat k=(-1,-26,17)$.

useful_results: If a line lies in a plane, the perpendicular from a point of the plane to that line is $\parallel\vec n\times\vec d$ ($\vec n$ = plane normal, $\vec d$ = line direction).
Point dividing $A,B$ in ratio $k:1$ internally is $\frac{k\vec B+\vec A}{k+1}$; a line lies in a plane iff one of its points is on the plane and $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$.
Foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $P_0+\lambda\vec d$ has $\lambda=\frac{(C-P_0)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$; here $\frac{11}{14}$.
Direction ratios are defined up to a common factor and sign; reduce to coprime integers before summing.

concepts: Equation of a plane perpendicular to a line
questions.question: Let $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=1$ be the equation of a plane passing through the point $(3,-2,5)$ and perpendicular to the line joining the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(-2,3,5)$. Then the value of $\alpha\beta\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: A plane perpendicular to a line has the line's direction as its normal, so $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\parallel$ the direction ratios.
solution: Direction ratios of the line joining $(1,2,3)$ and $(-2,3,5)$: $(-2-1,\,3-2,\,5-3)=(-3,1,2)$.
The plane is perpendicular to this line, so its normal is along the line: normal vector $=3\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k$ (this is $-1$ times the direction).
The plane is $3x-y-2z=1$, which has the required form $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=1$ with $\alpha=3,\ \beta=-1,\ \gamma=-2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's opening remark (the given equation 'is not an equation of a plane as gamma z is present; if we consider y is gamma ...') is wrong: alpha, beta, gamma are constants, so alpha x + beta y + gamma z = 1 is a perfectly valid linear equation of a plane in x, y, z. No relabelling is needed. The PDF working (normal 3i-j-2k, plane 3x-y-2z=1) and the answer 6 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=t(-3,1,2)$ directly and fix the single unknown $t$ from the point condition.
solution: The normal $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is parallel to the line's direction $(-3,1,2)$, so $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=t(-3,1,2)$ for some real $t$.

useful_results: A plane $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=1$ not through the origin has normal $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$; its normal coincides (as a direction) with any line perpendicular to it.
If $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=t\,(l,m,n)$ and the plane passes through $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ then $t=\frac{1}{lx_0+my_0+nz_0}$ (valid when the denominator is nonzero).
The form $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=1$ is linear in $x,y,z$ ($\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are constants), so no relabelling is needed.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points
questions.question: Let the position vectors of the points $A,B,C$ and $D$ be $5\hat i+5\hat j+2\lambda\hat k,\ \hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\ -2\hat i+\lambda\hat j+4\hat k$ and $-\hat i+5\hat j+6\hat k$. Let $S$ be the set of real values of $\lambda$ for which the points $A,B,C$ and $D$ are coplanar. Then $\sum_{\lambda\in S}(\lambda+2)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Four points are coplanar iff $\vec{BA}\cdot(\vec{BC}\times\vec{BD})=0$, which gives a quadratic in $\lambda$.
solution: $\vec a=5\hat i+5\hat j+2\lambda\hat k,\ \vec b=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\ \vec c=-2\hat i+\lambda\hat j+4\hat k,\ \vec d=-\hat i+5\hat j+6\hat k$.
$\vec{BA}=\vec a-\vec b=(4,3,2\lambda-3)$, $\vec{BC}=\vec c-\vec b=(-3,\lambda-2,1)$, $\vec{BD}=\vec d-\vec b=(-2,3,3)$.
Expanding along the first row: $4(3\lambda-6-3)-3(-9+2)+(2\lambda-3)(-9+2\lambda-4)=0$, i.e. $12\lambda-36+21+(2\lambda-3)(2\lambda-13)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec{BA}=p\,\vec{BC}+q\,\vec{BD}$ and eliminate $p,q$ using the three components; subtracting two equations factors out $(\lambda-3)$ at once.
solution: Case $\lambda=3$: (1) and (3) give $p=-\frac{18}{7},\,q=\frac{13}{7}$, and (2) holds ($-\frac{18}{7}+\frac{39}{7}=3$). So $\lambda=3$ works.
Case $p=-2$: (1) gives $q=1$, and (3) gives $2\lambda-3=-2+3=1$, so $\lambda=2$ (check (2): $-2(0)+3=3$ true).

useful_results: Four points $A,B,C,D$ are coplanar iff $[\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}]=0$; equivalently the $4\times4$ determinant of rows $(x,y,z,1)$ is zero.
Coplanarity of $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ also means $\vec w=p\vec u+q\vec v$ when $\vec u\nparallel\vec v$; subtracting component equations often factors the condition.

Sum of a symmetric function of the roots (e.g. $\sum(\lambda+2)^2$) needs only the roots or Vieta: here $(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^2-2\lambda_1\lambda_2+4(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)+8=25-12+20+8=41$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=5,\ \lambda_1\lambda_2=6$.

concepts: Cross product and Lagrange identity
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k,\ \vec b=\hat i-2\hat j-2\hat k$ and $\vec c=-\hat i+4\hat j+3\hat k$. If $\vec d$ is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, and $\vec a\cdot\vec d=18$, then $|\vec a\times\vec d|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec d\parallel\vec b\times\vec c$ fixes $\vec d$ up to a scalar, and $|\vec a\times\vec d|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)^2$.
solution: $\vec b\times\vec c=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-2&-2\\-1&4&3\end{matrix}\right|=(-6+8)\hat i-(3-2)\hat j+(4-2)\hat k=2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$.
$\vec d\perp\vec b$ and $\vec d\perp\vec c$, so $\vec d=\lambda(2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)$.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec d|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)^2=29\times36-18^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$ to get $\vec a\times\vec d$ directly as a vector.
solution: $\vec d=\lambda(\vec b\times\vec c)$ with $\lambda=2$ as before, so $\vec a\times\vec d=2\,\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)$.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec d|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)^2$ (valid for all vectors); avoids computing the cross product.
Vector triple product (BAC-CAB): $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$.
A vector perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors $\vec b,\vec c$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec b\times\vec c$; one extra condition (like $\vec a\cdot\vec d$) fixes the scalar.
Check: $\vec b\times\vec c$ here is perpendicular to $\vec b$: $2+2-4=0$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: One vertex of a rectangular parallelopiped is at the origin $O$ and the lengths of its edges along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes are $3$, $4$ and $5$ units respectively. Let $P$ be the vertex $(3,4,5)$. Then the shortest distance between the diagonal $OP$ and an edge parallel to the $z$ axis, not passing through $O$ or $P$, is:
questions.key_idea: Both lines are explicit: use the skew-line distance formula $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$.
solution: The diagonal $OP$ is $\frac x3=\frac y4=\frac z5$: point $\vec a_1=(0,0,0)$, direction $\vec b_1=(3,4,5)$.
An edge parallel to the $z$-axis not through $O$ or $P$ passes through $(3,0,0)$ and $(3,0,5)$. Take $\vec a_2=(3,0,5)$, direction $\vec b_2=(0,0,1)$: $\frac{x-3}{0}=\frac{y-0}{0}=\frac{z-5}{1}$.
Shortest distance $=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$.
$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&4&5\\0&0&1\end{matrix}\right|=4\hat i-3\hat j$, with magnitude $\sqrt{16+9}=5$.
$(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)=(3,0,5)\cdot(4,-3,0)=12$ (the PDF writes this as the determinant with rows $(3,0,5),(3,4,5),(0,0,1)$, equal to $3\times4=12$).
questions.correction_note: Typo in the PDF: the formula is printed as S.D. = ((a2 . a1) . (b1 x b2)) / |b1 x b2|; it should be (a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2) (the displayed numbers, rows (3,0,5),(3,4,5),(0,0,1) giving 12, are the correct a2-a1 scalar triple product). The value 12/5 and the answer (D) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: The edge is parallel to the $z$-axis, so project everything onto the $xy$-plane: the distance becomes a point-to-line distance in 2D.
solution: The common perpendicular to a line and a vertical line is horizontal, so the distance is unchanged when both are projected onto the $xy$-plane.
The vertical edge through $(3,0,*)$ projects to the point $(3,0)$.
The diagonal $OP$ projects to the line through $O$ with direction $(3,4)$: $4x-3y=0$.
The other eligible edge through $(0,4,*)$ gives $\frac{|0-12|}{5}=\frac{12}{5}$, the same.

useful_results: Skew lines $\vec a_1+s\vec b_1$, $\vec a_2+t\vec b_2$: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$; it is $0$ iff the lines are coplanar.
If one line is parallel to a coordinate axis, project along that axis: distance between a diagonal and a vertical edge reduces to a point-to-line distance in the plane.
For a cuboid with edges $a,b,c$, distance between diagonal $OP$ and the $z$-edge through $(a,0,0)$ is $\frac{ab}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ ($=\frac{12}{5}$ for $a=3,b=4$).
The two eligible edges (through $(a,0)$ and $(0,b)$) give the same distance.

concepts: Plane through the line of intersection of two planes
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: A plane $P$ contains the line of intersection of the planes $\vec r\cdot(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)=6$ and $\vec r\cdot(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)=-5$. If $P$ passes through the point $(0,2,-2)$, then the square of the distance of the point $(12,12,18)$ from the plane $P$ is:
questions.key_idea: A plane through the intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; the given point fixes $\lambda$.
solution: Any plane through their line of intersection is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$: $(1+2\lambda)x+(1+3\lambda)y+(1+4\lambda)z+(5\lambda-6)=0$.
questions.correction_note: Typo in the PDF: the substitution line reads 2(1+3L)+6(1+4L)(-2)+5L-6=0 with a stray factor 6; it should be 2(1+3L)-2(1+4L)+5L-6=0. The next line (2+6L-2-8L+5L-6=0) and all later values (L=2, plane 5x+7y+9z+4=0, d^2=620) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find a point and the direction of the line of intersection, then the plane through that line and the given point via a cross product.
solution: Normals: $\vec n_1=(1,1,1)$, $\vec n_2=(2,3,4)$; the line's direction is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=(4-3,\,2-4,\,3-2)=(1,-2,1)$.
A point on the line: set $z=0$: $x+y=6$, $2x+3y=-5$, so $y=-17,\ x=23$: the point $(23,-17,0)$.

useful_results: The family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ gives all planes through the line $P_1=P_2=0$ except $P_2=0$ itself.
The direction of the line of intersection of two planes is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; squaring removes the root: $d^2=\frac{310^2}{155}=620$.
Convert vector-form planes $\vec r\cdot\vec n=p$ to $\vec n\cdot(x,y,z)-p=0$ carefully with the sign of the constant.

concepts: Scalar triple product and volume of a parallelepiped
questions.question: Let the vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ represent three coterminous edges of a parallelepiped of volume $V$. Then the volume of the parallelepiped whose coterminous edges are represented by $\vec a,\ \vec b+\vec c$ and $\vec a+2\vec b+3\vec c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Volume is $|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$, and a triple product of combinations equals the determinant of the coefficient matrix times $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
solution: New volume $V_1=|[\vec a\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec a+2\vec b+3\vec c]|$.
Write the new edges in terms of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$; the coefficient rows are $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,2,3)$.
So $[\vec a\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec a+2\vec b+3\vec c]=\left|\begin{matrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\1&2&3\end{matrix}\right|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Special case: the ratio does not depend on the edges, so take the unit cube $\vec a=\hat i,\ \vec b=\hat j,\ \vec c=\hat k$ with $V=1$.
solution: For $\vec a=\hat i,\vec b=\hat j,\vec c=\hat k$ the original volume is $V=1$.
New edges: $\hat i$, $\hat j+\hat k$, $\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$.
Since the volume scales by the fixed factor $|\det|$ for any $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, the new volume is $1\cdot V=V$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce by repeatedly subtracting multiples of earlier edges, which leaves the triple product unchanged.
solution: $[\vec a,\ \vec b+\vec c,\ \vec a+2\vec b+3\vec c]=[\vec a,\ \vec b+\vec c,\ 2\vec b+3\vec c]$, removing $1\cdot\vec a$ from the third edge.
Subtract $2(\vec b+\vec c)$ from the third edge: $=[\vec a,\ \vec b+\vec c,\ \vec c]$.
Subtract the third from the second: $=[\vec a,\ \vec b,\ \vec c]$.

useful_results: $[\,p_1\vec a+q_1\vec b+r_1\vec c,\ \ldots\,]=\det\begin{pmatrix}p_1&q_1&r_1\\p_2&q_2&r_2\\p_3&q_3&r_3\end{pmatrix}[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ for any three linear combinations (valid for all vectors).
Adding a multiple of one vector to another inside a scalar triple product does not change its value.
A triple product with a repeated or linearly dependent vector is $0$ (coplanarity).
Volume of a tetrahedron is $\frac16$ of the parallelepiped; the same determinant factor scales both.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points
questions.question: The sum of all values of $\alpha$, for which the points whose position vectors are $\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k,\ 2\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k,\ (\alpha+1)\hat i+2\hat k$ and $9\hat i+(\alpha-8)\hat j+6\hat k$ are coplanar, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Four points are coplanar iff $\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}$ are coplanar, giving a quadratic in $\alpha$ whose root-sum is asked.
solution: $\vec{AB}=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k,\quad \vec{AC}=\alpha\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k,\quad \vec{AD}=8\hat i+(\alpha-6)\hat j+3\hat k$.
The points are coplanar iff $\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}$ are coplanar: $\left|\begin{matrix}1&-1&1\\\alpha&2&-1\\8&\alpha-6&3\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
This simplifies to $\alpha^2-2\alpha-8=0$, i.e. $(\alpha-4)(\alpha+2)=0$, so $\alpha=4$ or $-2$.
Sum of all values of $\alpha=4+(-2)=2$ (also $=-\frac{b}{a}=2$ directly from the quadratic).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line (6+a-6)+(3a+8)+(a^2-6a-16)=0 is correct, but the next line printed is a^2-2a-14=0; the constant should be -8 (a+3a+8+a^2-6a-16 = a^2-2a-8). The PDF's final 'sum of values of alpha = 2' is still correct since the sum of the roots is 2 whichever constant is used (true roots are 4 and -2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec{AD}=p\,\vec{AB}+q\,\vec{AC}$; the $\hat k$ and $\hat i$ components give $q(\alpha+1)=5$ and the $\hat j$ one gives $q=\alpha-3$.
solution: $\vec{AB}=(1,-1,1)$, $\vec{AC}=(\alpha,2,-1)$ are not parallel, so coplanarity means $\vec{AD}=(8,\alpha-6,3)=p\vec{AB}+q\vec{AC}$.
The roots add up to $2$ (they are $4$ and $-2$).

useful_results: If $\vec u,\vec v$ are non-parallel, $\vec w$ is coplanar with them iff $\vec w=p\vec u+q\vec v$; comparing components can be faster than expanding a $3\times3$ determinant.
For $a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c=0$ the sum of the roots is $-\frac ba$ (counting complex roots); the question asks for real values, so check the discriminant (here $36>0$, both roots real).
Points $P_1,\ldots,P_4$ are coplanar iff $[\vec{P_1P_2},\vec{P_1P_3},\vec{P_1P_4}]=0$; choosing the base point with simplest coordinates shortens the work.

concepts: Collinearity of three points
questions.question: If the points with position vectors $\alpha\hat i+10\hat j+13\hat k,\ 6\hat i+11\hat j+11\hat k,\ \frac92\hat i+\beta\hat j-8\hat k$ are collinear, then $(19\alpha-6\beta)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Collinear points give parallel difference vectors, so corresponding components are in proportion.
solution: $\vec{AB}=(6-\alpha)\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$ and $\vec{BC}=-\frac32\hat i+(\beta-11)\hat j-19\hat k$.
From the first and last ratios: $6-\alpha=-\frac{3}{19}$, so $\alpha=6+\frac3{19}=\frac{117}{19}$ and $19\alpha=117$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Collinearity means $B$ divides $AC$: $\vec B=t\vec A+(1-t)\vec C$; the $z$-coordinates (no unknown) give $t$ first.
solution: For collinear $A,B,C$ there is a real $t$ with $\vec B=t\vec A+(1-t)\vec C$.

useful_results: Three points are collinear iff $\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}=\vec 0$, i.e. their components are proportional.
Using the coordinate with no unknown first (here $z$) fixes the ratio $t$ and avoids solving simultaneous equations.
In $\vec B=t\vec A+(1-t)\vec C$, $B$ divides $AC$ internally if $0<t<1$ (here $t=\frac{19}{21}$) and externally otherwise.
If one component of $\vec{AB}$ is $0$, the same component of $\vec{BC}$ must be $0$ for collinearity.

concepts: Coplanarity of vectors and determinants
questions.question: Let the vectors $\vec u_1=\hat i+\hat j+a\hat k,\ \vec u_2=\hat i+b\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec u_3=c\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$ be coplanar. If the vectors $\vec v_1=(a+b)\hat i+c\hat j+c\hat k,\ \vec v_2=a\hat i+(b+c)\hat j+a\hat k$ and $\vec v_3=b\hat i+b\hat j+(c+a)\hat k$ are also coplanar, then $6(a+b+c)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity of the $\vec v$'s forces $abc=0$ (determinant $=4abc$), which turns the first condition into $a+b+c=2$.
solution: Apply $R_3\to R_3-(R_1+R_2)$: the third row becomes $(b-2a-b,\ b-b-2c,\ c+a-c-a)=(-2a,-2c,0)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar $\vec v_i$ means $p\vec v_1+q\vec v_2+r\vec v_3=\vec 0$ has a non-trivial solution; a change of variable turns it into a very sparse system.
solution: The components of $p\vec v_1+q\vec v_2+r\vec v_3=\vec0$ are: $a(p+q)+b(p+r)=0$, $c(p+q)+b(q+r)=0$, $c(p+r)+a(q+r)=0$.
Put $X=p+q,\ Y=p+r,\ Z=q+r$. The map $(p,q,r)\to(X,Y,Z)$ has determinant $-2\ne0$, so non-trivial $(p,q,r)$ corresponds to non-trivial $(X,Y,Z)$.
The system is $aX+bY=0,\ cX+bZ=0,\ cY+aZ=0$, with coefficient determinant $\left|\begin{matrix}a&b&0\\c&0&b\\0&c&a\end{matrix}\right|$.
This determinant is $a(0-bc)-b(ca-0)=-2abc$, so non-trivial solutions exist iff $abc=0$.

useful_results: $\left|\begin{matrix}a+b&c&c\\a&b+c&a\\b&b&c+a\end{matrix}\right|=4abc$ (verified at $a=b=c=1$: $\left|\begin{matrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{matrix}\right|=4$).
$\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&a\\1&b&1\\c&1&1\end{matrix}\right|=a+b+c-2-abc$; at $a=b=c=2$ the determinant is $1(2-1)-1(1-2)+2(1-4)=-4$ and the formula gives $6-2-8=-4$.
Three vectors are coplanar iff their coefficient determinant vanishes; a row operation such as $R_3\to R_3-(R_1+R_2)$ can create zeros.
Both conditions together: $abc=0$ and $a+b+c=2+abc$, so $a+b+c=2$ whichever variable is zero.

concepts: Projection of a vector and cross product
questions.question: Let $O$ be the origin and the position vector of the point $P$ be $-\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k$. If the position vectors of the points $A,B$ and $C$ are $-2\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k,\ 2\hat i+4\hat j-2\hat k$ and $-4\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$ respectively, then the projection of the vector $\vec{OP}$ on a vector perpendicular to the vectors $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ is:
questions.key_idea: A vector perpendicular to $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ is $\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}$; project $\vec{OP}$ on it.
solution: $\vec{AB}=(2+2)\hat i+(4-1)\hat j+(-2+3)\hat k=4\hat i+3\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec{AC}=(-4+2)\hat i+(2-1)\hat j+(-1+3)\hat k=-2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$.
$\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\4&3&1\\-2&1&2\end{matrix}\right|=5\hat i-10\hat j+10\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: Notation slip in the PDF: it prints 'AB x AC = |OP . (AB x AC) / |AB x AC||'; the left side should be 'Projection of OP on AB x AC', as the sentence 'Projection of OP on' (cut at the page break) indicates. The numbers (AB x AC = 5i-10j+10k, value 3) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the perpendicular direction by solving the two dot-product equations instead of taking a cross product.
solution: Let $\vec n=(x,y,z)$ be $\perp$ to $\vec{AB}=(4,3,1)$ and $\vec{AC}=(-2,1,2)$: $4x+3y+z=0$ and $-2x+y+2z=0$.
From the first, $z=-4x-3y$. Substituting in the second: $-2x+y-8x-6y=0$, so $-10x-5y=0$ and $y=-2x$.

useful_results: A vector perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors is along their cross product; equivalently solve the two dot-product equations (ratio form $\frac{x}{b_1c_2-b_2c_1}=\cdots$).
Scalar projection of $\vec p$ on $\vec n$ is $\frac{\vec p\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|}$ (sign shows direction); the magnitude is unchanged if $\vec n$ is replaced by $-\vec n$.

The projection of $\vec p$ on the normal of a plane is the signed distance travelled along the normal, e.g. $\vec{OP}\cdot\hat n$ is the distance of $P$ from the plane through $O$ with normal $\hat n$.
$\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}$ has magnitude $2\times$ area of $\triangle ABC$: here $15=2\times7.5$.

concepts: Linear combination of vectors and quadratic equation from its roots
questions.question: An arc $PQ$ of a circle subtends a right angle at its centre $O$. The mid point of the arc $PQ$ is $R$. If $\vec{OP}=\vec u,\ \vec{OR}=\vec v$ and $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec u+\beta\vec v$, then $\alpha,\beta^2$ are the roots of the equation:
questions.key_idea: Place $O$ at the origin with $P$ and $Q$ on the axes, so $R$ is at $45^\circ$; then read $\alpha,\beta$ off the component equation.
solution: Take the circle as the unit circle with $O$ at the origin: $\vec{OP}=\vec u=\hat i$ and $\vec{OQ}=\vec q=\hat j$ (a right angle at $O$).
$R$ is the mid point of arc $PQ$, so $\vec{OR}=\vec v=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat j$.
$\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec u+\beta\vec v$ gives $\hat j=\alpha\hat i+\beta\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat j\right)$.
Comparing $\hat j$: $\frac{\beta}{\sqrt2}=1$, so $\beta=\sqrt2$. Comparing $\hat i$: $\alpha+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt2}=0$, so $\alpha=-1$.
The roots are $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta^2=2$: sum $=1$, product $=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Dot $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec u+\beta\vec v$ with $\vec u$ and $\vec v$, using only the angles $\angle POQ=90^\circ$ and $\angle QOR=45^\circ$ (no coordinates).
solution: Let $|\vec u|=|\vec v|=r$. Then $\vec u\cdot\vec v=r^2\cos45^\circ=\frac{r^2}{\sqrt2}$.

useful_results: Taking dot products of a vector equation with known vectors turns it into scalar equations, without needing coordinates.
The mid point of the arc subtended by a chord's endpoints $P,Q$ on a circle centred at $O$ satisfies $\vec{OR}=\frac{\vec u+\vec q}{|\vec u+\vec q|}\,r$ (angle bisector of $\angle POQ$).
Here $\vec q=-\vec u+\sqrt2\vec v$ for a right-angle arc: check $|-\vec u+\sqrt2\vec v|^2=1+2-2\sqrt2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt2}=1$ for unit vectors.
A quadratic with roots $p,q$ is $x^2-(p+q)x+pq=0$; note one root is $\beta^2$, not $\beta$.

concepts: Position vectors of centroid, circumcentre and orthocentre
questions.question: If the points $P$ and $Q$ are respectively the circumcenter and the orthocentre of a $\triangle ABC$, then $\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The centroid $G$ lies on the line $PQ$ with $PG:GQ=1:2$ (Euler line), so $\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}=3\vec{PG}=\vec{PQ}$.
solution: Take the circumcentre $P$ as the origin, with $A,B,C$ having position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$.
The centroid $G$ has position vector $\vec{PG}=\frac{\vec a+\vec b+\vec c}{3}$.
The circumcentre, centroid and orthocentre are collinear with $G$ dividing $PQ$ in the ratio $1:2$, so $\vec{PQ}=3\vec{PG}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: With the circumcentre as origin, verify directly that the point with position vector $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$ is the orthocentre.
solution: Take $P$ as origin; then $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=|\vec c|=R$ (circumradius).
Let $\vec h=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$. Then $\vec{AH}\cdot\vec{BC}=(\vec h-\vec a)\cdot(\vec c-\vec b)=(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot(\vec c-\vec b)=|\vec c|^2-|\vec b|^2=0$.
Similarly $\vec{BH}\cdot\vec{CA}=0$ and $\vec{CH}\cdot\vec{AB}=0$, so $H$ lies on all three altitudes: $H$ is the orthocentre $Q$.
Check: right triangle $A(1,0),B(-1,0),C(0,1)$ has circumcentre $(0,0)$, orthocentre $C=(0,1)$ and $\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}=(0,1)=\vec{PQ}$.

useful_results: With the circumcentre $P$ as origin the orthocentre is $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$ (Sylvester); for any origin, $\vec H=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C-2\vec P$.
Euler line: $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear with $OG:GH=1:2$, i.e. $\vec{OH}=3\vec{OG}$ (equilateral triangle: all three coincide).
$\vec{GA}+\vec{GB}+\vec{GC}=\vec 0$ for the centroid $G$, and $\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}=3\vec{PG}$ for any point $P$.
In an acute triangle all three points are inside; in a right triangle $H$ is the right-angle vertex and $O$ the hypotenuse mid point.

concepts: Cross product and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+7\hat j-\hat k,\ \vec b=3\hat i+5\hat k$ and $\vec c=\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$. Let $\vec d$ be a vector perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, and $\vec c\cdot\vec d=12$. Then $(-\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec d=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$ with $\lambda$ from $\vec c\cdot\vec d=12$; then the asked value is a scalar triple product.
solution: $\vec a=2\hat i+7\hat j-\hat k,\ \vec b=3\hat i+5\hat k,\ \vec c=\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$.
$\vec d\perp\vec a,\vec b$, so $\vec d=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)=\lambda\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&7&-1\\3&0&5\end{matrix}\right|=\lambda(35\hat i-13\hat j-21\hat k)$.
$\vec c\cdot\vec d=12$: $\lambda(35+13-42)=6\lambda=12$, so $\lambda=2$ and $\vec d=2(35\hat i-13\hat j-21\hat k)=(70,-26,-42)$.
The required value is the scalar triple product $(-\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=\left|\begin{matrix}-1&1&-1\\1&-1&2\\70&-26&-42\end{matrix}\right|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec a(\vec c\cdot\vec b)-\vec b(\vec c\cdot\vec a)$ to get $\vec c\times\vec d$ as a vector, then one dot product.
solution: $\vec d=2(\vec a\times\vec b)$ (as before), so $\vec c\times\vec d=2\,\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=2\left[\vec a(\vec c\cdot\vec b)-\vec b(\vec c\cdot\vec a)\right]$.

useful_results: $\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec a(\vec c\cdot\vec b)-\vec b(\vec c\cdot\vec a)$ (valid for all vectors); it avoids a second cross product.
A vector perpendicular to $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$; one scalar condition fixes $\lambda$.
$\vec m\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=[\vec m\ \vec c\ \vec d]$ is the $3\times3$ determinant of the three vectors in that order.
Here $\lambda=\frac{12}{\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)}=\frac{12}{6}=2$, since $\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=35+13-42=6$.

concepts: Magnitude of a vector and component inequalities
questions.question: For any vector $\vec{a}=a_1\hat{i}+a_2\hat{j}+a_3\hat{k}$, with $10|a_i|<1$, $i=1,2,3$, consider the following statements: (A): $\max\{|a_1|,|a_2|,|a_3|\}\le|\vec{a}|$ and (B): $|\vec{a}|\le3\max\{|a_1|,|a_2|,|a_3|\}$.
questions.key_idea: Compare $|\vec{a}|^2=a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2$ with $M^2$ and $3M^2$, where $M$ is the largest $|a_i|$.
solution: (A): $M^2$ is one of the three non-negative terms $a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2$, so $|\vec{a}|^2\ge M^2$, i.e. $M\le|\vec{a}|$. Statement (A) is true.
Hence $|\vec{a}|\le\sqrt3\,M$, and since $\sqrt3<3$ and $M\ge0$, $|\vec{a}|\le\sqrt3\,M\le3M$. Statement (B) is true.
The condition $10|a_i|<1$ is not needed; it only says the components are small (so $|\vec{a}|<\frac{\sqrt3}{10}$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF proves (B) by $|\vec{a}|<\sqrt{3/100}=\frac{\sqrt3}{10}<\frac{3}{10}$ and then writes $|\vec{a}|<3\max$. That only bounds $|\vec{a}|$ by a constant, not by $3\max|a_i|$ (the maximum can be tiny), so the step is invalid. Correct proof: $|\vec{a}|^2\le3M^2$. Final answer (A) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometric view: the tip of $\vec{a}$ lies on a face of the cube $|x|,|y|,|z|\le M$, so its distance from the centre lies between $M$ and the corner distance $\sqrt3M$.
solution: Let $M=\max|a_i|$. The tip $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ lies inside the cube $[-M,M]^3$ and on at least one of its faces, say $x=\pm M$.
Every point of the plane $x=\pm M$ is at distance at least $M$ from the origin, so $|\vec{a}|\ge M$. This is (A).
Every point of the cube is at most as far as a corner, whose distance is $\sqrt{M^2+M^2+M^2}=\sqrt3M$, so $|\vec{a}|\le\sqrt3M\le3M$. This is (B).

useful_results: For $\vec{a}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and $M=\max|a_i|$: $M\le|\vec{a}|\le\sqrt3\,M$ (in $n$ dimensions the upper bound is $\sqrt n\,M$).
Left equality holds iff at most one component is non-zero; right equality iff all $|a_i|$ are equal. Example $(0.05,0.05,0.05)$: $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt3\,(0.05)$.
For any unit vector $\hat{u}$, $|\vec{a}\cdot\hat{u}|\le|\vec{a}|$ (Cauchy-Schwarz); each component is such a projection.
Triangle inequality: $\left||\vec{a}|-|\vec{b}|\right|\le|\vec{a}\pm\vec{b}|\le|\vec{a}|+|\vec{b}|$.

concepts: Line of intersection of planes
Dot and cross product of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}$ be a non-zero vector parallel to the line of intersection of the two planes described by $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\ \hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\ \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ (each plane is spanned by the two given vectors). If $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=6$, then the ordered pair $(\theta,|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The line of intersection is along $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; then use $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$ and the Lagrange identity.
solution: Normal of the second plane: $\vec{n}_2=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})\times(\hat{j}-\hat{k})=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ (the PDF uses $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{i}-\hat{k}$, the same plane, same normal).
questions.correction_note: Minor typos in the PDF: it writes $\vec{a}=\lambda|\vec{n}_2\times\vec{n}_2|$ (should be $\lambda(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)$, no modulus, since $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2=-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ as it computes) and uses $\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ for the second plane (same plane as $\hat{j}-\hat{k}$). Answer (A) is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: A vector common to both planes is visible by inspection: $(\hat{i}+\hat{j})-(\hat{i}+\hat{k})=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ also equals the second spanning vector, so the line is along $\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.
solution: Plane 1 contains $\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{k}$, hence their difference $\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.
Plane 2 is spanned by $\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ and $\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, so it also contains $\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.
A non-zero vector lying in both planes is along their line of intersection, so $\vec{a}=t(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$.

useful_results: The line of intersection of planes with normals $\vec{n}_1,\vec{n}_2$ has direction $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$ (when the planes are not parallel); a plane spanned by $\vec{u},\vec{v}$ has normal $\vec{u}\times\vec{v}$.
If two planes are given by spanning vectors, look for a common vector (a combination of the first pair equal to a combination of the second); it gives the line at once.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|^2+|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$, so $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$ follows from $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$ and the lengths with no determinant.
Here $\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}=\frac66=1$, consistent with $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points and scalar triple product
questions.question: If four distinct points with position vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ and $\vec{d}$ are coplanar, then $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Four points are coplanar iff $[\vec{b}-\vec{a},\ \vec{c}-\vec{a},\ \vec{d}-\vec{a}]=0$; expand it and use cyclic symmetry.
solution: Coplanar points $A,B,C,D$ make the vectors $\vec{b}-\vec{a},\ \vec{c}-\vec{a},\ \vec{d}-\vec{a}$ coplanar.
Expanding (terms with a repeated vector vanish): $[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]-[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{a}]-[\vec{b}\ \vec{a}\ \vec{d}]-[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]=0$.

Cyclic shifts leave a triple product unchanged: $[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]=[\vec{c}\ \vec{d}\ \vec{b}]$, $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}]=[\vec{b}\ \vec{d}\ \vec{a}]$, $[\vec{a}\ \vec{d}\ \vec{c}]=[\vec{d}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{a}]$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar points satisfy $\vec{d}=\alpha\vec{a}+\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c}$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$; substitute in option (C) and watch the triple products collapse.
solution: Other options: (A) gives $(\alpha+\beta-\gamma)=1-2\gamma$ times $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]$; (B) and (D) each give $(\alpha-\beta-\gamma)=2\alpha-1$ times it. These equal $1$ only for special $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, so only (C) is always true.

useful_results: Points $A,B,C,D$ are coplanar iff $[\vec{b}-\vec{a},\vec{c}-\vec{a},\vec{d}-\vec{a}]=0$, i.e. iff $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]-[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}]+[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]-[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]=0$ (alternating sum over the four triples).
Equivalently $\vec{d}=\alpha\vec{a}+\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c}$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$ (an affine combination) when $A,B,C$ are not collinear.
Volume of tetrahedron $ABCD$ is $\frac16\left|[\vec{b}-\vec{a},\vec{c}-\vec{a},\vec{d}-\vec{a}]\right|$; coplanar means volume $0$.
Triple product: cyclic shifts keep the sign, swapping two entries flips it, a repeated vector gives $0$.

concepts: Parallel vectors, dot and cross product
questions.question: Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\vec{a}=\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=-17$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=-20$. Then $|\vec{c}\times(\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Since $\vec{c}\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$, the condition says $\vec{c}\parallel\vec{a}+\vec{b}$, which turns the vector unknown into one scalar.
solution: Its square of magnitude is $1+9+36=46$, option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $\alpha$ using $\vec{a}=\vec{s}-\vec{b}$ with $\vec{s}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}$, and finish with the Lagrange identity instead of a determinant.

useful_results: $\vec{u}\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ with $\vec{u}\ne\vec{0}$ means $\vec{c}=\alpha\vec{u}$; this replaces a vector unknown by one scalar.
If $\vec{c}=\alpha\vec{s}$, the ratio $\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}}{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}}=\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{s}}{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{s}}$ does not depend on $\alpha$ (needs $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{s}\ne0$).
Lagrange identity: $|\vec{c}\times\vec{v}|^2=|\vec{c}|^2|\vec{v}|^2-(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{v})^2$; here $37\cdot11-19^2=46$.
A condition such as $\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}$ is a selector between the roots of a quadratic; test the chosen root in the original equations.

concepts: Coplanarity of three vectors and determinants
questions.question: Let $a,b,c$ be three distinct real numbers, none equal to one. If the vectors $a\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+c\hat{k}$ are coplanar, then $\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Coplanar means the determinant is zero; row operations create the factors $(a-1)$, $(b-1)$, $(c-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write each vector as $(1,1,1)$ plus a multiple of one basis vector and expand the triple product by multilinearity.
solution: Expand $[\vec{p}+x\hat{i},\ \vec{p}+y\hat{j},\ \vec{p}+z\hat{k}]$ by linearity; any term with $\vec{p}$ twice vanishes.
Each of the last three brackets equals $1$ (the matching component of $\vec{p}$), and $[\hat{i}\,\hat{j}\,\hat{k}]=1$, so the triple product is $xyz+xy+yz+zx$.

useful_results: $\left|\begin{matrix}a&1&1\\1&b&1\\1&1&c\end{matrix}\right|=abc-a-b-c+2=(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)\left[1+\sum\frac1{a-1}\right]$ (for $a,b,c\ne1$).
So the vectors are coplanar iff $\sum\frac{1}{1-a}=1$; then also $\sum\frac{a}{1-a}=\sum\left(\frac{1}{1-a}-1\right)=-2$.
Three vectors are coplanar iff their scalar triple product (the determinant of components) is $0$.
Check: $a=2,\ b=3$ gives $abc-a-b-c+2=5c-3=0$, so $c=\frac35$, and $\frac1{-1}+\frac1{-2}+\frac1{2/5}=-1-\frac12+\frac52=1$.

concepts: Cross product and parallel vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$. If a vector $\vec{d}$ satisfies $\vec{d}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}\times\vec{b}$ and $\vec{d}\cdot\vec{a}=24$, then $|\vec{d}|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $(\vec{d}-\vec{c})\times\vec{b}=\vec{0}$ means $\vec{d}=\vec{c}+\lambda\vec{b}$; the dot product with $\vec{a}$ fixes $\lambda$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $\vec{d}=(x,y,z)$ as three unknowns: the cross-product equation gives two independent linear equations and the dot product gives the third.
solution: Equating components: $7y+2z=1$, $3z-7x=-2$, $-2x-3y=-1$ (the third follows from the first two, since $\vec{d}\times\vec{b}\perp\vec{b}$).
Add $x-3y=23$ to $2x+3y=1$ (the third equation, rewritten): $3x=24$, so $x=8$; then $y=\frac{1-16}{3}=-5$ and $z=\frac{1-7y}{2}=18$.

useful_results: $\vec{u}\times\vec{b}=\vec{w}\times\vec{b}$ iff $\vec{u}=\vec{w}+\lambda\vec{b}$: $\vec{u}$ is determined only up to a multiple of $\vec{b}$, so one more scalar condition is needed.
If $\vec{u}\times\vec{b}=\vec{w}$ is given with $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{b}=k$, then $\vec{u}=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{w}+k\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}$ (solving for $\vec{u}$ uniquely).
Use $\lambda=\frac{k-\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}$ whenever $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}\ne0$.
Geometrically $\vec{d}$ moves on the line through the tip of $\vec{c}$ parallel to $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{d}\cdot\vec{a}=24$ cuts it at one plane.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines and distance of a point from a plane along a line
questions.question: The distance of the point $(-1,2,3)$ from the plane $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=10$ parallel to the line of the shortest distance between the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=(2\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\mu(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is:
questions.key_idea: The shortest-distance direction is the cross product of the two line directions; move from the point along it until the plane is hit.
solution: The line of shortest distance is perpendicular to both lines: direction $=(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})\times(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\2&0&1\\1&-1&1\end{matrix}\right|=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ (up to a factor $t$).
The line through $A(-1,2,3)$ with this direction: $\vec{r}=(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$.
A general point is $(\lambda-1,\ 2-\lambda,\ 3-2\lambda)$. Put it in the plane $x-2y+3z=10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the slant-distance formula: distance along direction $\vec{u}$ from $P$ to the plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=p$ is $\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot P-p|\,|\vec{u}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{u}|}$.
solution: $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{u}=1+2-6=-3\ne0$, so the line meets the plane.
Moving $P$ by $t\vec{u}$ changes $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}$ by $t(\vec{n}\cdot\vec{u})$; to cancel $-6$ we need $|t|=\frac{6}{3}=2$.

useful_results: Direction of the common perpendicular (shortest distance) of $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_1+\lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_2+\mu\vec{b}_2$ is $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$ (lines not parallel).
Distance from $P$ to the plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=p$ measured along direction $\vec{u}$ is $\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot P-p|\,|\vec{u}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{u}|}$ (needs $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{u}\ne0$).

It equals the perpendicular distance $\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot P-p|}{|\vec{n}|}$ divided by $\cos\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the angle between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{n}$. Here perpendicular distance is $\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}$.
Only the directions of the given lines matter for this question, not their positions.

concepts: Area of a triangle and dot product of vectors
questions.question: Let for a triangle $ABC$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{CB}=\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{CA}=4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\delta\hat{k}$. If $\delta>0$ and the area of the triangle $ABC$ is $5\sqrt6$, then $\overrightarrow{CB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec{0}$ fixes $\alpha,\beta$ and links $\gamma,\delta$; the area condition then fixes $\delta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid the $3\times3$ cross product: Lagrange identity $|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|^2=|\vec{u}|^2|\vec{v}|^2-(\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v})^2$, and $\overrightarrow{CB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=|\overrightarrow{CA}|^2+\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}$.
solution: $|\overrightarrow{CA}|^2=50$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=10$, so the dot product is $60$: option (A).

useful_results: For a triangle, $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec{0}$; with two sides given the third follows component by component.
Area $=\frac12|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|=\frac12\sqrt{|\vec{u}|^2|\vec{v}|^2-(\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v})^2}$, which needs no determinant.
$\overrightarrow{CB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=\frac12\left(CB^2+CA^2-AB^2\right)$ (cosine rule); here $\frac12(84+50-14)=60$.
A sign condition like $\delta>0$ is there to choose between the two roots of a quadratic.

concepts: Cross product properties and magnitude
questions.question: Let $|\vec{a}|=2$, $|\vec{b}|=3$ and the angle between the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be $\frac{\pi}{4}$. Then $|(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})\times(2\vec{a}-3\vec{b})|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Distribute the cross product: $\vec{a}\times\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{b}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{b}\times\vec{a}=-\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ collapse it to $-7\,\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid cross products altogether: expand with the Lagrange identity $|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|^2=|\vec{u}|^2|\vec{v}|^2-(\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v})^2$ using $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=3\sqrt2$.

useful_results: $(p\vec{a}+q\vec{b})\times(r\vec{a}+s\vec{b})=(ps-qr)(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$: the determinant of the coefficient matrix scales the cross product (and the parallelogram area).
$|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2\sin^2\theta=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$ (Lagrange identity).
$\vec{a}\times\vec{a}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{b}\times\vec{a}=-\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, valid for any vectors.
Here the coefficient determinant is $\left|\begin{matrix}1&2\\2&-3\end{matrix}\right|=-7$ and $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=18$, giving $49\cdot18=882$.

concepts: Position vectors and midpoints
questions.question: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral. If $E$ and $F$ are the mid points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively and $(\overrightarrow{AB}-\overrightarrow{BC})+(\overrightarrow{AD}-\overrightarrow{DC})=k\,\overrightarrow{FE}$, then $k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write every vector as a difference of position vectors; the sum becomes $2(\vec{b}+\vec{d})-2(\vec{a}+\vec{c})$, which is $4$ times the vector between the diagonal midpoints.
solution: Let $A,B,C,D$ have position vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{d}$. Then $E$ has $\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2}$ and $F$ has $\frac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $k$ does not depend on the shape of the quadrilateral, so test one concrete non-degenerate quadrilateral.
solution: $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$: $\left(\frac52,1\right)$. $F$ is the midpoint of $BD$: $(2,1)$. So $\overrightarrow{FE}=\left(\frac12,0\right)$.

useful_results: Midpoint of $PQ$ has position vector $\frac{\vec{p}+\vec{q}}{2}$; converting every displacement to a difference of position vectors makes identities mechanical.
For any quadrilateral $ABCD$ with diagonal midpoints $E$ (of $AC$) and $F$ (of $BD$): $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{CB}+\overrightarrow{CD}=4\overrightarrow{EF}$.
$E=F$ exactly when $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, so such a test case gives no information (both sides are $\vec{0}$); pick a non-parallelogram to test a constant.
A constant that is independent of the figure can be found from one non-degenerate instance.

concepts: Coplanarity of three vectors and determinants
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all $(\lambda,\mu)$ for which the vectors $\lambda\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$, where $\lambda-\mu=5$, are coplanar. Then $\sum_{(\lambda,\mu)\in S}80\left(\lambda^2+\mu^2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity gives $10\lambda+4\lambda\mu-3\mu=5$; with $\lambda=\mu+5$ this is a quadratic with two roots.
solution: Split the middle term: $4\mu^2+12\mu+15\mu+45=0$, so $4\mu(\mu+3)+15(\mu+3)=0$ and $(\mu+3)(4\mu+15)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Vieta's relations on $4\mu^2+27\mu+45=0$ for the sum over both roots, without finding them.
solution: As before $\lambda=\mu+5$ and the condition reduces to $4\mu^2+27\mu+45=0$, with two real roots $\mu_1,\mu_2$.

useful_results: Three vectors are coplanar iff their determinant (scalar triple product) vanishes; a linear condition between the parameters then leaves a quadratic.

For a quadratic $A\mu^2+B\mu+C=0$ the sum over both roots of any polynomial in $\mu$ follows from $\mu_1+\mu_2=-\frac BA$ and $\mu_1\mu_2=\frac CA$, so the roots need not be found (check the roots are real first).
Determinant here: $\left|\begin{matrix}\lambda&-1&1\\1&2&\mu\\3&-4&5\end{matrix}\right|=4\lambda\mu+10\lambda-3\mu-5$; test with $(\lambda,\mu)=(2,-3)$: $-24+20+9-5=0$.
The two pairs are $(2,-3)$ and $\left(\frac54,-\frac{15}{4}\right)$.

concepts: Cross product equation and dot product conditions
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=6\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\alpha\hat{i}+11\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be vectors such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$. If $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=-12$ and $\vec{c}\cdot(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=5$, then $\vec{c}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{c}-\vec{b})=\vec{0}$ gives $\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$; the two dot conditions then fix $\alpha$ and $\lambda$.
solution: $\vec{b}=29\hat{i}+11\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ gives $38$, $\vec{a}$ gives $27$, so the value is $38-27=11$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Notice $\vec{a}\perp(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})$, so the second condition gives $\alpha$ at once; then find $\vec{c}$ from three linear equations.
solution: This equals $5$, so $\alpha=29$ and $\vec{b}=29\hat{i}+11\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ with no $\lambda$ involved.

useful_results: $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ iff $\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$ (for $\vec{a}\ne\vec{0}$); the cross-product condition fixes $\vec{c}$ up to a multiple of $\vec{a}$.
If a test vector $\vec{w}\perp\vec{a}$, then $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{w}=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{w}$ no matter what $\lambda$ is; look for such a $\vec{w}$ (here $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$).
A cross-product equality plus one dot-product equality determines a vector uniquely (when $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}\ne0$).

concepts: Lines perpendicular to given lines and foot of perpendicular
questions.question: Let a line $\ell$ pass through the origin and be perpendicular to the lines $\ell_1:\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-11\hat{j}-7\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}),\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\ell_2:\vec{r}=(-\hat{i}+\hat{k})+\mu(2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}),\ \mu\in\mathbb{R}$. If $P$ is the point of intersection of $\ell$ and $\ell_1$, and $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the foot of perpendicular from $P$ on $\ell_2$, then $9(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Direction of $\ell$ is $d_1\times d_2$; the intersection $P$ and the foot $Q$ each come from one scalar equation.
solution: Let the direction ratios of $\ell$ be $a,b,c$. Perpendicular to $\ell_1,\ell_2$: $a+2b+3c=0$ and $2a+2b+c=0$.
Cross multiplying: $\frac{a}{-4}=\frac{b}{5}=\frac{c}{-2}$, so the direction ratios can be taken as $4,-5,2$.
Any point of $\ell$ is $(4t,-5t,2t)$. A point of $\ell_1$ is $(1+\lambda,\ 2\lambda-11,\ 3\lambda-7)$.
From the first and third: $2(3\lambda-7)=\lambda+1$, so $5\lambda=15$, $\lambda=3$ and $t=1$ (the second equation holds: $-5=-5$). So $P(4,-5,2)$.
A point of $\ell_2$ is $Q(2\mu-1,\ 2\mu,\ \mu+1)$, so the direction ratios of $PQ$ are $2\mu-5,\ 2\mu+5,\ \mu-1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A line through the origin that meets $\ell_1$ at $P$ and is perpendicular to it gives $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\vec{d}_1=0$; then use the projection formula for the foot.
solution: $P$ lies on $\ell_1$ and on $\ell$ (through $O$), and $\ell\perp\ell_1$, so $\overrightarrow{OP}\perp(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$.

useful_results: A line perpendicular to two non-parallel lines has direction $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$.

If a line through the origin meets $\ell_1$ at $P$ and is perpendicular to $\ell_1$, then $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\vec{d}_1=0$; this finds $P$ from one linear equation, no need for the direction of $\ell$.
Foot of perpendicular from $P$ to the line $\vec{r}=A+\mu\vec{d}$: $\mu=\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|^2}$.
Intersecting-line equations are over-determined; a consistent third equation (here $-5=-5$) is a free check.

concepts: Scalar and vector triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$. If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=11$, $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})=27$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=-\sqrt3|\vec{b}|$, then $|\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$, so $\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})=\vec{a}(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})$, which together with $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})$ gives $|\vec{b}||\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|$ through its perpendicular and parallel parts.
solution: Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}$. Then $|\vec{b}||\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|\sin\theta=|-3\vec{a}|=3\sqrt{14}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: As $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$, the vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ are an orthogonal basis; expand $\vec{c}$ in it, find $|\vec{c}|^2$ and use Lagrange's identity.
solution: $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{c}=[\vec{a}\,\vec{b}\,\vec{c}]=-\,\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})=-27$ (swapping $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ in the triple product flips the sign).

useful_results: Vector triple product: $\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})=\vec{a}(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})$; if $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$ it is just $(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}$.
If $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$, then $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\}$ is an orthogonal basis and $|\vec{c}|^2=\sum\frac{(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{e})^2}{|\vec{e}|^2}$ (Parseval).
Lagrange identity: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{c}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})^2$.

$[\vec{a}\,\vec{b}\,\vec{c}]=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})$ and swapping two vectors changes the sign, so $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})=-[\vec{a}\,\vec{b}\,\vec{c}]$. Here $\vec{c}=(3,-2,4)$ works: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=11$, $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=-3$.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and Lagrange identity
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$. If $\vec{b}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ and $|\vec{b}|^2=50$, then $\left|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2\right|$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Taking magnitudes in $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ gives $\sin\theta$, and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}$ then follows from $\cos\theta$ (its sign does not matter).
solution: Therefore $\left|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2\right|=|72-138|=66$; for $\cos\theta<0$ it is $|72-6|=66$ as well, so the answer is $66$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's penultimate line writes the cross term as $\frac{2\times5\times11\times3}{10}$ (=33), giving $|72-(72+33)|=33$, yet jumps to $|66|$; the term should equal 66 ($2\cdot10\sqrt{11}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}=66$). PDF also ignores $\cos\theta<0$, which gives the same final value 66. Answer 66 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Construct $\vec{b}$ explicitly: since $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0$, every solution of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$ is $\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{|\vec{c}|^2}+t\vec{c}$.
solution: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=6-3-3=0$, so $\vec{a}\perp\vec{c}$, as it must be if $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$.

Using $(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}|\vec{c}|^2-\vec{c}(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})=22\vec{a}$, the vector $\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{22}+t\vec{c}$ satisfies $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$ for every real $t$.

useful_results: Lagrange identity: $|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|^2+(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})^2=|\vec{b}|^2|\vec{c}|^2$. Here $11+(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})^2=1100$, so $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=\pm33$.
If $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ then $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\perp\vec{c}$; $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0$ is a necessary consistency check ($6-3-3=0$ here).
Parallelogram law: $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^2=2(|\vec{b}|^2+|\vec{c}|^2)$; here $138+6=144=2\cdot72$, which is why the sign of $\cos\theta$ does not matter.
If $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0$, all solutions of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$ are $\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{|\vec{c}|^2}+t\vec{c}$ (a line of vectors).

concepts: Family of planes through the line of intersection of two planes
Parallelism of a line and a plane
questions.question: If the equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $2x-y+z=3$, $4x-3y+5z+9=0$ and parallel to the line $\frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+3}{4}=\frac{z-2}{5}$ is $ax+by+cz+6=0$, then $a+b+c$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: A plane through the intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; parallel to a line means its normal is perpendicular to the direction.
solution: The plane is parallel to the line with direction $(-2,4,5)$, so the normal is perpendicular to it.
Multiply by $\frac52$: $11x-7y+10z+6=0$, which has the required constant term $6$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Build the normal directly as the cross product of the two directions the plane must contain: the intersection line and the given line.
solution: Direction of the line of intersection: $(2,-1,1)\times(4,-3,5)=(-2,-6,-2)\parallel(1,3,1)$.
The plane contains this direction and is parallel to $(-2,4,5)$, so its normal is $(1,3,1)\times(-2,4,5)=(15-4,\,-2-5,\,4+6)=(11,-7,10)$.
Find one point on the line of intersection: put $z=0$, then $2x-y=3$ and $4x-3y=-9$ give $x=9$, $y=15$, point $(9,15,0)$.

useful_results: Plane through the line $P_1=P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (all such planes except $P_2=0$ itself).
A plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=k$ is parallel to a line with direction $\vec{d}$ iff $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}=0$.
Normal of a plane containing directions $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$ is $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$; direction of the line of two planes is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
Quick check: the point $(9,15,0)$ lies on both original planes ($18-15=3$; $36-45+9=0$) and on $11x-7y+10z+6=0$.

concepts: Line in space: intersection and parallelism with a plane
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the line $L$ pass through the point $(0,1,2)$, intersect the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ and be parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$. Then the distance of the point $P(1,-9,2)$ from the line $L$ is :
questions.key_idea: The intersection point makes the direction $\vec{AB}$, and parallelism to the plane forces $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec{n}=0$, which collapses to $\lambda=0$.
solution: Let $A(0,1,2)$ and let $B(1+2\lambda,2+3\lambda,3+4\lambda)$ be the point where $L$ meets the given line.
