$L$ is parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$ (normal $(2,1,-3)$), so $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec{n}=0$.
Then $\vec{AB}=(1,1,1)$ and $L:\ (\mu,\,1+\mu,\,2+\mu)$. Let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P(1,-9,2)$ on $L$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of a point from a line by the cross product: $\frac{|\vec{AP}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$, with no foot of the perpendicular.
solution: As before, $\lambda=0$ gives direction $\vec{d}=(1,1,1)$ for $L$ through $A(0,1,2)$.

useful_results: A line through $A$ parallel to a plane with normal $\vec{n}$ has direction $\vec{d}$ with $\vec{d}\cdot\vec{n}=0$; if it also meets a given line at $B$, then $\vec{AB}\parallel\vec{d}$.

Distance of $P$ from the line $\vec{r}=\vec{A}+t\vec{d}$ is $\frac{|\vec{AP}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$ (Pythagoras: $|AP|^2-\left(\frac{\vec{AP}\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|}\right)^2$ equals the same, here $101-\frac{81}{3}=74$).
Parameter of the foot of the perpendicular from $P$: $t=\frac{\vec{AP}\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|^2}$ (here $\frac{-9}{3}=-3$, matching $\mu=-3$ with $\vec{AP}$ taken from $A$).
Condition 'parallel to a plane' always reduces to one scalar equation in the free parameter; solve it first.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-4}{4}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ is :
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance $=\frac{|(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)|}{|\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2|}$.
solution: Line 1 passes through $\vec{a}=(4,-2,-3)$ with direction $\vec{n}_1=(4,5,3)$; line 2 through $\vec{b}=(1,3,4)$ with direction $\vec{n}_2=(3,4,2)$.

Shortest distance $d=\frac{|(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)|}{|\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2|}$ (the PDF prints $\times$ in place of $\cdot$ between $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ and $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$).
questions.correction_note: Only a notation slip: the PDF's formula has a cross product between $(\vec a-\vec b)$ and $(\vec n_1\times\vec n_2)$; it must be a dot product (scalar triple product). All numbers and the answer $3\sqrt6$ are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the plane through line 1 parallel to line 2; the required distance is the distance of any point of line 2 from this plane.
solution: Normal of the plane containing line 1 and parallel to line 2: $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2=(-2,1,1)$.
Line 2 is parallel to this plane, so all its points are equidistant from it; use $(1,3,4)$.

useful_results: Skew lines $\vec{a}+t\vec{p}$, $\vec{b}+s\vec{q}$: $d=\frac{|(\vec{b}-\vec{a})\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$; if $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}=\vec{0}$ the lines are parallel and a different formula $\frac{|(\vec{b}-\vec{a})\times\vec{p}|}{|\vec{p}|}$ applies.
The lines intersect (coplanar, not parallel) iff $(\vec{b}-\vec{a})\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})=0$; here it is $18\neq0$, so they are skew.
The common perpendicular has direction $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$; $d$ is the length of the projection of $\vec{b}-\vec{a}$ along it.
Equivalent: $d$ is the volume of the parallelepiped on $\vec{b}-\vec{a},\vec{p},\vec{q}$ divided by the area $|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|$ of its base parallelogram.

concepts: Plane through the line of intersection of two planes
Perpendicular planes
questions.question: If the equation of the plane containing the line $x+2y+3z-4=0=2x+y-z+5$ and perpendicular to the plane $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ is $ax+by+cz=4$, then $(a-b+c)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The required plane belongs to the family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, and perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals.
solution: Planes through the given line: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, i.e. $(1+2\lambda)x+(2+\lambda)y+(3-\lambda)z+(5\lambda-4)=0$ ... (1).
Plane (1) is perpendicular to plane (2), so the normals are perpendicular: $5(1+2\lambda)-2(2+\lambda)-3(3-\lambda)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The normal of the required plane is perpendicular to both the line's direction and the normal of the given plane, so it is their cross product.
solution: Direction of the line of intersection: $(1,2,3)\times(2,1,-1)=(-2-3,\ 6+1,\ 1-4)=(-5,7,-3)$.
Normal of the given plane: $\vec{m}=(5,-2,-3)$ (cross product of its two direction vectors).
The required plane contains $(-5,7,-3)$ and is perpendicular to the given plane, so its normal is $(-5,7,-3)\times(5,-2,-3)=(-21-6,\ -15-15,\ 10-35)=(-27,-30,-25)\parallel(27,30,25)$.
A point on the line: $x=0$ gives $2y+3z=4$ and $y-z=-5$, so $z=\frac{14}{5}$, $y=-\frac{11}{5}$.

useful_results: Two planes are perpendicular iff $\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2=0$; a plane perpendicular to a given plane and containing a given line has normal $\vec{d}\times\vec{n}_{given}$.
$\vec{r}=\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{p}+\mu\vec{q}$ is a plane with normal $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$.
The line $P_1=0=P_2$ has direction $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; a point on it is found by setting one coordinate to a convenient value.

concepts: Equation of a plane through a line and a point
Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane passing through the line $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-3}=\frac{z+5}{7}$ and the point $(2,4,-3)$. If the image of the point $(-1,3,4)$ in the plane $P$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The image of a point in a plane is $Q=P-2\,\frac{\vec{n}\cdot P-d}{|\vec{n}|^2}\,\vec{n}$.
solution: The line passes through $A(1,2,-5)$ with direction $(1,-3,7)$; the point $B(2,4,-3)$ gives $\vec{AB}=(1,2,2)$ in the plane.

alternate_solutions.idea: The image lies on the normal through the point and the midpoint lies on the plane; parametrise the normal line and solve for the midpoint.
solution: Plane: $4x-y-z=7$, normal $\vec{n}=(4,-1,-1)$ (found as in the main method).
Image $Q=(-1+4s,\ 3-s,\ 4-s)$ lies on the line through $(-1,3,4)$ along $\vec{n}$.
The midpoint of $P$ and $Q$ is $\left(-1+2s,\ 3-\frac s2,\ 4-\frac s2\right)$ and it lies on the plane: $4(-1+2s)-\left(3-\frac s2\right)-\left(4-\frac s2\right)=7$.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $Q=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$; the foot is the midpoint of $PQ$.
A plane through a point $B$ and a line (point $A$, direction $\vec{d}$) has normal $\vec{AB}\times\vec{d}$.
Reflection preserves distances to every point of the plane, so $QA=PA$ for all $A$ in the plane. Here $|PA|^2=4+1+81=86=|QA|^2$ for $A(1,2,-5)$ and $Q=(7,1,2)$ ($36+1+49=86$).
Sum of coordinates of the image: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=(1,1,1)\cdot P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)(\vec{n}\cdot(1,1,1))}{|\vec{n}|^2}$, which is useful when only a combination is asked.

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral using the vector (cross) product
questions.question: The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ with vertices $A(2,1,1)$, $B(1,2,5)$, $C(-2,-3,5)$ and $D(1,-6,-7)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Split the planar quadrilateral along a diagonal into two triangles and use area $=\frac12|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|$.
solution: Note $\vec{DC}=(-3,3,12)=3\vec{AB}$, so $AB\parallel DC$: $ABCD$ is a trapezium (the PDF's rectangle figure is only schematic), so the diagonal $BD$ splits it into two triangles.
So the area is $|{-30}\hat{i}+18\hat{j}-12\hat{k}|=6|5\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}|=6\sqrt{38}$ (same direction $(5,-3,2)$ as for $\triangle ABD$, so the four points are coplanar).

alternate_solutions.idea: For a planar convex quadrilateral, area $=\frac12|\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}|$ (cross product of the diagonals).
solution: Area $=\frac12\cdot16\sqrt{38}=8\sqrt{38}$ (valid because $ABCD$ is planar and convex, as $\vec{DC}=3\vec{AB}$).

useful_results: Area of a planar convex quadrilateral $=\frac12|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|$, with $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$ the diagonal vectors (here the two diagonals give $16\sqrt{38}/2=8\sqrt{38}$).
Area of a triangle with sides $\vec{u},\vec{v}$ from one vertex is $\frac12|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|$; coplanarity of four points $\iff(\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC})\cdot\vec{AD}=0$.

If $\vec{DC}=k\vec{AB}$ ($k>0$), $ABCD$ is a trapezium with parallel sides in ratio $1:k$ and area $=\frac{(1+k)}{2}\cdot|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AD}|$; here $k=3$ and $|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AD}|=4\sqrt{38}$, giving $8\sqrt{38}$.
Do not assume a rectangle from a sketch; check parallel/perpendicular relations with vectors.

concepts: Angle between a line and a plane, distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: For $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|a-b|\le10$, let the angle between the plane $P:\ ax+y-z=b$ and the line $l:\ x-1=a-y=z+1$ be $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac13\right)$. If the distance of the point $(6,-6,4)$ from the plane $P$ is $3\sqrt6$, then $a^4+b^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The angle between a line and a plane uses $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{d}|}$, so $\cos\theta=\frac13$ means $\sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$; then integrality and $|a-b|\le10$ filter the roots.
solution: The angle $\theta$ between a line and a plane satisfies $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{d}|}$; with $\cos\theta=\frac13$, $\sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.
The condition $|a-b|\le10$ with $a=-2$ means $-12\le b\le8$: $b=-40$ is rejected, $b=-4$ is accepted.
questions.correction_note: PDF has two slips. (i) It writes the distance numerator as $12+6+4+b$ instead of $-12-6-4-b=-(b+22)$ (same absolute value, so harmless). (ii) The line 'b >= -8n' used to reject $b=-40$ is garbled/meaningless; the correct filter is $|a-b|\le10$, i.e. $-12\le b\le8$ for $a=-2$. Final answer 32 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\tan$ of the angle between $\vec{n}$ and $\vec{d}$, i.e. $\frac{|\vec{n}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}$, which gives a linear (not quadratic) equation in $a$.
solution: The line-plane angle $\theta$ has $\cos\theta=\frac13$, so the angle $\varphi$ between $\vec{n}$ and $\vec{d}$ (complement) has $\cos\varphi=\pm\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, hence $\tan\varphi=\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}$ in absolute value.
$a-2=4a+4\Rightarrow a=-2$, or $a-2=-4a-4\Rightarrow a=-\frac25$ (not an integer). So $a=-2$.

useful_results: Angle $\theta$ between line (direction $\vec{d}$) and plane (normal $\vec{n}$): $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{d}|}$, $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec{n}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}||\vec{d}|}$. Do not use cosine of the dot-product formula.

Using $\tan\varphi=\frac{|\vec{n}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}$ turns an angle condition into a linear one when the cross product is simple (check: for $a=-2$, $\frac{\sqrt2\cdot1}{4}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}$).
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $Ax+By+Cz=D$ is $\frac{|Ax_0+By_0+Cz_0-D|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2+C^2}}$; an absolute value gives two candidates, so extra constraints (integers, $|a-b|\le10$) decide.
With integer parameters, solve the quadratic and discard non-integer roots before using the second condition.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+2}{1}=\frac{y}{-2}=\frac{z-5}{2}$ and $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+3}{0}$ is :
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance $=\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2)|}{|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|}$.
solution: Line 1 passes through $(-2,0,5)$ with direction $(1,-2,2)$; line 2 through $(4,1,-3)$ with direction $(1,2,0)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the plane through line 1 parallel to line 2; the distance of a point of line 2 from it is the shortest distance.
solution: Line 2 is parallel to this plane (normal $\cdot$ direction $=-2+2+0=0$), so use its point $(4,1,-3)$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines is the projection of the join of any two points onto the common perpendicular direction $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$.
Equivalent: distance from a point of line 2 to the plane containing line 1 and parallel to line 2.
Cross product of $(1,-2,2)$ and $(1,2,0)$ has magnitude $\sqrt{16+4+16}=6$, a convenient integer here, so no surds appear.
Zero scalar triple product means the lines meet or are parallel; non-zero ($-54$ here) means skew.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the line $\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}$ and the plane $x+y+z=2$. If the distance of the point $P$ from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is $q$, then $q$ and $2q$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.key_idea: Find $P$ by substituting the parametric point in the plane, then $q$ by the point-plane distance; roots $q,2q$ give $x^2-3qx+2q^2=0$.
solution: Let $\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}=\lambda$, so a point of the line is $(3\lambda-3,\ \lambda-2,\ 1-2\lambda)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $y$ and $z$ in favour of $x$ using the symmetric form of the line, instead of introducing a parameter.
solution: Then $y=1$, $z=-5$, $P=(6,1,-5)$ and $q=6$ as in the main solution.

useful_results: A line $\frac{x-x_0}{l}=\frac{y-y_0}{m}=\frac{z-z_0}{n}$ meets a plane at the parameter where substitution makes the plane equation true; if the coefficient of the parameter vanishes the line is parallel to the plane (no unique point).
Watch sign conventions: $\frac{1-z}{2}$ means the direction ratio of $z$ is $-2$, giving $z=1-2\lambda$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $Ax+By+Cz=D$ is $\frac{|Ax_0+By_0+Cz_0-D|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2+C^2}}$; $\sqrt{9+16+144}=13$ is a Pythagorean quadruple-type coincidence.

concepts: Centroid of a triangle in 3D
Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let two vertices of a triangle $ABC$ be $(2,4,6)$ and $(0,-2,-5)$, and its centroid be $(2,1,-1)$. If the image of the third vertex in the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The centroid gives the third vertex; its image in the plane is $C-2\,\frac{\vec{n}\cdot C-d}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$.
solution: Let the third vertex be $C(x,y,z)$; the centroid is $\left(\frac{2+0+x}{3},\frac{4-2+y}{3},\frac{6-5+z}{3}\right)=(2,1,-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The image lies on the normal through $C$ and the midpoint of $CD$ lies in the plane; solve for the single parameter.
solution: The normal is $\vec{n}=(1,2,4)$, so the image is $D=(4+t,\ 1+2t,\ -4+4t)$.
The midpoint of $CD$ is $\left(4+\frac t2,\ 1+t,\ -4+2t\right)$ and lies on $x+2y+4z=11$.

useful_results: Centroid $G=\frac{A+B+C}{3}$, so $C=3G-A-B$.
Image of $P$ in $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $P'=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$; here $\vec{n}\cdot C-d=-21=-|\vec{n}|^2$, so $P'=C+2\vec{n}$.
$\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac{(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)}{2}$ (check: $\frac{225-77}{2}=74$).
A point and its image are at equal distances from the plane: here both are $\frac{21}{\sqrt{21}}=\sqrt{21}$ away.

concepts: Intersection of lines in 3D
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{6-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{5}$ intersect the lines $\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ and $\frac{x+3}{6}=\frac{3-y}{3}=\frac{z-6}{1}$ at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then the distance of the mid-point of the line segment $AB$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=14$ is :
questions.key_idea: Write the first line as $(\lambda,\ 6-2\lambda,\ 5\lambda-8)$ and find $\lambda$ at each intersection by equating two coordinates and checking the third.
solution: Intersection $A$ of (1) and (2): $\lambda=4\mu+5$ and $6-2\lambda=3\mu+7$ give $6-8\mu-10=3\mu+7$, so $\mu=-1$, $\lambda=1$; check $z$: $5-8=-3=\mu-2$.
Intersection $B$ of (1) and (3): $\lambda=6\gamma-3$ and $6-2\lambda=3-3\gamma$ give $12-12\gamma=3-3\gamma$, so $\gamma=1$, $\lambda=3$; check $z$: $15-8=7=\gamma+6$.
So $B=(3,0,7)$ and the mid-point of $AB$ is $(2,2,2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Signed distance to a plane is a linear function, so the distance of the midpoint is the average of the signed distances of $A$ and $B$.
solution: With $A=(1,4,-3)$ and $B=(3,0,7)$ (found by equating two coordinates on each pair of lines as in the main method).

useful_results: If $f(X)=\frac{\vec{n}\cdot X-d}{|\vec{n}|}$ (signed distance), then $f$ of the midpoint (or any weighted average with weights summing to 1) is the same average of $f$ values. Check: $-4=\frac{-23/3-1/3}{2}$.
Two lines intersect: equate two coordinates to find both parameters and verify the third; if the third fails, the lines are skew.
Parametrise symmetric forms carefully when a variable is reversed, e.g. $\frac{6-y}{2}=\lambda\Rightarrow y=6-2\lambda$.

concepts: Equation of a plane through three points
Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,6)$ in the plane passing through the points $A(1,2,0)$, $B(1,4,1)$ and $C(0,5,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Find the plane through the three points, then reflect $P$ using $Q=P-2\,\frac{\vec{n}\cdot P-d}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$.
solution: Plane through $A(1,2,0)$: $A'(x-1)+B'(y-2)+C'(z-0)=0$ (coefficients named $A',B',C'$ to avoid clashing with the points).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use that the image is equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$ as $P$ is (spheres), giving linear equations, so no plane equation is needed.
solution: Subtracting the first two squared equations gives $\vec{Q}\cdot(\vec{B}-\vec{A})=\vec{P}\cdot(\vec{B}-\vec{A})$; similarly for $C$. With $\vec{B}-\vec{A}=(0,2,1)$ and $\vec{C}-\vec{A}=(-1,3,1)$: $2\beta+\gamma=10$ and $-\alpha+3\beta+\gamma=11$.
$\beta=2$ gives $Q=(1,2,6)=P$, which is the original point, so reject; $\beta=6$ gives $Q=(5,6,-2)$.

useful_results: Plane through three points: normal $=\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}$; here $(0,2,1)\times(-1,3,1)=(-1,-1,2)$, giving $x+y-2z=3$.
Image of $P$: $Q=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$; here $\vec{n}\cdot P-d=-12$ and $|\vec{n}|^2=6$, so $Q=P+4\vec{n}$ (check: $|P|^2=41$, $|Q|^2=65$).
The image of $P$ is equidistant from every point of the plane as $P$ is; three non-collinear fixed points determine $Q\ne P$.
Reflection preserves distances to the plane: $P$ and $Q$ are both at distance $\frac{12}{\sqrt6}$ from it.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the image of the point $P(2,3,5)$ in the plane $2x+y-3z=6$. Then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Image of a point: $\frac{\alpha-x_1}{a}=\frac{\beta-y_1}{b}=\frac{\gamma-z_1}{c}=\frac{-2(ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the perpendicular through $P$ and place the midpoint of $P$ and its image on the plane.
solution: The normal is $(2,1,-3)$, so the image is $Q=(2+2t,\ 3+t,\ 5-3t)$.
The midpoint $\left(2+t,\ 3+\frac t2,\ 5-\frac{3t}{2}\right)$ lies on the plane: $2(2+t)+3+\frac t2-3\left(5-\frac{3t}{2}\right)=6$.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $Q=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$; the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $PQ$.
Here $\vec{n}\cdot P-d=-14=-|\vec{n}|^2$, so $Q=P+2\vec{n}$ exactly. Such coincidences are quick checks.
The image lies on the normal through $P$ and $|PQ|=\frac{2|\vec{n}\cdot P-d|}{|\vec{n}|}=2\sqrt{14}$ (check: $|2\vec{n}|=2\sqrt{14}$).
Reflection is an isometry that fixes the plane pointwise, so the image of a point on the plane is itself (then $\vec{n}\cdot P=d$ and the formula gives $Q=P$).

concepts: Plane through a point perpendicular to two given planes
questions.question: If the equation of the plane that contains the point $(-2,3,5)$ and is perpendicular to each of the planes $2x+4y+5z=8$ and $3x-2y+3z=5$ is $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z+97=0$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is:
questions.key_idea: A plane perpendicular to two planes has normal parallel to the cross product of their normals.
solution: Let the required plane be $a(x+2)+b(y-3)+c(z-5)=0$, where $(a,b,c)$ is its normal.
It is perpendicular to $2x+4y+5z=8$ and $3x-2y+3z=5$, so the normals are perpendicular: $2a+4b+5c=0$ and $3a-2b+3c=0$.
Hence $\frac a{22}=\frac b9=\frac c{-16}$, so take $(a,b,c)=(22,9,-16)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The required plane contains the direction vectors $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ (its normal is perpendicular to both normals), so use the coplanarity determinant.
solution: A plane perpendicular to a given plane is parallel to the normal of that plane, so the required plane is parallel to both $\vec n_1=(2,4,5)$ and $\vec n_2=(3,-2,3)$.
A point $(x,y,z)$ lies on it iff $\left|\begin{matrix}x+2&y-3&z-5\\2&4&5\\3&-2&3\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
The constant already equals $97$, so no rescaling is needed: $\alpha=22,\beta=9,\gamma=-16$.

useful_results: A plane perpendicular to the planes with normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ (non-parallel) has normal $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$; equivalently it contains the directions $\vec n_1$ and $\vec n_2$.
A plane through $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ with normal $(a,b,c)$ is $a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0$.
Plane through a point containing two given directions $\vec u,\vec v$: $\left|\begin{matrix}x-x_0&y-y_0&z-z_0\\u_1&u_2&u_3\\v_1&v_2&v_3\end{matrix}\right|=0$.

concepts: Line meeting a plane and distance measured parallel to a given line
questions.question: Let the line passing through the points $P(2,-1,2)$ and $Q(5,3,4)$ meet the plane $x-y+z=4$ at the point $R$. Then the distance of the point $R$ from the plane $x+2y+3z+2=0$, measured parallel to the line $\frac{x-7}{2}=\frac{y+3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Distance measured parallel to a direction is the length of the segment from $R$ along that direction to the plane.
solution: Direction of $PQ$ is $(3,4,2)$, so line $PQ$ is $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\lambda$.
The line through $R$ parallel to $\frac{x-7}2=\frac{y+3}2=\frac z1$ is $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y+5}{2}=\frac{z}{1}=k$; it meets the plane $x+2y+3z+2=0$ at $S$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the formula for distance along a direction, $\frac{|\vec n\cdot R+D|}{|\vec n\cdot\vec d|}\,|\vec d|$, so no point $S$ is needed.
solution: $R=(-1,-5,0)$ as before (from the line $PQ$ and the plane $x-y+z=4$).
Plane $x+2y+3z+2=0$ has normal $\vec n=(1,2,3)$; value at $R$ is $-1-10+0+2=-9$.
The given direction is $\vec d=(2,2,1)$, with $|\vec d|=3$ and $\vec n\cdot\vec d=2+4+3=9$.
Moving $t\vec d$ from $R$ reaches the plane when $-9+t(\vec n\cdot\vec d)=0$, i.e. $t=1$.

useful_results: Distance of point $X_0$ from plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r+D=0$ measured along direction $\vec d$ (with $\vec n\cdot\vec d\neq0$) is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot X_0+D|}{|\vec n\cdot\vec d|}\,|\vec d|$. Here $\frac{9}{9}\cdot3=3$.
If $\vec d=\vec n$ the formula reduces to the usual perpendicular distance.
A line through $P$ and $Q$ meets a plane at the point $\lambda$ found by substituting $P+\lambda(Q-P)$ into the plane equation (if $\vec n\cdot(Q-P)\neq0$).
The distance along $\vec d$ is never less than the perpendicular distance; here the perpendicular distance of $R$ is $\frac{9}{\sqrt{14}}\approx2.4<3$.

concepts: Plane through three points and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane passing through the points $(5,3,0)$, $(13,3,-2)$ and $(1,6,2)$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}$, if the distances of the points $A(3,4,\alpha)$ and $B(2,\alpha,a)$ from the plane $P$ are $2$ and $3$ respectively, then the positive value of $a$ is:
questions.key_idea: The plane's normal is the cross product of two edge vectors; the natural-number condition picks the valid $\alpha$ before $a$ is found.
solution: Normal $=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\8&0&-2\\-4&3&2\end{matrix}\right|=6\hat i-8\hat j+24\hat k\ \parallel\ 3\hat i-4\hat j+12\hat k$.
$12\alpha-10=26$ gives $\alpha=3$; $12\alpha-10=-26$ gives $\alpha=-\frac43$ (not a natural number), so $\alpha=3$.
$12a-9=39$ gives $a=4$; $12a-9=-39$ gives $a=-\frac52$. The positive value is $a=4$, option (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF step 'alpha = -8 (rejected)' is wrong: $|12\alpha-10|=26$ gives $\alpha=3$ or $\alpha=-\frac43$ (not $-8$). The rejection conclusion and the final answer $a=4$ are unchanged. The PDF also silently takes $B(2,3,a)$ (i.e. $\alpha=3$) and omits the $a=-5/2$ root; both are made explicit. Its cross product and normal $(3,-4,12)$ are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the plane as a three-point determinant, then use the distance formula and test the options for $a$.
solution: Dividing by $2$: $3x-4y+12z=3$. Norm of the normal $=\sqrt{9+16+144}=13$.
For $B(2,3,a)$ the distance is $\frac{|12a-9|}{13}$. Test the options: $a=5\to\frac{51}{13}$, $a=3\to\frac{27}{13}$, $a=4\to\frac{39}{13}=3$, $a=6\to\frac{63}{13}$.

useful_results: Plane through three non-collinear points $A,B,C$: normal $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$, or equivalently $\left|\begin{matrix}x-x_1&y-y_1&z-z_1\\x_2-x_1&y_2-y_1&z_2-z_1\\x_3-x_1&y_3-y_1&z_3-z_1\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; a given distance gives two linear equations, one on each side of the plane.
A condition like $\alpha\in\mathbb N$ or 'positive value' is used to discard the second root of the modulus equation.
Numerical check: for $P:3x-4y+12z=3$, point $(3,4,3)$ gives $\frac{|9-16+36-3|}{13}=2$.

concepts: Coplanar lines, family of planes and foot of perpendicular on a line
questions.question: Let the lines $l_1:\frac{x+5}{3}=\frac{y+4}{1}=\frac{z-\alpha}{-2}$ and $l_2:3x+2y+z-2=0=x-3y+2z-13$ be coplanar. If the point $P(a,b,c)$ on $l_1$ is nearest to the point $Q(-4,-3,2)$, then $|a|+|b|+|c|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Coplanar non-parallel lines lie in a plane through $l_2$ parallel to $l_1$, which fixes $\alpha$; the nearest point is the foot of the perpendicular.
solution: $l_1$ has direction $(3,1,-2)$. For the plane to be parallel to $l_1$: $3(3+\mu)+(2-3\mu)-2(1+2\mu)=0$, i.e. $9-4\mu=0$, so $\mu=\frac94$.
Coplanarity requires the point $(-5,-4,\alpha)$ of $l_1$ to lie on this plane.
A point of $l_1$ is $P(3\lambda-5,\ \lambda-4,\ -2\lambda+7)$ and $Q=(-4,-3,2)$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ has direction ratios $(3\lambda-1,\ \lambda-1,\ -2\lambda+5)$ (as $\overrightarrow{QP}$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Non-parallel coplanar lines must intersect: find the intersection point of $l_1$ with the two planes of $l_2$, then minimise $PQ^2$ as a quadratic in $\lambda$.
solution: $l_1$: $(3\lambda-5,\ \lambda-4,\ \alpha-2\lambda)$. $l_2$ has direction $(3,2,1)\times(1,-3,2)=(7,-5,-11)$, not parallel to $(3,1,-2)$, so coplanar means they intersect.
A common point lies on both planes of $l_2$. First plane: $3(3\lambda-5)+2(\lambda-4)+(\alpha-2\lambda)-2=0$, i.e. $9\lambda+\alpha-25=0$.

useful_results: Planes through the line $P_1=0=P_2$: $P_1+\mu P_2=0$ (all except $P_2=0$); choosing $\mu$ so that the normal is perpendicular to $\vec d_1$ gives the plane through $l_2$ parallel to $l_1$.
Two skew-or-intersecting lines are coplanar iff the plane through one, parallel to the other, contains a point of the other (or iff $\det[\vec{P_2P_1},\vec d_1,\vec d_2]=0$).

Nearest point of a line $\vec a+\lambda\vec d$ to $Q$: $\lambda=\frac{(\vec Q-\vec a)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$. Here $\vec a=(-5,-4,7),\ \vec d=(3,1,-2)$: $\frac{(1,1,-5)\cdot(3,1,-2)}{14}=\frac{14}{14}=1$.
A distance-squared function of the parameter is a quadratic; its vertex $\lambda=-\frac{b}{2a}$ gives the nearest point without calculus.

concepts: Family of planes through a line of intersection and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the plane $P: 4x-y+z=10$ be rotated by an angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$ about its line of intersection with the plane $x+y-z=4$. If $\alpha$ is the distance of the point $(2,3,-4)$ from the new position of the plane $P$, then $35\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: After a rotation by $\frac\pi2$ about the common line, the new plane passes through that line and is perpendicular to the old plane.
solution: The new plane passes through the line of intersection, so it is $(4x-y+z-10)+\lambda(x+y-z-4)=0$.
Its normal is $(4+\lambda,\ -1+\lambda,\ 1-\lambda)$; it is perpendicular to $P$, whose normal is $(4,-1,1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The new normal is $\vec n_P\times(\vec n_P\times\vec n_Q)$, perpendicular to both $\vec n_P$ and the common line.
solution: Normals: $\vec n_P=(4,-1,1)$, $\vec n_Q=(1,1,-1)$; $\vec n_P\cdot\vec n_Q=2$, $|\vec n_P|^2=18$.
The line of intersection has direction $\vec n_P\times\vec n_Q$. The rotated plane contains that line and is perpendicular to $P$, so its normal is $\vec n_P\times(\vec n_P\times\vec n_Q)$.
Using the triple product identity: $\vec n_P(\vec n_P\cdot\vec n_Q)-\vec n_Q|\vec n_P|^2=2(4,-1,1)-18(1,1,-1)=(-10,-20,20)\parallel(1,2,-2)$.
A point on the line: adding the two plane equations $5x=14$, so $x=\frac{14}5$; with $z=0$, $y=\frac65$. Point $\left(\frac{14}{5},\frac65,0\right)$.

useful_results: A plane through the line $P_1=0=P_2$ perpendicular to $P_1$: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ with $\lambda=-\frac{\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_1}{\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2}$ (here $-\frac{18}{2}=-9$).
Rotating a plane by $\frac\pi2$ about a line lying in it gives the plane through the line perpendicular to the original (two choices of direction give the same plane).
For a rotation by an angle $\theta$ the condition becomes $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec n_1\cdot(\vec n_1+\lambda\vec n_2)}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_1+\lambda\vec n_2|}$.
Distance of a point from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; check: $\frac{54}{15}=\frac{18}{5}$ in both methods.

concepts: Family of planes through a line of intersection and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2y+az=2$ and $x-y+z=3$ be $5x-11y+bz=6a-1$. For $c\in\mathbb Z$, if the distance of this plane from the point $(a,-c,c)$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, then $\frac{a+b}{c}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Compare the family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ with the given plane, coefficient by coefficient, to get $\lambda,a,b$.
solution: The plane through the line is $(x+2y+az-2)+\lambda(x-y+z-3)=0$, i.e. $(1+\lambda)x+(2-\lambda)y+(a+\lambda)z=2+3\lambda$.
The plane is $5x-11y+z=17$ and the point is $(3,-c,c)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Points with $z=0$ on the line lie on every plane of the family, so one such point fixes $a$; the line's direction lying in the plane fixes $b$.
solution: At $z=0$ the planes $x+2y+az=2$ and $x-y+z=3$ do not involve $a$: $x+2y=2,\ x-y=3$ gives the point $\left(\frac83,-\frac13,0\right)$ on the line.
The required plane contains it: $5\cdot\frac83+11\cdot\frac13=17=6a-1$, so $a=3$.
The plane contains this direction: $(5,-11,b)\cdot(5,2,-3)=25-22-3b=0$, so $b=1$.
Plane $5x-11y+z=17$; distance from $(3,-c,c)$ is $\frac{|12c-2|}{7\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, so $|12c-2|=14$ and the integer root is $c=-1$.

useful_results: If two planes $P_1=0,P_2=0$ meet in a line, then every plane containing the line is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; equal ratios of coefficients is how an unknown family member is matched.
Two planes $a_1x+b_1y+c_1z=d_1$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2z=d_2$ are the same plane iff all four coefficients are proportional.
A plane contains a line iff it contains one point of the line and its normal is perpendicular to the line direction ($\vec n\cdot(\vec n_1\times\vec n_2)=0$ for a line of intersection).
When the question restricts a variable to $\mathbb Z$, solve the modulus equation and reject the non-integer root: $c=\frac43$ rejected, $c=-1$ kept.

concepts: Plane through two points parallel to a given line
questions.question: The plane, passing through the points $(0,-1,2)$ and $(-1,2,1)$ and parallel to the line passing through $(5,1,-7)$ and $(1,-1,-1)$, also passes through the point:
questions.key_idea: The normal is the cross product of the vector joining the two points and the direction of the given line.
solution: Direction of the line through $(5,1,-7)$ and $(1,-1,-1)$: $(-4,-2,6)\parallel(4,2,-6)$, which is parallel to the plane.
Normal $\vec n=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-1&3&-1\\4&2&-6\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i(-18+2)-\hat j(6+4)+\hat k(-2-12)=-16\hat i-10\hat j-14\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's first line uses the point $(0,-1,0)$; it should be $(0,-1,2)$ (its later equation $8(x-0)+5(y+1)+7(z-2)=0$ uses $(0,-1,2)$ correctly). PDF's cross product line reads $\hat i(16)-\hat j(10)+\hat k(-14)$; the correct first component is $\hat i(-18+2)=-16$, so $\vec n=(-16,-10,-14)\parallel(8,5,7)$, which is what the PDF then uses. Final plane $8x+5y+7z=9$ and answer (B) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the plane parametrically as point $+\,s\,$(vector in plane) $+\,t\,$(line direction) and solve for $(s,t)$ for each option.
solution: Parametric form: $(x,y,z)=(0,-1,2)+s(-1,3,-1)+t(2,1,-3)$, using the direction $(2,1,-3)$ of the line.
From the first, $s=2t+2$. Second: $3(2t+2)+t=6$, so $7t=0$, i.e. $t=0$ and $s=2$.
Third equation: $-2-0=-2$ holds, so $(-2,5,0)$ is on the plane.
For $(2,0,1)$: $-s+2t=2$, $3s+t=1$ give $t=1$, $s=0$, but then $-s-3t=-3\neq-1$: not on the plane.
For $(0,5,-1)$: $s=\frac{12}7,t=\frac67$ gives $-s-3t=-\frac{30}7\neq-3$; for $(1,-2,1)$: $s=-\frac37,t=\frac27$ gives $-\frac37\neq-1$. Both fail.
Hence only option (B) lies on the plane.

useful_results: Plane through $A,B$ parallel to a line with direction $\vec d$: normal $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\vec d$ (needs $\overrightarrow{AB}\not\parallel\vec d$).
A point $X$ lies on the plane iff $[\overrightarrow{AX},\overrightarrow{AB},\vec d]=0$ (scalar triple product).
Checking an option needs only substitution into the linear form $8x+5y+7z$ and comparison with $9$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point on a line and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let $N$ be the foot of perpendicular from the point $P(1,-2,3)$ on the line passing through the points $(4,5,8)$ and $(1,-7,5)$. Then the distance of $N$ from the plane $2x-2y+z+5=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: The foot $N$ is the point of the line with $\overrightarrow{PN}\perp$ line direction.
solution: Direction of the line: $(4-1,\ 5+7,\ 8-5)=(3,12,3)\parallel(1,4,1)$; through $(1,-7,5)$ it is $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+7}{4}=\frac{z-5}{1}=\lambda$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the projection formula: $N=A+\frac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$.
solution: Take $A=(1,-7,5)$ on the line and $\vec d=(1,4,1)$, $|\vec d|^2=18$.
$\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d=0+20-2=18$, so the projection coefficient is $\frac{18}{18}=1$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $\vec a+\lambda\vec d$: $\lambda=\frac{(\vec P-\vec a)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$. Here $\frac{18}{18}=1$.
Distance from a point to a line $=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$; for this $P$: $|(0,5,-2)\times(1,4,1)|/\sqrt{18}=|(13,-2,-5)|/\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{198}/\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{11}$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
Direction ratios can be scaled: $(3,12,3)$ and $(1,4,1)$ give the same line, which simplifies arithmetic.

concepts: Coplanarity of two lines
questions.question: The line that is coplanar to the line $\frac{x+3}{-3}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Two lines are coplanar iff the scalar triple product of the join of two points and the two directions is zero.
solution: The given line passes through $A(-3,1,5)$ with direction $\vec d_1=(-3,1,5)$.
For option (C), the line passes through $B(-1,2,5)$ with direction $\vec d_2=(-1,2,5)$; $\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,1,0)$ (the PDF uses $\overrightarrow{BA}=(-2,-1,0)$, same result).
Rows 1 and 2 are identical, so the determinant is $0$ and the lines are coplanar.
For the other options the same determinant has absolute value $10,\ 10$ and $5$ for (A), (B), (D) respectively, all non-zero, so they are not coplanar.

alternate_solutions.idea: Check whether the lines intersect: option (C) meets the given line at the origin.
solution: For $s=t=-1$ both lines pass through $(0,0,0)$, so they intersect and are therefore coplanar.
The other options give non-intersecting non-parallel lines (determinants of absolute value $10,10,5$), so (C) is the answer.

useful_results: Lines $\vec a_1+s\vec d_1$ and $\vec a_2+t\vec d_2$ are coplanar iff $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$, i.e. they intersect or are parallel.
In a determinant, row operations such as $R_2\to R_2-R_3$ can reveal two identical rows quickly.
If a candidate line passes through a point of the given line (here the origin, lying on both), the lines are automatically coplanar; try to spot a common point first.
Check: for option (A), $|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|=10\neq0$, so skew.

concepts: Plane through three points, foot of perpendicular and distance from origin
questions.question: Let the foot of perpendicular of the point $P(3,-2,-9)$ on the plane passing through the points $(-1,-2,-3)$, $(9,3,4)$ and $(9,-2,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then the distance of $Q$ from the origin is:
questions.key_idea: Foot of the perpendicular lies along the plane normal from $P$, which is the cross product of two edge vectors.
solution: Check that $Q$ is on the plane: $2-15+20=7$ (correct).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the normal by solving the two perpendicularity equations instead of a cross product, then use the foot formula $Q=P-\frac{\vec n\cdot P-d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.
solution: Let the normal be $(a,b,c)$; it is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{AC}=(10,0,4)$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}=(10,5,7)$.
$\vec n\cdot P-d=6-6+45-7=38$ and $|\vec n|^2=38$, so the ratio is $1$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$: $Q=P-\frac{\vec n\cdot P-d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$; the image (reflection) is $P-2\frac{\vec n\cdot P-d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.
Distance of $P$ from the plane equals $|PQ|=\frac{|\vec n\cdot P-d|}{|\vec n|}=\frac{38}{\sqrt{38}}=\sqrt{38}$ here.
Plane through three points: normal is $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$ and any scalar multiple works.
Check: $\vec n\cdot B=18+9-20=7$ and $\vec n\cdot C=18-6-5=7$, confirming that all three points lie on $2x+3y-5z=7$.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all values of $\lambda$ for which the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{0}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z+6}{1}$ and $\frac{x+\lambda}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\frac{z-6}{0}$ is $13$. Then $8\left|\sum_{\lambda\in S}\lambda\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance is the projection of the join of two points on the common perpendicular $\vec p\times\vec q$, giving a modulus equation linear in $\lambda$.
solution: Line 1 passes through $A(\lambda,3,-6)$ with direction $\vec p=(0,4,1)$; line 2 through $B(-\lambda,0,6)$ with direction $\vec q=(3,-4,0)$.
$\overrightarrow{AB}=(-2\lambda,-3,12)$ (the PDF uses $\overrightarrow{BA}=(2\lambda,3,-12)$; the modulus is the same).
$\vec p\times\vec q=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\0&4&1\\3&-4&0\end{matrix}\right|=4\hat i+3\hat j-12\hat k$, with magnitude $\sqrt{16+9+144}=13$.
Shortest distance $=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)|}{|\vec p\times\vec q|}=13$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance between the lines is the distance of $A$ from the plane through line 2 that is parallel to line 1 (normal $\vec p\times\vec q$).
solution: Common normal $\vec n=\vec p\times\vec q=(4,3,-12)$, $|\vec n|=13$.
Plane through $B(-\lambda,0,6)$ with this normal contains line 2 and is parallel to line 1: $4(x+\lambda)+3y-12(z-6)=0$.
The shortest distance between the lines equals the distance of any point of line 1, e.g. $A(\lambda,3,-6)$, from this plane.
Value at $A$: $4(2\lambda)+9-12(-12)=8\lambda+153$, so the distance is $\frac{|8\lambda+153|}{13}$.
Setting it equal to $13$: $8\lambda+153=\pm169$, so $8\lambda=16$ or $-322$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec a_1+s\vec p$ and $\vec a_2+t\vec q$: $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)|}{|\vec p\times\vec q|}$ (it is $0$ iff coplanar).
Equivalent view: distance from a point of one line to the plane through the other line that is parallel to the first.

If a distance condition contains the parameter linearly inside the modulus, there are two values $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ with sum $-\frac{2\cdot153}{8}$; here $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=2-\frac{161}{4}=-\frac{153}{4}$.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane and area of a triangle
questions.question: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,3)$ in the plane $2x-y+z=9$ be $Q$. If the coordinates of the point $R$ are $(6,10,7)$, then the square of the area of the triangle $PQR$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $R$ lies on the plane, so $R$ is equidistant from $P$ and $Q$ and $PQ$ is perpendicular to the plane; the area splits into two right triangles.
solution: Check: $R(6,10,7)$ lies on the plane since $12-10+7=9$. Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the plane, so $PQ=2PM$ and $\angle PMR=90^\circ$.
Let $\theta=\angle MPR$, the angle between $\overrightarrow{PR}$ and the normal $(2,-1,1)$: $\cos\theta=\frac{(5\hat i+8\hat j+4\hat k)\cdot(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)}{\sqrt{105}\sqrt6}$.
Hence the square of the area is $594$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $Q$ explicitly and use the cross product: $\Delta=\frac12|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|$ (area).
solution: Check the midpoint $M=(3,1,4)$ lies on the plane: $6-1+4=9$.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\4&-2&2\\5&8&4\end{matrix}\right|=(-8-16)\hat i-(16-10)\hat j+(32+10)\hat k=-24\hat i-6\hat j+42\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Right triangles: $\Delta=\frac12\,PQ\cdot MR$ with $PM$ equal to the point-plane distance.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$: $Q=P-2\frac{\vec n\cdot P-d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$; here $Q=(5,0,5)$.
If $R$ lies on the plane, then $RP=RQ$ and $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles with altitude from $R$ to $PQ$ equal to $MR$.
Area of a triangle $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|$, so area$^2=\frac14|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|^2$, avoiding square roots.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$; check $24\cdot105-(20-16+8)^2=2520-144=2376$.

concepts: Coplanarity (intersection) of two lines
questions.question: If the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{x-4}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{\beta}$ intersect, then the magnitude of the minimum value of $8\alpha\beta$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Intersection of two lines forces the triple product of the join and the two directions to vanish, giving a linear relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
solution: First line passes through $(1,2,3)$ with direction $(2,3,\alpha)$ (since $\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{y-2}{3}$); second passes through $(4,1,0)$ with direction $(5,2,\beta)$.
Vector joining the points: $(4,1,0)-(1,2,3)=(3,-1,-3)$, i.e. $-3\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k$ up to sign.
For the lines to intersect, the three vectors must be coplanar: $\left|\begin{matrix}2&3&\alpha\\5&2&\beta\\-3&1&3\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
The minimum value is $-18$ (at $\beta=-\frac32$), so its magnitude is $18$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Equate the general points of the two lines: they meet at a definite point, which gives $\alpha-\beta=3$ directly.

useful_results: Two non-parallel lines intersect iff $\left|\begin{matrix}\vec d_1\\\vec d_2\\\vec a_2-\vec a_1\end{matrix}\right|=0$ (coplanarity); parallel lines give a separate case.
The $x$ and $y$ equations alone fix the common parameters $(s,t)$ (here $s=t=-1$); the $z$ equation then gives the relation between the unknowns.
Minimum of $p(\beta)=k(\beta^2+3\beta)$ with $k>0$ is $-\frac{9k}{4}$ at $\beta=-\frac32$; with $k=8$: $-18$.
Check: $\alpha=\frac32,\beta=-\frac32$ gives $8\alpha\beta=-18$ and $\alpha-\beta=3$.

concepts: Distance of a point from a plane
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ be the values of $\lambda$ for which the points $\left(\frac52,1,\lambda\right)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are at equal distance from the plane $2x+3y-6z+7=0$. If $\lambda_1>\lambda_2$, then the distance of the point $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2,\ \lambda_2,\ \lambda_1)$ from the line $\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+7}{2}$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Equal-distance condition gives $|15-6\lambda|=3$; the point-to-line distance is then a foot-of-perpendicular computation.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of a point from a line by the cross-product formula $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
solution: Take $A(5,1,-7)$ on the line, $\vec d=(1,2,2)$, $|\vec d|=3$. $\overrightarrow{AP}=(-4,1,10)$.
$\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-4&1&10\\1&2&2\end{matrix}\right|=(2-20)\hat i-(-8-10)\hat j+(-8-1)\hat k=-18\hat i+18\hat j-9\hat k$.

useful_results: Two points are equidistant from a plane iff $|f(P_1)|=|f(P_2)|$, where $f(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz+d$: either $f(P_1)=f(P_2)$ (same side) or $f(P_1)=-f(P_2)$ (opposite sides).

Distance of a point $P$ from the line $\vec a+t\vec d$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$; also $\sqrt{|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2-\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}\right)^2}$.
Check: $|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2=16+1+100=117$, $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d=-4+2+20=18$, so $\sqrt{117-\frac{324}{9}}=\sqrt{81}=9$.
Foot of the perpendicular on a line: choose $t$ with $\overrightarrow{PM}\cdot\vec d=0$; here $t=2$.

concepts: Line of intersection of two planes and foot of the perpendicular in 3D
questions.question: Let $P_1$ be the plane $3x-y-7z=11$ and $P_2$ be the plane passing through the points $(2,-1,0)$, $(2,0,-1)$ and $(5,1,1)$. If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(7,4,-1)$ on the line of intersection of the planes $P_1$ and $P_2$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The line of intersection is along $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$, and the foot $N$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{AN}\cdot(\vec n_1\times\vec n_2)=0$.
solution: $P_2$ passes through $(2,-1,0)$ with in-plane vectors $(0,1,-1)$ and $(3,2,1)$: $\left|\begin{matrix}x-2&y+1&z\\0&1&-1\\3&2&1\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
Normals: $\vec n_1=3\hat i-\hat j-7\hat k$, $\vec n_2=\hat i-\hat j-\hat k$.
Direction of the common line: $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=-6\hat i-4\hat j-2\hat k\parallel \vec p=3\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$.
A common point: put $z=0$: $3x-y=11$ and $x-y=3$ give $x=4,\ y=1$, so $(4,1,0)$ lies on both planes.
Line: $\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=\lambda$, so a general point is $N=(3\lambda+4,\,2\lambda+1,\,\lambda)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\overrightarrow{AN}\perp$ the line means $\overrightarrow{AN}$ lies in the span of $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$; write $N=A-s\vec n_1-t\vec n_2$ and use both plane equations.
solution: $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$ is the line direction; any vector perpendicular to it lies in the plane spanned by $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$, so $N=A-s\vec n_1-t\vec n_2$.
Values: $\vec n_1\cdot A=21-4+7=24$, $\vec n_2\cdot A=7-4+1=4$, $\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_1=59$, $\vec n_2\cdot\vec n_2=3$, $\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2=11$.

useful_results: The line of intersection of planes with normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$ (nonzero when the planes are not parallel).
To get a point on the common line, set one coordinate to $0$ and solve the two plane equations (works if the line is not parallel to that coordinate plane).

Foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to a line through $Q$ with direction $\vec d$: $Q+\mu\vec d$ with $\mu=\frac{(A-Q)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$. Here $\mu=\frac{(3,3,-1)\cdot(3,2,1)}{14}=1$ from $Q=(4,1,0)$.
Plane through three points: set the $3\times3$ determinant of $(\vec r-\vec r_1,\ \vec r_2-\vec r_1,\ \vec r_3-\vec r_1)$ to $0$.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular and area of a triangle in 3D
Distance and lattice points on a plane
questions.question: Let the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A(4,3,1)$ on the plane $P: x-y+2z+3=0$ be $N$. If $B(5,\alpha,\beta)$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}$ is a point on the plane $P$ such that the area of the triangle $ABN$ is $3\sqrt2$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\alpha\beta$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $AN\perp$ plane, so $\triangle ABN$ is right-angled at $N$ and area $=\frac12\,AN\cdot BN$.
solution: $AN\perp$ plane and $BN$ lies in the plane, so $AN\perp BN$: $\overrightarrow{AN}\cdot\overrightarrow{BN}=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes '$\overrightarrow{AN}\cdot\overrightarrow{BN}=6\sqrt2$' (a dot product) from the area formula; the dot product is actually $0$ (AN is perpendicular to BN). What it means is $|AN|\,|BN|=6\sqrt2$, which is what the next line uses. Also the PDF skips the step $\alpha=2\beta+8$ substituted into $BN^2$ and the integrality filter; both added. Final answer 7 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: With $B-N=(2,m,n)$ in the plane and $BN^2=12$, integrality forces $m^2+n^2=8$, so $(m,n)=(\pm2,\pm2)$; the plane condition picks one.
solution: $BN^2=12$ gives $m^2+n^2=8$; the only integer squares summing to $8$ are $4+4$, so $|m|=|n|=2$.
Check $m=2n+2$: $n=-2\Rightarrow m=-2$ works; $n=2\Rightarrow m=6$ fails; $n=0$ or $m=2$ pairs with $n=0$ fail.

useful_results: The foot of the perpendicular from $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $(x_1,y_1,z_1)-\frac{ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d}{a^2+b^2+c^2}(a,b,c)$; the distance is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$. Here $\frac{6}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt6$.
If $AN$ is perpendicular to a plane and $B$ lies in it, then $AB^2=AN^2+NB^2$ and $[ABN]=\frac12\,AN\cdot NB$.
With integrality constraints, reduce to a sum-of-squares equation such as $m^2+n^2=8$ (only $2^2+2^2$) and test few cases.
Area of a triangle with vertices $A,B,C$ is $\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$, valid in any dimension 3 position.

concepts: Angle between a line and a plane, intersection of line and plane
questions.question: Let the line $\ell: x=\frac{1-y}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{\lambda},\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ meet the plane $P: x+2y+3z=4$ at the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. If the angle between the line $\ell$ and the plane $P$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{14}}\right)$, then $\alpha+2\beta+6\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The sine of the angle between line and plane equals $\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$; this fixes $\lambda$, then substitute the line in the plane.
solution: Rewrite the line: $x=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-3}{\lambda}$, so its direction ratios are $(1,2,\lambda)$.
The normal of $P$ has direction ratios $(1,2,3)$.
A general point of the line is $\left(t,\,2t+1,\,\frac23t+3\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\alpha+2\beta+3\gamma=4$ (point on the plane) to write the target as $4+3\gamma$, and get $\lambda$ from Lagrange's identity $|\vec d\times\vec n|^2$.
solution: $\vec d=(1,2,\lambda)$, $\vec n=(1,2,3)$: $\vec d\times\vec n=(6-2\lambda,\ \lambda-3,\ 0)$, so $|\vec d\times\vec n|^2=5(\lambda-3)^2$.
For the angle $\theta$ between line and plane, $|\vec d\times\vec n|=|\vec d||\vec n|\cos\theta$ (cosine of the angle with the plane).

useful_results: Angle $\theta$ between a line (direction $\vec d$) and a plane (normal $\vec n$): $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec d\times\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$.
If a point lies on $ax+by+cz=k$, any linear expression with coefficients proportional to $(a,b,c)$ can be reduced using $k$: here $\alpha+2\beta+6\gamma=4+3\gamma$.
Line meets plane: substitute the parametric point of the line into the plane; unique solution iff $\vec d\cdot\vec n\ne0$.
When the cosine of the line-plane angle is given, convert to sine first; mixing the two is the commonest slip.

concepts: Plane intercepts on the axes and orthocentre of a triangle in 3D
questions.question: Let the plane $x+3y-2z+6=0$ meet the co-ordinate axes at the points $A$, $B$, $C$. If the orthocenter of the triangle $ABC$ is $\left(\alpha,\beta,\frac67\right)$, then $98(\alpha+\beta)^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Orthocentre $H$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ and $\overrightarrow{CH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=0$ (the $z$-coordinate is given).
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=6\hat i-2\hat j$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=2\hat j+3\hat k$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=6\hat i+3\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $OA,OB,OC$ are mutually perpendicular, so the orthocentre of $ABC$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the plane.
solution: $OA\perp$ plane $OBC$, so $OA\perp BC$. If $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to plane $ABC$, then $OH\perp BC$ too.
Hence $BC\perp$ plane $OAH$, so $BC\perp AH$: $H$ lies on the altitude from $A$. Similarly it lies on the altitude from $B$ (and $C$).
So $H$ is the orthocentre. The foot from $O$ to $x+3y-2z+6=0$ is $H=-\frac{6}{14}(1,3,-2)=\left(-\frac37,-\frac97,\frac67\right)$.
The $z$-coordinate $\frac67$ matches the given data, confirming the identification.

useful_results: If the three edges $OA,OB,OC$ from a vertex are mutually perpendicular, the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to plane $ABC$.
For the plane $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ this foot is $\frac{(1/a,\,1/b,\,1/c)}{1/a^2+1/b^2+1/c^2}$; with $(a,b,c)=(-6,-2,3)$ it gives $\left(-\frac37,-\frac97,\frac67\right)$.
Altitude conditions in coordinates: $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ and $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=0$; $H$ is also in the plane (here automatically).
Plane meeting the axes at $(a,0,0),(0,b,0),(0,0,c)$ is $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$; $x+3y-2z+6=0$ becomes $\frac{x}{-6}+\frac{y}{-2}+\frac{z}{3}=1$.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane and distance between points in 3D
questions.question: Let the image of the point $\left(\frac53,\frac53,\frac83\right)$ in the plane $x-2y+z-2=0$ be $P$. If the distance of the point $Q(6,-2,\alpha),\ \alpha>0$, from $P$ is $13$, then $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The image lies along the normal: $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c}=\frac{-2(ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflection in a plane is a Householder map: $P=X_0+\left(I-\frac{2\vec n\vec n^{T}}{|\vec n|^2}\right)(T-X_0)$ for any point $X_0$ on the plane.
solution: Take $X_0=(2,0,0)$ on the plane ($2-0+0-2=0$). Then $T-X_0=\left(-\frac13,\frac53,\frac83\right)$ with $T=\left(\frac53,\frac53,\frac83\right)$.

useful_results: Image of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ in $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $(x_1,y_1,z_1)-\frac{2(ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}(a,b,c)$; the foot is the midpoint of the point and its image.
Reflection preserves distances and fixes points of the plane; image of $T$ is at the same distance from the plane, on the opposite side.
Distance formula in 3D: $PQ^2=\sum(\Delta x)^2$; always check the sign condition (here $\alpha>0$) to reject the extra root.
Numerical check: $P=(2,1,3)$ gives $2-2+3-2=1=-(-1)$, so $P$ is on the other side of the plane at equal signed value.

concepts: Pencil of planes and plane parallel to a line
Distance from a point to a plane measured along a line
questions.question: Let the plane $P$ contain the line $2x+y-z-3=0=5x-3y+4z+9$ and be parallel to the line $\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{3-y}{-4}=\frac{z-7}{5}$. Then the distance of the point $A(8,-1,-19)$ from the plane $P$ measured parallel to the line $\frac{x}{-3}=\frac{y-5}{4}=\frac{2-z}{-12}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Plane $=P_1+\lambda P_2$ with $\vec n\cdot\vec b=0$; then intersect the line through $A$ in the given direction with the plane.
solution: The given line has direction $\vec b=(2,4,5)$; parallel to it means $\vec n\cdot\vec b=0$.
The line through $A$ parallel to $\frac{x}{-3}=\frac{y-5}{4}=\frac{z-2}{12}$ is $\frac{x-8}{-3}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z+19}{12}=\lambda$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Get the normal as (direction of the given line) $\times$ (direction $\vec b$), then use distance along a direction $=\frac{|\vec n\cdot A-k|\,|\vec d|}{|\vec n\cdot\vec d|}$.
solution: $P$ contains this direction and is parallel to $\vec b=(2,4,5)$: $\vec n=(1,-13,-11)\times(2,4,5)=(-21,-27,30)\parallel(7,9,-10)$.
A point of the given line: $z=0$ gives $2x+y=3$, $5x-3y=-9$, so $(0,3,0)$. Then $k=7\cdot0+9\cdot3=27$ and $P: 7x+9y-10z=27$.

useful_results: A plane containing the line of intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (pencil of planes); it is parallel to a vector $\vec b$ iff $\vec n\cdot\vec b=0$.

Distance of $A$ from plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ measured along direction $\vec d$ is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot A-k|}{|\vec n\cdot\vec d|}\,|\vec d|$ (requires $\vec n\cdot\vec d\ne0$); it equals the perpendicular distance divided by $|\cos\phi|$.
Plane through a line (direction $\vec u$, point $Q$) and parallel to $\vec b$ has normal $\vec u\times\vec b$.
Check here: perpendicular distance $\frac{210}{\sqrt{230}}$, $\cos\phi=\frac{105}{13\sqrt{230}}$, ratio $=26$.

concepts: Intersection of a line with planes in 3D
Trigonometric identities for the angles of a triangle
questions.question: If the line $x=y=z$ intersects the line $x\sin A+y\sin B+z\sin C-18=0=x\sin 2A+y\sin 2B+z\sin 2C-9$, where $A,B,C$ are the angles of a triangle $ABC$, then $80\left(\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: A common point $x=y=z=k$ lies on both planes; dividing the two equations turns triangle sine-sums into $\prod\sin\frac A2$.
solution: Using $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C=4\cos\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2$: $k\left(4\cos\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2\right)=18$ ...(i)
Using $\sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C$: $k(4\sin A\sin B\sin C)=9$ ...(ii)
(ii)/(i): $\frac{\sin A\sin B\sin C}{\cos\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2}=\frac{9}{18}$.
Since $\sin A=2\sin\frac A2\cos\frac A2$ etc., the left side is $8\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$.
So $8\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2=\frac12$, hence $80\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In terms of triangle elements the ratio is $\frac{\sum\sin2A}{\sum\sin A}=\frac{2r}{R}$, and $\frac rR=4\prod\sin\frac A2$.
solution: With $x=y=z=k$ the two equations give $\frac{\sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C}{\sin A+\sin B+\sin C}=\frac{9}{18}=\frac12$.

useful_results: In a triangle: $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C=4\cos\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2$ and $\sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C$ (since $A+B+C=\pi$).
$\frac rR=4\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2=\cos A+\cos B+\cos C-1$; always $\frac rR\le\frac12$ (Euler), with equality only for the equilateral triangle.
Two lines meet iff the system of their equations has a common point; with $x=y=z=k$ each plane equation becomes a linear equation in $k$ (consistency needs the ratio of constants to match).
Numerical check: for $r/R=\frac14$ take $A=B\approx 0.548$ rad: $\sum\sin2A/\sum\sin A\approx0.5$ and $80\prod\sin\frac A2\approx5$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and cross product identities
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=3(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$. Let $\vec c$ be the vector such that $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$. Then $\vec a\cdot\big((\vec c\times\vec b)-\vec b-\vec c\big)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Dot $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ with $\vec b$: $[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec b]=|\vec b|^2$, and $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec b]$.
solution: Dot the given $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ with $\vec b$: $(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec b$.
The expression expands as $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)-\vec a\cdot\vec b-\vec a\cdot\vec c$.
$\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec b]=27$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $\vec c$ explicitly from $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$, then compute directly.
solution: Since $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$, the solution is $\vec c=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a+\vec b\times\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}$ (check: $\vec a\times\vec c=\frac{\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec a)}{|\vec a|^2}=\vec b$).
Check: $\vec a\times\vec c=(3,-3,3)=\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-1+2+2=3$.
$\vec c\times\vec b=(-1,1,2)\times(3,-3,3)=(9,9,0)$, so $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=9+18=27$.

useful_results: $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$ is unchanged by cyclic permutation and changes sign on swapping two vectors: $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=-[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$.
If $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ then $\vec b\perp\vec a$, $\vec b\perp\vec c$, and $[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec b]=|\vec b|^2$; a solution exists only if $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
General solution of $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ (with $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$): $\vec c=\frac{\vec b\times\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}+t\vec a$, and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=t|\vec a|^2$ fixes $t$.
Here $t=\frac12$, giving $\vec c=(-1,1,2)$.

concepts: Orthocentre and distances in a triangle (vectors)
questions.question: Let the position vectors of the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of a triangle be $2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$ and $2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ respectively. Let $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and $\ell_3$ be the lengths of perpendiculars drawn from the orthocenter of the triangle on the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ respectively, then $\ell_1^2+\ell_2^2+\ell_3^2$ equals :
questions.key_idea: All three sides equal $\sqrt2$, so the triangle is equilateral and its orthocentre is the centroid, equidistant from the sides.
solution: $AB^2=1+0+1=2$, $BC^2=0+1+1=2$, $CA^2=0+1+1=2$: the triangle is equilateral with side $\sqrt2$.
In an equilateral triangle the orthocentre is the centroid $G$, and $G$ is at one third of the height from each side.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each $\ell$ is the inradius $r=\frac{\Delta}{s}$ (orthocentre = incentre), and $\Delta=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$.
solution: For the equilateral triangle the orthocentre coincides with the incentre, so $\ell=r=\frac{\Delta}{s}=\frac{\sqrt3/2}{3\sqrt2/2}=\frac1{\sqrt6}$.

useful_results: In an equilateral triangle of side $a$, the orthocentre, centroid, circumcentre and incentre coincide; each is at distance $\frac{a\sqrt3}{6}$ from every side.

Three equal side lengths of the form $\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2+(\Delta z)^2}=\sqrt2$ for points $(2,2,1),(1,2,2),(2,1,2)$ signal a symmetric triangle: check side lengths before computing the orthocentre.
Area of a triangle with vertex vectors: $\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$; here $=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot2$.
The three points lie on $x+y+z=5$, with normal $(1,1,1)$ matching the cross product.

concepts: Angle bisector and distance in a triangle (vectors)
questions.question: The position vectors of the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of a triangle are $2\hat i-3\hat j+3\hat k$, $2\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$ and $-\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k$ respectively. Let $l$ denote the length of the angle bisector $AD$ of $\angle BAC$ where $D$ is on the line segment $BC$, then $2l^2$ equals :
questions.key_idea: $AB=AC=5$, so the bisector from $A$ is also the median and $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.
solution: In an isosceles triangle the bisector of the apex angle meets $BC$ at its midpoint $D$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the bisector-length formula $AD^2=bc\left[1-\frac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}\right]$, which needs only the three side lengths.

useful_results: Length of the internal bisector from $A$: $AD^2=bc\left[1-\frac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}\right]=\frac{4bc\,s(s-a)}{(b+c)^2}$ (valid for any triangle).
Angle bisector theorem: $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$; if $AB=AC$ then $D$ is the midpoint and $AD$ is also the altitude.

Check on a 3-4-5 triangle with right angle at $A$ ($b=3,c=4,a=5$): $AD^2=12\left[1-\frac{25}{49}\right]=\frac{288}{49}$, and direct: $AD=\frac{bc\sqrt2}{b+c}=\frac{12\sqrt2}{7}$, squares to $\frac{288}{49}$.
Third vertex data ($z=3$ throughout) means the triangle is planar in $z=3$: treat it as a 2D problem.

concepts: Internal angle bisector theorem (vectors)
questions.question: Let $O$ be the origin and the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ be $2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ and $2\hat i+4\hat j+4\hat k$ respectively. If the internal bisector of $\angle AOB$ meets the line $AB$ at $C$, then the length of $OC$ is :
questions.key_idea: Angle bisector theorem: $AC:CB=OA:OB$, so $C$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $|OA|:|OB|$.
solution: By the internal angle bisector theorem $AC:CB=OA:OB=3:6=1:2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The bisector of $\angle AOB$ has direction $\hat a+\hat b$ (sum of unit vectors); intersect that line with $AB$.

useful_results: Internal bisector of $\angle AOB$ has direction $\frac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}+\frac{\vec b}{|\vec b|}$ and meets $AB$ at $C=\frac{|\vec b|\,\vec a+|\vec a|\,\vec b}{|\vec a|+|\vec b|}$.
Length of the bisector: $OC^2=|\vec a||\vec b|\left[1-\frac{AB^2}{(|\vec a|+|\vec b|)^2}\right]$. Here $AB^2=0+4+9=13$: $18\left(1-\frac{13}{81}\right)=\frac{136}{9}$.
The external bisector divides $AB$ externally in the same ratio $|\vec a|:|\vec b|$.
In a quadrilateral/triangle problem with a vertex at the origin, always compare $|OA|$ and $|OB|$ first for the ratio.

concepts: Collinear and linearly dependent vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ be three non-zero vectors such that $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are non-collinear. If $\vec a+5\vec b$ is collinear with $\vec c$, $\vec b+6\vec c$ is collinear with $\vec a$ and $\vec a+\alpha\vec b+\beta\vec c=\vec 0$, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Collinearity gives $\vec a+5\vec b=\lambda\vec c$ and $\vec b+6\vec c=\mu\vec a$; eliminating $\vec a$ and comparing coefficients of independent $\vec b,\vec c$ gives the scalars.
solution: $\vec a+5\vec b$ collinear with $\vec c$: $\vec a+5\vec b=\lambda\vec c$.
$\vec b+6\vec c$ collinear with $\vec a$: $\vec b+6\vec c=\mu\vec a$, so $\vec a=\frac{\vec b+6\vec c}{\mu}$ (note $\mu\ne0$).
Eliminate $\vec a$: $\frac{\vec b+6\vec c}{\mu}+5\vec b=\lambda\vec c$, i.e. $\lambda\vec c-5\vec b=\frac6\mu\vec c+\frac1\mu\vec b$.
$\vec b,\vec c$ are non-collinear, so coefficients match: $-5=\frac1\mu$ and $\lambda=\frac6\mu$.
Then $\vec a+5\vec b=-30\vec c$, i.e. $\vec a+5\vec b+30\vec c=\vec0$.
Comparing with $\vec a+\alpha\vec b+\beta\vec c=\vec 0$: $\alpha=5$, $\beta=30$ (the relation is unique since $\vec b,\vec c$ are independent).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $\vec a=-(\alpha\vec b+\beta\vec c)$ into both collinearity conditions and compare coefficients of the independent vectors $\vec b,\vec c$.
solution: From the given relation $\vec a=-\alpha\vec b-\beta\vec c$.
$\vec a+5\vec b=(5-\alpha)\vec b-\beta\vec c$ is collinear with $\vec c$, so the coefficient of $\vec b$ vanishes: $5-\alpha=0$, $\alpha=5$.
$\vec b+6\vec c$ is collinear with $\vec a=-(5\vec b+\beta\vec c)$, so $(1,6)\parallel(5,\beta)$ in the basis $\{\vec b,\vec c\}$.

useful_results: If $\vec b,\vec c$ are non-collinear, then $x\vec b+y\vec c=\vec0$ implies $x=y=0$; use this to compare coefficients.
$\vec u\parallel\vec c$ with $\vec u=p\vec b+q\vec c$ and $\vec b,\vec c$ independent forces $p=0$.
$p\vec b+q\vec c\parallel p'\vec b+q'\vec c$ iff $pq'=p'q$ (same ratio of coefficients).
Check: $\vec a=-5\vec b-30\vec c$ gives $\vec a+5\vec b=-30\vec c$ and $\vec b+6\vec c=-\frac15\vec a$.

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral and parallelogram using vector product
questions.question: Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\vec a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=12\vec a+4\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\vec b$, where $O$ is the origin. If $S$ is the parallelogram with adjacent sides $OA$ and $OC$, then (area of the quadrilateral $OABC$) / (area of $S$) is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Split the quadrilateral $OABC$ by the diagonal $OB$ into triangles $OAB$ and $OBC$ and use half the magnitude of the cross product.
solution: Area of the parallelogram: $S=|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
$[\triangle OAB]=\frac12|\vec a\times(12\vec a+4\vec b)|=\frac12\cdot4|\vec a\times\vec b|=2|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
$[\triangle OBC]=\frac12|(12\vec a+4\vec b)\times\vec b|=\frac12\cdot12|\vec a\times\vec b|=6|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
Total area $=2|\vec a\times\vec b|+6|\vec a\times\vec b|=8|\vec a\times\vec b|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Area ratios are preserved by an affine map, so take $\vec a=(1,0)$, $\vec b=(0,1)$ and use the shoelace formula.
solution: Choose $\vec a=(1,0)$, $\vec b=(0,1)$ (independent, so any pair is an affine image; area ratios are unchanged).
Then $O(0,0)$, $A(1,0)$, $B(12,4)$, $C(0,1)$ and $S$ is the unit square, area $1$.

useful_results: Area of a quadrilateral $OABC$ (convex) $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$: here $\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec b-\vec a$ and $\frac12|(12\vec a+4\vec b)\times(\vec b-\vec a)|=\frac12|12+4||\vec a\times\vec b|=8|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
Area of a triangle with sides $\vec p,\vec q$ from a vertex is $\frac12|\vec p\times\vec q|$; of the parallelogram is $|\vec p\times\vec q|$.
Ratios of areas are invariant under linear (affine) maps, so special coordinates can be used for $\vec a,\vec b$ independent.
For $\overrightarrow{OB}=x\vec a+y\vec b$ with $x,y>0$, area of $OABC$ is $\frac{x+y}{2}|\vec a\times\vec b|$; here $x+y=16$.

concepts: Dot product and angle between vectors
Linear equations in direction components
questions.question: Let a unit vector $\hat u=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ make angles $\frac\pi2,\frac\pi3$ and $\frac{2\pi}3$ with the vectors $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$, $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$ and $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j$ respectively. If $\vec v=\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$ then $|\hat u-\vec v|^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Each angle condition is a linear equation in $x,y,z$; solve the three equations, then compute $|\hat u-\vec v|^2$.
solution: Let $\vec p_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,1)$, $\vec p_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,1)$, $\vec p_3=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,0)$; each is a unit vector and $|\hat u|=1$.
Angle $\frac\pi2$ with $\vec p_1$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_1=0$, so $\frac{x}{\sqrt2}+\frac{z}{\sqrt2}=0$, i.e. $x+z=0$ ...(i)
Angle $\frac\pi3$ with $\vec p_2$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_2=\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12$, so $\frac y{\sqrt2}+\frac z{\sqrt2}=\frac12$, i.e. $y+z=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ ...(ii)
Angle $\frac{2\pi}3$ with $\vec p_3$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_3=\cos\frac{2\pi}3=-\frac12$, so $\frac x{\sqrt2}+\frac y{\sqrt2}=-\frac12$, i.e. $x+y=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ ...(iii)
questions.correction_note: PDF's third condition has a typo: it writes '$\frac{x}{\sqrt2}+\frac{4}{\sqrt2}=\frac{-1}{2}$' where the second term should be $\frac{y}{\sqrt2}$ (giving $x+y=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$, which is what it then uses). Also the PDF's line $|\hat u-\vec v|^2=\left(\sqrt{\frac42+\frac12}\right)^2$ is terse; written out in full. Final answer is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $|\hat u-\vec v|^2=|\hat u|^2+|\vec v|^2-2\hat u\cdot\vec v$; adding the three conditions gives $x+y+z=0$, so $\hat u\cdot\vec v=0$.
solution: $|\hat u|^2=1$ and $|\vec v|^2=\frac32$ (note $\vec v$ is not a unit vector).

useful_results: Angle conditions with known vectors become linear equations: $\hat u\cdot\vec p=|\vec p|\cos\theta$; use $|\hat u|=1$ only as a consistency check (here $x^2+y^2+z^2=\frac12+0+\frac12=1$).
$|\vec u-\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2+|\vec v|^2-2\vec u\cdot\vec v$; remember $|\vec v|^2=\frac32$ when $\vec v=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,1)$.
Three independent linear equations of the form $x+z=p,\ y+z=q,\ x+y=r$ give $x+y+z=\frac{p+q+r}{2}$; subtract each to get the individual values.
Cosines of $\frac\pi2,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3$ are $0,\frac12,-\frac12$ - watch the sign for obtuse angles.

concepts: Angle between two vectors (dot product)
questions.question: Let $P(3,2,3)$, $Q(4,6,2)$ and $R(7,3,2)$ be three vertices of $\triangle PQR$. Then the angle $\angle QPR$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\angle QPR$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{PR}$, so one dot product decides it.
solution: $\angle QPR$ is the angle at $P$ between $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{PR}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute all three side lengths: if they are equal, the triangle is equilateral and every angle is $60^\circ$.
solution: All three sides equal $\sqrt{18}$, so $\triangle PQR$ is equilateral.

useful_results: Angle between $\vec u,\vec v$: $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{|\vec u||\vec v|}$; the angle at a vertex uses the two vectors that start from that vertex.
Three equal side lengths force an equilateral triangle, so all angles are $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and no dot product is needed.
If $|\vec u|=|\vec v|$ then $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{|\vec u|^2}$; here $\frac{9}{18}=\frac12$.

concepts: Dot product, cross product and Lagrange identity
questions.question: Let $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ and $\vec b=b_1\hat i+b_2\hat j+b_3\hat k$ be two vectors such that $|\vec a|=1$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$ and $|\vec b|=4$. If $\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$, then the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-3|\vec b|^2$ and $|\vec c|^2=4|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+9|\vec b|^2$.
solution: Given $|\vec a|=1$, $|\vec b|=4$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$ and $\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$.
Dot with $\vec a$: $\vec c\cdot\vec a=2(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a-3\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=0-6=-6$ (the PDF records this as relation (1); it is not needed further).
Dot with $\vec b$: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b-3|\vec b|^2=0-48=-48$.
Since $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$ the cross term vanishes, so $|\vec c|^2=4|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+9|\vec b|^2$.
By the Lagrange identity $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=16-4=12$.
questions.correction_note: Typo only: the PDF writes $|\vec c|^2=4|\vec a\times\vec b|+9|\vec b|^2$ (missing square on $|\vec a\times\vec b|$) and omits the reason the cross term vanishes; the subsequent numbers (12, 144, 192) are right. Answer (C) is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose coordinates: $\vec a=\hat i$ and $\vec b=(2,2\sqrt3,0)$ fit the given data, which makes every vector explicit.
solution: Take $\vec a=(1,0,0)$. We need $|\vec b|=4$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$, so $b_1=2$ and $b_2^2=12$; take $\vec b=(2,2\sqrt3,0)$.
The angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ depends only on the given magnitudes and $\vec a\cdot\vec b$, so this choice loses no generality.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec c$ splits into a part $-3\vec b$ along $\vec b$ and a part $2(\vec a\times\vec b)$ perpendicular to $\vec b$, so $\tan$ of the angle is a ratio of lengths.
solution: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=16-4=12$, so $|2(\vec a\times\vec b)|=4\sqrt3$ and this part is perpendicular to $\vec b$.
The part along $\vec b$ is $-3\vec b$, of length $12$, pointing opposite to $\vec b$.
The angle $\theta$ between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is obtuse with $\tan(\pi-\theta)=\frac{4\sqrt3}{12}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.

useful_results: Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$; here $16-4=12$.

$\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a=(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$ and $|\vec x+\vec y|^2=|\vec x|^2+|\vec y|^2$ for $\vec x=2(\vec a\times\vec b),\vec y=-3\vec b$.
If $\vec c=\vec p+\vec q$ with $\vec p\perp\vec q$, the angle of $\vec c$ with $\vec q$ satisfies $\tan\phi=\frac{|\vec p|}{|\vec q|}$.
Here $\cos\theta=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so $\theta=150^\circ$.

concepts: Area of a parallelogram using diagonals (cross product)
questions.question: Let $A(2,3,5)$ and $C(-3,4,-2)$ be opposite vertices of a parallelogram $ABCD$. If the diagonal $\vec{BD}=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, then the area of the parallelogram is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area of a parallelogram $=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ with $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ its diagonals.
solution: So $\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}=17\hat i+8\hat j-11\hat k$; the PDF has the opposite overall sign $(-17,-8,11)$ and the magnitude is the same.
questions.correction_note: Sign slip: $\vec{AC}\times\vec{BD}=(17,8,-11)$, not $(-17,-8,11)$ as printed (the PDF's cross-product row is $-5,1,-7$ over $1,2,3$). Magnitude and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $B$ and $D$ from the common midpoint of the diagonals and compute the area as $|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AD}|$.

useful_results: Area of a parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ (since $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=2\,\vec{AB}\times\vec{AD}$ in magnitude).
Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other: $\frac{A+C}{2}=\frac{B+D}{2}$.
Area of a triangle with vertices $A,B,C$ is $\frac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$.

concepts: Perpendicular lines in 3D and direction of the common perpendicular (cross product)
questions.question: Let $L_1:\vec r=(\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k),\ \lambda\in\mathbb R$, $L_2:\vec r=(\hat j-\hat k)+\mu(3\hat i+\hat j+p\hat k),\ \mu\in\mathbb R$ and $L_3:\vec r=\delta(\ell\hat i+m\hat j+n\hat k),\ \delta\in\mathbb R$ be three lines such that $L_1$ is perpendicular to $L_2$ and $L_3$ is perpendicular to both $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then the point which lies on $L_3$ is:
questions.key_idea: $L_3$ passes through the origin and is parallel to $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$, so its points are multiples of that cross product.
solution: Direction vectors: $\vec d_1=(1,-1,2)$ for $L_1$ and $\vec d_2=(3,1,p)$ for $L_2$.
$L_3$ is perpendicular to both lines, so its direction is parallel to $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ with $\vec d_2=(3,1,-1)$.
$\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-1&2\\3&1&-1\end{matrix}\right|=(1-2)\hat i-(-1-6)\hat j+(1+3)\hat k=-\hat i+7\hat j+4\hat k$.
$L_3:\vec r=\delta(\ell\hat i+m\hat j+n\hat k)$ passes through the origin with direction $(\ell,m,n)\parallel(-1,7,4)$.
The PDF takes $(\ell,m,n)=(-1,7,4)$; with $\delta=1$ the point $(-1,7,4)$ lies on $L_3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let the options do the work: the point on $L_3$ must give a vector perpendicular to both $\vec d_1$ and $\vec d_2$.
solution: As before $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=0$ gives $p=-1$, so $\vec d_2=(3,1,-1)$ and $\vec d_1=(1,-1,2)$.
Any point $(x,y,z)$ of $L_3$ (a line through the origin) satisfies $\vec r\cdot\vec d_1=0$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec d_2=0$, i.e. $x-y+2z=0$ and $3x+y-z=0$.

useful_results: A line perpendicular to two non-parallel lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is parallel to $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
Lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ are perpendicular iff $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=0$ (no need for them to meet).
A line $\vec r=\delta\vec v$ through the origin contains the point $P$ iff $P$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec v$; here $(-1,7,4)=1\cdot\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
The cross product is checked by $\vec d_1\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0=\vec d_2\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)$.

concepts: Cross product magnitude and orthogonality of $\vec b\times\vec a$ with $\vec b$
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two vectors such that $|\vec b|=1$ and $|\vec b\times\vec a|=2$. Then $\left|\left(\vec b\times\vec a\right)-\vec b\right|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec b\times\vec a\perp\vec b$, so $|\vec x-\vec b|^2=|\vec x|^2+|\vec b|^2$ with no cross term.
solution: Expand: $\left|(\vec b\times\vec a)-\vec b\right|^2=|\vec b\times\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2\,(\vec b\times\vec a)\cdot\vec b$.
$\vec b\times\vec a$ is perpendicular to $\vec b$, so $(\vec b\times\vec a)\cdot\vec b=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Special case: $\vec b\times\vec a$ is always perpendicular to $\vec b$, so a convenient pair of perpendicular vectors will do, e.g. $\vec b=\hat i$, $\vec a=2\hat j$.
