solution: Only $|\vec b|=1$ and $|\vec b\times\vec a|=2$ are given, and the expression depends only on these two lengths together with $\vec b\perp(\vec b\times\vec a)$, so any consistent pair works.
Take $\vec b=\hat i$ and $\vec a=2\hat j$: then $|\vec b|=1$ and $\vec b\times\vec a=2\hat k$ with $|\vec b\times\vec a|=2$.
Geometrically the two vectors $\vec b\times\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are perpendicular, so by Pythagoras $|\cdot|^2=2^2+1^2=5$.

useful_results: For perpendicular $\vec x,\vec y$: $|\vec x\pm\vec y|^2=|\vec x|^2+|\vec y|^2$ (Pythagoras).
$\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a=(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$.
$\vec b\times\vec a=-(\vec a\times\vec b)$, so its magnitude is the same: $|\vec b\times\vec a|=|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
General: $|\vec x\pm\vec y|^2=|\vec x|^2+|\vec y|^2\pm2\,\vec x\cdot\vec y$.

concepts: Dot and cross product of vectors, angle between vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\alpha\hat j+\beta\hat k,\ \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$. Let a vector $\vec b$ be such that the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $|\vec b|^2=6$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3\sqrt2$, then the value of $(\alpha^2+\beta^2)\left|\vec a\times\vec b\right|^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$ gives $|\vec a|^2=6$, hence $\alpha^2+\beta^2=5$; then $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2\sin^2\frac{\pi}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the Lagrange identity $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ so no angle is needed once $|\vec a|^2$ is known.
solution: From $|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=3\sqrt2$ with $|\vec b|=\sqrt6$ we get $|\vec a|^2=6$, so $\alpha^2+\beta^2=5$.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=6\cdot6-(3\sqrt2)^2$.

useful_results: Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$.
At $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\vec a\cdot\vec b$ because $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$ (here both equal $3\sqrt2$, and $18=(3\sqrt2)^2$).
For $\vec a=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$, $|\vec a|^2=x^2+y^2+z^2$, so a given length fixes the sum of squares of the unknown components.
Length of $\vec a$ from the dot product: $|\vec a|=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|\cos\theta}$.

concepts: Line perpendicular to two lines (cross product)
Distance of a point from a line in 3D
questions.question: The distance of the point $Q(0,2,-2)$ from the line passing through the point $P(5,-4,3)$ and perpendicular to the lines $\vec r=(-3\hat i+2\hat k)+\lambda(2\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k),\ \lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $\vec r=(\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k)+\mu(-\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k),\ \mu\in\mathbb R$ is:
questions.key_idea: The required line is parallel to the cross product of the two directions; then drop a perpendicular from $Q$ by $\vec{AP}\cdot\vec d=0$.
solution: The direction of the required line is the cross product of $(2,3,5)$ and $(-1,3,2)$.
$\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&3&5\\-1&3&2\end{matrix}\right|=(6-15)\hat i-(4+5)\hat j+(6+3)\hat k=-9\hat i-9\hat j+9\hat k$, parallel to $\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$.
Required line: $\vec r=(5\hat i-4\hat j+3\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)$.
Let the foot of the perpendicular from $A(0,2,-2)$ be $P'=(5+\lambda,\,\lambda-4,\,3-\lambda)$; then $\vec{AP'}=(5+\lambda,\;\lambda-6,\;5-\lambda)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the point-to-line distance formula $\frac{|\vec{PQ}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ directly, avoiding the foot of the perpendicular.
solution: Direction of the line (as in the main solution): $\vec d=(1,1,-1)$ with $|\vec d|^2=3$.
$\vec{PQ}\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-5&6&-5\\1&1&-1\end{matrix}\right|=(-6+5)\hat i-(5+5)\hat j+(-5-6)\hat k=(-1,-10,-11)$.

useful_results: A line perpendicular to two lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ has direction $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
Distance of $Q$ from the line through $P$ with direction $\vec d$: $\frac{|\vec{PQ}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ (equivalently $\sqrt{|\vec{PQ}|^2-\left(\frac{\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}\right)^2}$).
The foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ is at parameter $\lambda=\frac{\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$ along the line.

concepts: Vector equation $\vec p\times\vec b=\vec c\times\vec b$ (parallel vectors) and dot product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$, $\vec b=4\hat i+\hat j+7\hat k$ and $\vec c=\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$ be three vectors. If a vector $\vec p$ satisfies $\vec p\times\vec b=\vec c\times\vec b$ and $\vec p\cdot\vec a=0$, then $\vec p\cdot(\hat i-\hat j-\hat k)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec p\times\vec b=\vec c\times\vec b$ means $(\vec p-\vec c)\parallel\vec b$, so $\vec p=\vec c+\lambda\vec b$ and $\vec p\cdot\vec a=0$ fixes $\lambda$.
solution: $\vec p\times\vec b-\vec c\times\vec b=\vec 0$, so $(\vec p-\vec c)\times\vec b=\vec 0$ and hence $(\vec p-\vec c)\parallel\vec b$.
So $\vec p-\vec c=\lambda\vec b$, i.e. $\vec p=\lambda\vec b+\vec c$.
$\vec p\cdot\vec a=0$ gives $\lambda\,\vec b\cdot\vec a+\vec c\cdot\vec a=0$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec a=12+1-14=-1$ and $\vec c\cdot\vec a=3-3-8=-8$, so $-\lambda-8=0$ and $\lambda=-8$.
The PDF writes the equation as $0=\lambda(12+1-14)+(3-3-8)$, which is the same, giving $\lambda=-8$.
$\vec p=\vec c-8\vec b=(1-32)\hat i+(-3-8)\hat j+(4-56)\hat k=-31\hat i-11\hat j-52\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the component equations of $\vec p\times\vec b=\vec c\times\vec b$ and notice that only $y$ is needed for $x-y-z$.
solution: Let $\vec p=(x,y,z)$. $\vec c\times\vec b=(1,-3,4)\times(4,1,7)=(-25,\,9,\,13)$ and $\vec p\times\vec b=(7y-z,\;4z-7x,\;x-4y)$.
Equating: $7y-z=-25$, $4z-7x=9$, $x-4y=13$ (these are dependent; two are enough). Also $\vec p\cdot\vec a=0$: $3x+y-2z=0$.
Hence $\vec p\cdot(\hat i-\hat j-\hat k)=32$ (and $\vec p=(-31,-11,-52)$).

useful_results: $\vec x\times\vec b=\vec y\times\vec b\iff(\vec x-\vec y)\parallel\vec b$: the solutions form the line $\vec y+\lambda\vec b$.
Adding $\vec p\cdot\vec a=0$ picks the single point where that line meets the plane through the origin perpendicular to $\vec a$ (valid when $\vec a\cdot\vec b\neq0$; here $-1$).
Similarly $\vec x\cdot\vec b=\vec y\cdot\vec b$ would fix only the component along $\vec b$; a cross and a dot condition together determine $\vec p$ uniquely.

concepts: Vector triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=-5\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k$, $\vec b=\hat i+2\hat j-4\hat k$ and $\vec c=\left(\left(\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)\times\hat i\right)\times\hat i\right)\times\hat i$. Then $\vec c\cdot\left(-\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $(\vec v\times\hat i)\times\hat i=(\vec v\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec v$, so three crosses with $\hat i$ collapse to a single cross product.
solution: Triple product: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\hat i=(\vec a\cdot\hat i)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\hat i)\vec a$.
$\vec a\cdot\hat i=-5$ and $\vec b\cdot\hat i=1$, so $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\hat i=-5\vec b-\vec a$.
Next cross: $(-11\hat j+23\hat k)\times\hat i=11\hat k+23\hat j$ (using $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$, $\hat k\times\hat i=\hat j$).
Last cross: $(23\hat j+11\hat k)\times\hat i=-23\hat k+11\hat j$ (using $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$, $\hat k\times\hat i=\hat j$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $(\vec u\times\hat i)\times\hat i=(\vec u\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec u$ twice, so the three crossings reduce to $\vec c=\hat i\times(\vec a\times\vec b)$.
solution: Let $\vec w=\vec a\times\vec b$. Identity: $(\vec w\times\hat i)\times\hat i=-\hat i\times(\vec w\times\hat i)=-\left[\vec w(\hat i\cdot\hat i)-\hat i(\hat i\cdot\vec w)\right]=(\vec w\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec w$.
Then $\vec c=\left[(\vec w\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec w\right]\times\hat i=(\vec w\cdot\hat i)(\hat i\times\hat i)-\vec w\times\hat i=\hat i\times\vec w$.
$\vec w=\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-5&1&-3\\1&2&-4\end{matrix}\right|=(-4+6)\hat i-(20+3)\hat j+(-10-1)\hat k=2\hat i-23\hat j-11\hat k$.
$\vec c=\hat i\times(2\hat i-23\hat j-11\hat k)=-23\hat k+11\hat j$ (using $\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$, $\hat i\times\hat k=-\hat j$).

useful_results: $(\vec v\times\hat n)\times\hat n=(\vec v\cdot\hat n)\hat n-\vec v$ for a unit vector $\hat n$: minus the component of $\vec v$ perpendicular to $\hat n$.

Hence $\left(\left(\vec v\times\hat n\right)\times\hat n\right)\times\hat n=\hat n\times\vec v$, and repeated crossing with $\hat n$ rotates the perpendicular part of $\vec v$ by $90^\circ$ each time.
BAC-CAB: $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec y(\vec x\cdot\vec z)-\vec z(\vec x\cdot\vec y)$ and $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec z=\vec y(\vec x\cdot\vec z)-\vec x(\vec y\cdot\vec z)$.
Check with $\vec v=\hat j$, $\hat n=\hat i$: $((\hat j\times\hat i)\times\hat i)\times\hat i=((-\hat k)\times\hat i)\times\hat i=(-\hat j)\times\hat i=\hat k=\hat i\times\hat j$.

concepts: Angle bisector theorem and projection of a vector
questions.question: Consider a $\triangle ABC$ where $A(1,3,2)$, $B(-2,8,0)$ and $C(3,6,7)$. If the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the line $BC$ at $D$, then the length of the projection of the vector $\vec{AD}$ on the vector $\vec{AC}$ is:
questions.key_idea: $AB=AC=\sqrt{38}$, so the bisector $AD$ is also the median: $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.
solution: Projection of $\vec{AD}$ on $\vec{AC}$ has length $AD\cos\frac A2$, because $AD$ bisects $\angle A$.
Length of the bisector: $AD=\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cos\frac A2$, so the projection is $\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cos^2\frac A2=\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cdot\frac{1+\cos A}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $AB=AC$ the bisector hits the midpoint $D$ of $BC$; then use $\frac{|\vec{AD}\cdot\vec{AC}|}{|\vec{AC}|}$ with coordinates.
solution: $AB^2=38=AC^2$, so by the angle bisector theorem $BD:DC=AB:AC=1:1$ and $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In an isosceles triangle $AD\perp BC$ and $AD^2=AB^2-BD^2$; the projection of $\vec{AD}$ on $\vec{AC}$ is then $\frac{AD^2}{AC}$ by the right-triangle altitude relation.
solution: $AB=AC$, so $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $AD\perp BC$; $BD=\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}$.
In right triangle $ADC$ (right angle at $D$), the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$ is at distance $\frac{AD^2}{AC}$ from $A$.

useful_results: Angle bisector theorem: the bisector from $A$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $AB:AC$, so $D=\frac{AC\cdot B+AB\cdot C}{AB+AC}$.
Length of the internal bisector from $A$: $AD=\frac{2bc\cos\frac A2}{b+c}$, with $b=AC$, $c=AB$.
Projection of $\vec u$ on $\vec v$ (length): $\frac{|\vec u\cdot\vec v|}{|\vec v|}$; for a right triangle with hypotenuse $h$ and leg $l$ it is $\frac{l^2}{h}$.
If $AB=AC$ the bisector, median and altitude from $A$ coincide.

concepts: Angle between vectors (acute angle condition)
questions.question: The least positive integral value of $\alpha$, for which the angle between the vectors $\alpha\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\alpha\hat i+2\alpha\hat j-2\hat k$ is acute, is ________.
questions.key_idea: The angle is acute iff the dot product is positive (the vectors are non-zero), which here is a quadratic inequality in $\alpha$.
solution: Let $\vec u=(\alpha,-2,2)$ and $\vec v=(\alpha,2\alpha,-2)$; the angle is acute iff $\cos\theta>0$, i.e. $\vec u\cdot\vec v>0$.
The denominator is positive, so we need $\alpha^2-4\alpha-4>0$.
$2+2\sqrt2\approx4.83$, so for positive integers $\alpha>4.83$ (the other branch $\alpha<2-2\sqrt2<0$ gives no positive value).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test integers directly: evaluate $f(\alpha)=\alpha^2-4\alpha-4$ at $\alpha=1,2,3,\dots$ until it first becomes positive.
solution: Acute angle $\iff\vec u\cdot\vec v=\alpha^2-4\alpha-4>0$ (denominators are positive).
Since $f$ is a parabola opening upward with vertex at $\alpha=2$, it is increasing for $\alpha>2$, so it stays positive from $5$ onwards.
Hence the least positive integer is $5$.

useful_results: Angle between non-zero vectors is acute iff $\vec u\cdot\vec v>0$, right iff $=0$, obtuse iff $<0$.
$\vec u\cdot\vec v>0$ alone suffices: only the sign of the numerator of $\cos\theta$ matters since $|\vec u||\vec v|>0$.
$\alpha^2-4\alpha-4>0\iff|\alpha-2|>2\sqrt2$; roots are $2\pm2\sqrt2$ (about $-0.83$ and $4.83$).
For a bounded integer search, check the root nearest the vertex with a quick numeric test: $f(4)=-4$, $f(5)=1$.

concepts: Dot product, cross product and angle between vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two vectors such that $|\vec a|=1$, $|\vec b|=4$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$. If $\vec c=(2\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$ and the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $\alpha$, then $192\sin^2\alpha$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-3|\vec b|^2$ gives $|\vec c|\cos\alpha$, and $|\vec c|^2=192$ then gives $\sin^2\alpha$.
solution: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=(2\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b-3|\vec b|^2=0-3(16)=-48$.
So $|\vec b||\vec c|\cos\alpha=-48$, hence $|\vec c|\cos\alpha=-12$ since $|\vec b|=4$.
Angle $\theta$ between $\vec a,\vec b$: $\cos\theta=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac12$, so $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\sin^2\theta=\frac34$.
$\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so $|\vec c|^2=48+9|\vec b|^2=48+144=192$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec c$ splits into a component $-3\vec b$ along $\vec b$ (length $12$) and a perpendicular component $2\vec a\times\vec b$ (length $4\sqrt3$), so $\tan\alpha$ is their ratio.
solution: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=16-4=12$, so $|2\vec a\times\vec b|=4\sqrt3$.
$2\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, and $|-3\vec b|=12$ lies along $\vec b$ (reversed).
The angle between $\vec c$ and the line of $\vec b$ has $\tan=\frac{4\sqrt3}{12}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\tan^2\alpha=\frac13$.

useful_results: If $\vec c=\vec p+\vec q$ with $\vec p\perp\vec q$ then the angle of $\vec c$ with $\vec q$ satisfies $\tan\phi=\frac{|\vec p|}{|\vec q|}$ and $\sin^2\phi=\frac{|\vec p|^2}{|\vec p|^2+|\vec q|^2}$.
Here $\sin^2\alpha=\frac{48}{48+144}=\frac14$, so $192\sin^2\alpha=|\vec p|^2=48$ directly.
Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$.
Compare Q128: the same vectors with coefficient $2$ gives $\cos\alpha=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, i.e. $\sin^2\alpha=\frac14$ (consistent).

concepts: Vector equation with cross product and dot product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=3\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be a vector such that $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)+24\hat j-6\hat k$ and $(\vec a-\vec b+\hat i)\cdot\vec c=-3$. Then $|\vec c|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The cross-product equation gives only a dependent set of equations; the dot-product condition supplies the missing independent one.
solution: $\vec a+\vec b=5\hat i+\hat j+4\hat k$ and $\vec a\times\vec b=(2\cdot3+1,\;1\cdot2-3\cdot3,\;-3-4)=7\hat i-7\hat j-7\hat k$.
Right side: $2(7\hat i-7\hat j-7\hat k)+24\hat j-6\hat k=14\hat i+10\hat j-20\hat k$.
Let $\vec c=(x,y,z)$. $(5\hat i+\hat j+4\hat k)\times\vec c=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\5&1&4\\x&y&z\end{matrix}\right|=(z-4y)\hat i-(5z-4x)\hat j+(5y-x)\hat k$.
These three are dependent, so we need the second condition: $\vec a-\vec b+\hat i=(3-2+1)\hat i+(2+1)\hat j+(1-3)\hat k=2\hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec d$ with the formula $\vec c=\frac{\vec d\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}+t\vec s$ and fix $t$ with the dot condition.
solution: Let $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b=(5,1,4)$ and $\vec d=(14,10,-20)$; note $\vec s\cdot\vec d=70+10-80=0$, so a solution exists.
A particular solution is $\frac{\vec d\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}$, because $\vec s\times(\vec d\times\vec s)=\vec d|\vec s|^2-\vec s(\vec s\cdot\vec d)=\vec d|\vec s|^2$.

useful_results: $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec d$ is solvable iff $\vec s\cdot\vec d=0$ and then $\vec c=\frac{\vec d\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}+t\vec s$ for any real $t$ (the cross equation never fixes the component along $\vec s$).
A cross-product equation plus one dot-product equation (with $\vec n\cdot\vec s\neq0$) determines $\vec c$ uniquely.
$\vec a\times\vec b$ components: $(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2-a_2b_1)$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines (common perpendicular)
questions.question: Let the line of the shortest distance between the lines $L_1:\vec r=(\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$ and $L_2:\vec r=(4\hat i+5\hat j+6\hat k)+\mu(\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)$ intersect $L_1$ and $L_2$ at $P$ and $Q$ respectively. If $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the mid point of the line segment $PQ$, then $2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The common perpendicular $PQ$ is parallel to $\vec b\times\vec d$, which fixes $\lambda,\mu$ by proportionality.
solution: $P=(1+\lambda,\,2-\lambda,\,3+\lambda)$ on $L_1$ and $Q=(4+\mu,\,5+\mu,\,6-\mu)$ on $L_2$; directions $\vec b=(1,-1,1)$, $\vec d=(1,1,-1)$.
$\vec b\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-1&1\\1&1&-1\end{matrix}\right|=0\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$, the direction of the common perpendicular.
$\frac{3+\mu-\lambda}{0}=\frac{3+\mu+\lambda}{2}=\frac{3-\mu-\lambda}{2}$: the first numerator must vanish, so $3+\mu-\lambda=0$.
Equating the last two: $3+\mu+\lambda=3-\mu-\lambda$, so $\mu=-\lambda$, and then $3-2\lambda=0$ gives $\lambda=\frac32$, $\mu=-\frac32$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Impose perpendicularity directly: $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec b=0$ and $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d=0$ give two linear equations in $\lambda,\mu$ with no cross product needed.
solution: From the first, $\mu=3-3\lambda$; substitute: $3+9-9\lambda+\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=\frac32$ and $\mu=-\frac32$.

useful_results: Feet of the common perpendicular of two skew lines: solve $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec b=0$ and $\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec d=0$ (two equations, two unknowns).

Shortest distance $=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec d)|}{|\vec b\times\vec d|}$; here $\frac{|(3,3,3)\cdot(0,2,2)|}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{12}{2\sqrt2}=3\sqrt2=|\vec{PQ}|$ (check: $PQ=(0,3,3)$).
The common perpendicular is parallel to $\vec b\times\vec d$; use this to set up proportionality, treating a zero component as a zero numerator.
The midpoint of $PQ$ lies on the 'middle' plane equidistant from both lines when they are skew.

concepts: Cross product and parallel vectors
Angle between two vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=-\hat i-8\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec c=4\hat i+c_2\hat j+c_3\hat k$ be three vectors such that $\vec b\times\vec a=\vec c\times\vec a$. If the angle between the vector $\vec c$ and the vector $3\hat i+4\hat j+\hat k$ is $\theta$, then the greatest integer less than or equal to $\tan^2\theta$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $\vec b\times\vec a=\vec c\times\vec a$ gives $(\vec c-\vec b)\times\vec a=\vec 0$, so $\vec c-\vec b$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec a$.
solution: $\vec b\times\vec a=\vec c\times\vec a\Rightarrow(\vec c-\vec b)\times\vec a=\vec 0$, so $\vec c-\vec b=\lambda\vec a$ and $\vec c=\vec b+\lambda\vec a$.
Compare with $\vec c=4\hat i+c_2\hat j+c_3\hat k$: $-1+\lambda=4$, so $\lambda=5$, $c_2=-3$, $c_3=7$. Hence $\vec c=4\hat i-3\hat j+7\hat k$.
$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec c\cdot(3\hat i+4\hat j+\hat k)}{|\vec c|\,|3\hat i+4\hat j+\hat k|}=\frac{12-12+7}{\sqrt{16+9+49}\sqrt{9+16+1}}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{74}\sqrt{26}}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec c\times\vec d|}{\vec c\cdot\vec d}$ directly, so no cosine or secant is needed.
solution: As before, $(\vec c-\vec b)\parallel\vec a$ gives the equal increments: $c_1-b_1=4+1=5$, so $c_2=-8+5=-3$ and $c_3=2+5=7$, i.e. $\vec c=(4,-3,7)$.

useful_results: $\vec b\times\vec a=\vec c\times\vec a\iff(\vec c-\vec b)\parallel\vec a$ (or $\vec c=\vec b$): equal cross products with the same vector mean the difference is parallel to it.

$\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec u\times\vec v|}{\vec u\cdot\vec v}$ for the angle between $\vec u,\vec v$ (with $\theta$ acute when the dot product is positive); it avoids square roots when only $\tan^2\theta$ is needed.
Identity: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2+(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2$ (here $1875+49=1924=74\times26$).
Greatest integer function: compute the value as a fraction and compare with the neighbouring integers ($38\le\frac{1875}{49}<39$ since $49\times38=1862$).

concepts: Distance of a point from a line measured along a given direction
questions.question: The distance of the point $(7,-2,11)$ from the line $\frac{x-6}{1}=\frac{y-4}{0}=\frac{z-8}{3}$ along the line $\frac{x-5}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-3}=\frac{z-5}{6}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The required segment lies on the line through $P$ parallel to the second line, so it meets the first line at a parameter-fixed point $Q$.
solution: The required line $L$ passes through $P$ and is parallel to $L_2$: $\frac{x-7}{2}=\frac{y+2}{-3}=\frac{z-11}{6}$.
$Q$ lies on $L_1$, whose points have $y=4$: $-3\lambda-2=4$, so $\lambda=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance along direction $\vec d$ equals $|\vec d|$ times a ratio of cross products, avoiding the explicit point $Q$.
solution: Let $A(6,4,8)$ be a point on $L_1$ with direction $\vec u=(1,0,3)$; $\vec d=(2,-3,6)$ and $|\vec d|=7$.
If $P+t\vec d$ lies on $L_1$, then $(\overrightarrow{PA}-t\vec d)\times\vec u=\vec 0$, so $t=\frac{|\overrightarrow{PA}\times\vec u|}{|\vec d\times\vec u|}$ in magnitude.

useful_results: Distance of $P$ from line $A+s\vec u$ measured along $\vec d$ is $|\vec d|\frac{|\overrightarrow{PA}\times\vec u|}{|\vec d\times\vec u|}$ (valid when $\vec d\not\parallel\vec u$).

Perpendicular distance is the special case where $\vec d\perp$ the line; the along-a-direction distance is $\frac{h}{\sin\phi}$ with $h$ the perpendicular distance and $\phi$ the angle between $\vec d$ and the line.

Here the perpendicular distance is $h=\frac{|\overrightarrow{PA}\times\vec u|}{|\vec u|}=\frac{\sqrt{360}}{\sqrt{10}}=6$ and $\sin\phi=\frac{|\vec d\times\vec u|}{|\vec d||\vec u|}=\frac{\sqrt{90}}{7\sqrt{10}}=\frac37$, giving $\frac{6}{3/7}=14$.
Any component that is constant along the target line (here $y=4$) gives the parameter in one equation.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z}{-3}$ and $\frac{x-\lambda}{2}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z-2}{-5}$ is $\frac{6}{\sqrt5}$, then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: The formula $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$ makes the distance linear in $\lambda$, giving $|\lambda-4|=3$.
solution: Line 1 passes through $(4,-1,0)$ with $\vec d_1=(1,2,-3)$; line 2 passes through $(\lambda,-1,2)$ with $\vec d_2=(2,4,-5)$.
Shortest distance $=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}\right|$ with $\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(\lambda-4,0,2)$.
$\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&2&-3\\2&4&-5\end{matrix}\right|=(-10+12)\hat i-(-5+6)\hat j+(4-4)\hat k=2\hat i-\hat j$, with magnitude $\sqrt5$.
Scalar triple product $=(\lambda-4)(2)-0\cdot(-1)+2(0)=2(\lambda-4)$ (equal to the PDF's determinant $(\lambda-4)(-10+12)-0+2(4-4)$).
Sum of all possible values of $\lambda=7+1=8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance between skew lines = distance of a point of line 2 from the plane through line 1 parallel to line 2.
solution: Normal to the plane containing line 1 and parallel to line 2: $\vec n=\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(2,-1,0)$.
Point $(\lambda,-1,2)$ of line 2 has distance $\frac{|2\lambda+1-9|}{\sqrt5}=\frac{|2\lambda-8|}{\sqrt5}$ from this plane.
Setting this equal to $\frac{6}{\sqrt5}$ gives $|\lambda-4|=3$, so $\lambda=1$ or $7$ and the sum is $8$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec a_1+t\vec d_1,\ \vec a_2+s\vec d_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$ (zero iff the lines are coplanar).
If the distance is fixed and one point parameter $\lambda$ occurs linearly, the equation is $|\lambda-c|=k$, always giving two values with sum $2c$ (here $c=4$, sum $8$).
When $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ has a zero component the triple product loses terms - always expand the determinant along the row with the zero.
Parallel lines ($\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\vec 0$) need the different formula $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.

concepts: Image of a point in a line
Direction cosines of a line
questions.question: Let the image of the point $(1,0,7)$ in the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{3}$ be the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then which one of the following points lies on the line passing through $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and making angles $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ with the $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively and an acute angle with the $x$-axis?
questions.key_idea: The foot of the perpendicular gives the image; then $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ with the acute condition fixes the signs of the direction cosines.
solution: Let $B(1,0,7)$ and $M(\lambda,1+2\lambda,2+3\lambda)$ be the foot of the perpendicular on the line, whose direction is $\vec p=(1,2,3)$.
$M=(1,3,5)$. $M$ is the midpoint of $B$ and the image, so the image is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(1,6,3)$.
Direction cosines of the new line: $m=\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12$, $n=\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$.
$l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ gives $l^2=1-\frac14-\frac12=\frac14$, so $l=\pm\frac12$; the angle with the $x$-axis is acute, so $l=+\frac12$ (the PDF keeps $\pm$).
Direction $\left(\frac12,-\frac12,-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\propto(1,-1,-\sqrt2)$, so the line is $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-6}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{-\sqrt2}$, i.e. $(1+t,\,6-t,\,3-\sqrt2\,t)$.
Test the options: $(3,4,3-2\sqrt2)$ is obtained for $t=2$ (since $x=3$, $y=4$ and $z=3-2\sqrt2$), so (D) lies on the line.
(A) and (C) have $x=1$, so $t=0$, which needs $y=6$: fail. (B) with $x=3$ needs $y=4$ but has $-4$: fail.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's final line is written with $\pm1$ in the $x$-denominator and the sign is never resolved; it also never checks which option fits. The acute angle with the $x$-axis fixes $l=+\frac12$, so the direction is $(1,-1,-\sqrt2)$ and only option (D) lies on the line. Answer D unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: On the line $x+y$ is constant ($=7$), so options can be eliminated at once after finding the image.
solution: Image of $B(1,0,7)$ in the line is $(1,6,3)$ (reflection: $M=(1,3,5)$, image $=2M-B$).
The line makes angles $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ with $y$ and $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ with $z$, so $m=-\frac12$, $n=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$, $l=+\frac12$ (acute with $x$).
Direction ratios $(l,m)=\left(\frac12,-\frac12\right)$ are in ratio $1:-1$, so $x$ rises exactly as $y$ falls and $x+y=1+6=7$ on the whole line.
Options: (A) $1+2=3$, (B) $3-4=-1$, (C) $1-2=-1$, (D) $3+4=7$. Only (D) can lie on the line.

useful_results: Image of $B$ in the line $A+\lambda\vec p$ is $2M-B$, where $M=A+\frac{(B-A)\cdot\vec p}{|\vec p|^2}\vec p$ is the foot of the perpendicular.
Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; two given angles with axes fix the third up to sign, which the 'acute/obtuse' condition resolves.
A line with direction ratios $(a,b,c)$ keeps $bx-ay$ constant etc. - a quick invariant for rejecting options.
Check: foot $M=(1,3,5)$ lies on the line ($\lambda=1$) and $\overrightarrow{BM}=(0,3,-2)$, $(0,3,-2)\cdot(1,2,3)=0$.

concepts: Intersection of two lines in space
Centroid of a triangle and section formula
questions.question: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with $R(-1,4,2)$. Suppose $M(2,1,2)$ is the midpoint of $PQ$. The distance of the centroid of $\triangle PQR$ from the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x-2}{0}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}$ and $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+3}{-3}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The centroid lies on the median $RM$ at $\frac23$ of the way from $R$, so $P$ and $Q$ need not be found.
solution: Check $z$: $-\lambda-3=0$ and $\mu-1=0$, so the lines meet at $(2,-6,0)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The centroid divides the median $RM$ in the ratio $2:1$, so $G=\frac{R+2M}{3}$ directly.
solution: The line $\frac{x-2}{0}=\dots$ has $x=2$ throughout; substituting $x=2$ in the second line gives $\mu=1$, point $(2,-6,0)$, and its $y$ and $z$ also match the first line ($\lambda=-3$).

useful_results: Centroid of a triangle with a vertex $R$ and opposite-side midpoint $M$ is $\frac{R+2M}{3}$; no need to know the other two vertices.
A line with a zero direction ratio (here $x$-component $0$) keeps that coordinate constant; substitute it into the other line to fix the parameter.
Two lines meet iff the parameters solving two coordinate equations also satisfy the third (otherwise they are skew).
Distance formula check: $\sqrt{1+64+4}=\sqrt{69}\approx8.31$.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line
questions.question: Let $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from the point $(1,2,3)$ on the line $\frac{x+3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3}$. Then $19(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A general point of the line plus the perpendicularity condition $\overrightarrow{PF}\cdot\vec d=0$ fixes the foot.
solution: The line is $\vec r=\langle-3,1,-4\rangle+\lambda\langle5,2,3\rangle$; a general point is $F(5\lambda-3,\,2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda-4)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The foot minimises the distance, so minimise $|PF|^2$ as a quadratic in $\lambda$; also the sum of coordinates is linear in $\lambda$.
solution: Sum of the coordinates of any point of the line: $(5\lambda-3)+(2\lambda+1)+(3\lambda-4)=10\lambda-6$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $A+\lambda\vec d$: $\lambda=\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$ (here $\frac{(4,1,7)\cdot(5,2,3)}{38}=\frac{43}{38}$).
Setting $\frac{d}{d\lambda}|P-F|^2=0$ is the same condition as $\overrightarrow{PF}\cdot\vec d=0$.
When only a combination such as $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is asked, evaluate it on the parametric form and substitute $\lambda$ - no need for each coordinate.
Distance from $P$ to the line is $|P-F|=\sqrt{|P-A|^2-\frac{((P-A)\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}}$.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between lines $L_1$ and $L_2$, where $L_1:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-3}=\frac{z+4}{2}$ and $L_2$ is the line passing through the points $A(-4,4,3)$, $B(-1,6,3)$ and perpendicular to the line $\frac{x-3}{-2}=\frac{y}{3}=\frac{z-1}{1}$, is:
questions.key_idea: $L_2$ is just the line $AB$ (its direction $(3,2,0)$ is already perpendicular to $(-2,3,1)$), so the skew-line formula applies directly.
solution: $L_2$ passes through $A(-4,4,3)$ and $B(-1,6,3)$, so $\vec b_2=\overrightarrow{AB}=(3,2,0)$. (It is perpendicular to $(-2,3,1)$: $-6+6+0=0$, consistent.) So $L_2:\frac{x+4}{3}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z-3}{0}$.
$L_1$: $\vec a_1=\hat i-\hat j-4\hat k$, $\vec b_1=2\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$. $L_2$: $\vec a_2=-4\hat i+4\hat j+3\hat k$, $\vec b_2=3\hat i+2\hat j$.
$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&-3&2\\3&2&0\end{matrix}\right|=-4\hat i+6\hat j+13\hat k$ and $|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|=\sqrt{16+36+169}=\sqrt{221}$.
S.D. $=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|=\left|\frac{20+30+91}{\sqrt{221}}\right|=\frac{141}{\sqrt{221}}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of a point of $L_2$ from the plane through $L_1$ parallel to $L_2$.
solution: Normal to that plane: $\vec n=\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=(-4,6,13)$, with $|\vec n|^2=221$.

useful_results: A line through two given points has direction equal to their difference; the 'perpendicular to a given line' phrase can be a consistency check, not new data.
Distance between skew lines = distance from any point of one line to the plane containing the other and parallel to the first.
$|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$; check: $|\vec b_1|^2=17$, $|\vec b_2|^2=13$, $\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=6-6+0=0$, so $17\times13=221$.
If a zero direction ratio appears (here $z$-component $0$), the line lies in a constant-$z$ plane, which simplifies the cross product.

concepts: Mirror image of a point in a line
questions.question: Let $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the mirror image of the point $(2,3,5)$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$. Then $2\alpha+3\beta+4\gamma$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of the point and its image.
solution: Let $A(2,3,5)$ and let $B(2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda+2,\,4\lambda+3)$ be the foot of the perpendicular on the line.
$B$ is the midpoint of $A$ and the image: $\frac{\alpha+2}{2}=\frac{55}{29}$, $\frac{\beta+3}{2}=\frac{97}{29}$, $\frac{\gamma+5}{2}=\frac{139}{29}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF step $\beta$: from $\frac{\beta+3}{2}=\frac{97}{29}$ it prints $\beta=\frac{167}{29}$; the correct value is $\frac{194}{29}-3=\frac{107}{29}$. The next line uses $321=3\times107$, so only the printed value is a typo. Also the last line writes $4\lambda$ for $4\gamma$. Answer 33 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $AB\perp$ the line, $A$ and the foot $B$ have equal dot product with $\vec d=(2,3,4)$; the image has it too.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AA'}\perp\vec d$ gives $\vec d\cdot A'=\vec d\cdot A$.
Therefore $2\alpha+3\beta+4\gamma=\vec d\cdot A'=33$, with no need to find $\lambda$ or the image.

useful_results: The mirror image $A'$ of $A$ in a line with direction $\vec d$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{AA'}\cdot\vec d=0$, so $\vec d\cdot A'=\vec d\cdot A$.
Image formula: $A'=2B-A$ with $B=P_0+\frac{(A-P_0)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$.
Here $\vec d\cdot B=29\lambda+20=33$ also equals $\vec d\cdot A=33$, confirming consistency.
The same shortcut works for any linear combination whose coefficients are the direction ratios.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $\frac{x-\sqrt3}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is $1$, then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec V_1\times\vec V_2=3(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$, so the distance is $\frac{|\lambda-\sqrt3|}{\sqrt3}$.
solution: $\vec V_1=-2\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec V_2=\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k$, and $\overrightarrow{AB}=(\lambda-\sqrt3,\,2-1,\,1-2)=(\lambda-\sqrt3,1,-1)$.
$\vec V_1\times\vec V_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-2&1&1\\1&-2&1\end{matrix}\right|=3\hat i+3\hat j+3\hat k=3(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$.

Distance $=\left|\frac{\vec V_1\times\vec V_2}{|\vec V_1\times\vec V_2|}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}\right|=\left|\frac{(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)\cdot((\lambda-\sqrt3)\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)}{\sqrt3}\right|=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the plane $x+y+z=\text{const}$ through line 2 and parallel to line 1, then the distance of a point of line 1.
solution: Normal common to both directions: $\vec V_1\times\vec V_2\parallel(1,1,1)$, so the plane through line 2 parallel to line 1 is $x+y+z=\sqrt3+1+2=3+\sqrt3$.
Point of line 1: $(\lambda,2,1)$, whose value of $x+y+z$ is $\lambda+3$.

useful_results: When $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2\parallel(1,1,1)$ the distance between lines is $\frac{|\Delta(x+y+z)|}{\sqrt3}$, where $\Delta$ is the difference of $x+y+z$ at the two base points.
For skew lines, a parameter in a base point appears linearly: the equation is $|\lambda-c|=k\Rightarrow\lambda=c\pm k$ with sum $2c$ (here $2\sqrt3$).
Check numerically: for $\lambda=0$ the numerator $|0-\sqrt3|/\sqrt3=1$.
Always confirm the lines are not parallel ($\vec V_1\times\vec V_2\ne\vec 0$) before using the skew-lines formula.

concepts: Mirror image of a point in a line
questions.question: If the mirror image of the point $P(3,4,9)$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $14(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The foot $N$ of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $P$ and its image.
solution: Let $N(1+3\lambda,\,2\lambda-1,\,2+\lambda)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ on the line.
$N$ is the midpoint of $P(3,4,9)$ and $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$: $\frac{\alpha+3}{2}=\frac{83}{14}$ gives $\alpha=\frac{62}{7}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Vector reflection formula $Q=2A+\frac{2(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d-P$, applied to the sum of coordinates directly.
solution: Take $A(1,-1,2)$ on the line and $\vec d=(3,2,1)$, so $|\vec d|^2=14$ and $(P-A)\cdot\vec d=(2,5,7)\cdot(3,2,1)=23$.

useful_results: Reflection of $P$ in the line $A+\lambda\vec d$: $Q=2A-P+\frac{2(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$.
Reflection preserves distances from every point of the line: $|QA|=|PA|$; here $|PA|^2=4+25+49=78$ and $|QA|^2=\frac{55^2+11^2+26^2}{49}=\frac{3822}{49}=78$.
Foot of perpendicular parameter is $\lambda=\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}=\frac{23}{14}$.
$Q-P$ is parallel to the normal direction and perpendicular to $\vec d$: $(Q-P)\cdot\vec d=0$.

concepts: Points on a line at a given distance
Centroid of a triangle
questions.question: Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points on the line $\frac{x+3}{8}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z+1}{2}$ which are at a distance of $6$ units from the point $R(1,2,3)$. If the centroid of the triangle $PQR$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: $P,Q$ are symmetric about the foot of the perpendicular from $R$, so the centroid is $\frac{R+2F}{3}$.
solution: A general point of the line is $(8\lambda-3,\,2\lambda+4,\,2\lambda-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $P,Q$ are equidistant from $R$, so the midpoint of $PQ$ is the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $R$; centroid $=\frac{R+2F}{3}$.
solution: Both $P$ and $Q$ are at distance $6$ from $R$ on the line, so $F$ (midpoint of $PQ$) is the foot of the perpendicular from $R$.

useful_results: The two points of a line at equal distance from an outside point are symmetric about the foot of the perpendicular from that point.
Centroid with the midpoint $F$ of one side: $G=\frac{R+2F}{3}$.

Parameter equation $a\lambda^2+b\lambda+c=0$ for distance conditions: the sum of roots $=-\frac ba$ is the sum of the parameters, i.e. $\lambda_P+\lambda_Q=1$ here, so the midpoint parameter is $\frac12$.
The distance of $R$ from the line is $\sqrt{(8\lambda-4)^2+\dots}$ at $\lambda=\frac12$: $\sqrt{0+9+9}=\sqrt{18}<6$ confirming two real points.

concepts: Intersection of two lines in space
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: The line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y}{-2}=\frac{z-7}{16}$ and $\frac{x+3}{4}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ intersect at the point $P$. If the distance of $P$ from the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ is $l$, then $14l^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Find $P$ by equating coordinates, then $l^2=\frac{|\vec V\times\vec p|^2}{|\vec p|^2}$ with $14=|\vec p|^2$ cancelling.
solution: Adding: $-7b=-7$, so $b=1$ and then $a=-\frac12$. Third coordinate check: $16(-\frac12)+7=-1=b-2$. So the lines meet.
The third line passes through $A(-1,1,1)$ with direction $\vec p=(2,3,1)$, $|\vec p|^2=14$. $\vec V=\overrightarrow{AP}=(2,0,-2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pythagoras: $l^2=|AP|^2-(\text{projection of }AP\text{ on the line})^2$.
solution: $P=(1,1,-1)$ as before and $A(-1,1,1)$ on the third line with unit-direction $\hat p=\frac{(2,3,1)}{\sqrt{14}}$.

useful_results: Distance of a point $P$ from line $A+t\vec p$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec p|}{|\vec p|}$, or $\sqrt{|AP|^2-\frac{(\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec p)^2}{|\vec p|^2}}$.
Two lines $\frac{x-x_1}{a_1}=\ldots$ intersect iff the three coordinate equations in $(a,b)$ are consistent (determinant of coplanarity $=0$).
Using two coordinate equations to solve the parameters and the third to verify avoids a separate coplanarity test.
Here the foot is $\left(-\frac57,\frac{10}{7},\frac87\right)$ and $l^2=\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)^2\!+\!\left(\frac37\right)^2\!+\!\left(\frac{15}{7}\right)^2\!=\frac{54}{7}$.

concepts: Intersection of lines with a given direction
Perpendicular distance of a point from a line
questions.question: A line with direction ratios $2,1,2$ meets the lines $x=y+2=z$ and $x+2=2y=2z$ respectively at the points $P$ and $Q$. If the length of the perpendicular from the point $(1,2,12)$ to the line $PQ$ is $l$, then $l^2$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Point $P(t,t-2,t)$ and $Q(2s-2,s,s)$ on the two lines, with $\overrightarrow{PQ}\parallel(2,1,2)$ giving $t=6,\ s=2$.
solution: $PQ:\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\lambda$. Let $F(2\lambda+2,\lambda+2,2\lambda+2)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A(1,2,12)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pythagoras with the projection of $\overrightarrow{QA}$ on the unit direction $\frac{(2,1,2)}{3}$.
solution: With $P,Q$ found as before, $Q=(2,2,2)$ lies on the line with unit direction $\hat u=\frac{(2,1,2)}{3}$.

useful_results: To find a line of known direction meeting two given lines, parametrise one point on each and impose parallelism of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$: two proportionality equations for two unknowns.
Perpendicular length from $A$ to a line through $Q$ with unit direction $\hat u$: $l^2=|QA|^2-(\overrightarrow{QA}\cdot\hat u)^2$.
A common-direction check: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(-4,-2,-4)=-2(2,1,2)$ confirms the direction.
Here the foot of the perpendicular happens to coincide with $P$ ($\overrightarrow{PA}=(-5,-2,6)\perp(2,1,2)$ since $-10-2+12=0$).

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines (feet of the common perpendicular)
Dot product of vectors
questions.question: Let $O$ be the origin and $M$ and $N$ be the points on the lines $\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-4}{1}=\frac{z-5}{3}$ and $\frac{x+8}{12}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+11}{9}$ respectively such that $MN$ is the shortest distance between the given lines. Then $\overrightarrow{OM}\cdot\overrightarrow{ON}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $MN$ is perpendicular to both lines, so $\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec d_1=0=\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec d_2$ gives the two parameters.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the known direction of the common perpendicular, $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$, and set $\overrightarrow{NM}\parallel$ it.
solution: The middle component gives $\lambda=5\mu-6$; substituting, the first gives $-8\mu+11=-3k$ and the third gives $-6\mu+2=4k$.

useful_results: The common perpendicular of two skew lines is parallel to $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; its feet satisfy $\overrightarrow{MN}\parallel\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ (three equations, two parameters plus a scale).
Equivalent condition: $\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec d_1=\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec d_2=0$ (two linear equations in $\lambda,\mu$).
A zero component in $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ (here $y$-component $0$) makes $M$ and $N$ share the same $y$-coordinate ($3$ and $3$), a quick check.

Shortest distance here: $|MN|=\sqrt{9+0+16}=5$, equal to $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$ with $\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(-13,-6,-16)$: $\frac{|78-128|}{10}=5$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If $d_1$ is the shortest distance between the lines $x+1=2y=-12z$ and $x=y+2=6z-6$, and $d_2$ is the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+8}{-7}=\frac{z-4}{5}$ and $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-6}{-3}$, then the value of $\frac{32\sqrt{3}\,d_1}{d_2}$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Both are skew-line distances: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$, applied twice.
solution: Write $L_1$ in symmetric form: $x+1=2y=-12z$ becomes $\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y}{1/2}=\frac{z}{-1/12}$. It passes through $\vec a_1=(-1,0,0)$ with $\vec b_1=\left(1,\frac12,-\frac1{12}\right)\parallel(12,6,-1)$.
$L_2$: $x=y+2=6z-6$ becomes $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1/6}$. It passes through $\vec a_2=(0,-2,1)$ with $\vec b_2=\left(1,1,\frac16\right)\parallel(6,6,1)$.
The shortest distance between two skew lines is $d_1=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$.
For the second pair, $L_3$ passes through $(1,-8,4)$ with $\vec b_3=(2,-7,5)$ and $L_4$ through $(1,2,6)$ with $\vec b_4=(2,1,-3)$, so $\vec a_4-\vec a_3=(0,10,2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A skew-line distance is the distance of a point of one line from the plane through the other line parallel to the first.
solution: For $d_1$: the common normal is $(2,-3,6)$ (from $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$). The plane through $L_1$ parallel to $L_2$ passes through $(-1,0,0)$: $2x-3y+6z=-2$.
The point $(0,-2,1)$ of $L_2$ lies at distance $\frac{|0+6+6+2|}{\sqrt{4+9+36}}=\frac{14}{7}=2$ from this plane, so $d_1=2$.
For $d_2$: the common normal is $(1,1,1)$. The plane through $L_3$ parallel to $L_4$ passes through $(1,-8,4)$: $x+y+z=-3$.
The point $(1,2,6)$ of $L_4$ lies at distance $\frac{|1+2+6+3|}{\sqrt3}=\frac{12}{\sqrt3}=4\sqrt3$ from it, so $d_2=4\sqrt3$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec r=\vec a_1+\lambda\vec b_1$ and $\vec r=\vec a_2+\mu\vec b_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$; it is $0$ exactly when the lines are coplanar (intersecting or parallel is excluded only if $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\vec 0$).
Direction vectors may be rescaled (here $(1,\frac12,-\frac1{12})\to(12,6,-1)$): the formula is unchanged because numerator and denominator scale together.
Equivalent form: distance from any point of one line to the plane through the other line parallel to the first (normal $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$).

Recognition cue: if $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\parallel(1,1,1)$, the distance is $\frac{|\Delta x+\Delta y+\Delta z|}{\sqrt3}$ ($\Delta$ = difference of the two base points). Here $\frac{0+10+2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{12}{\sqrt3}$.

concepts: Line meeting two given lines in 3D (collinearity of points)
questions.question: Let a line passing through the point $(-1,2,3)$ intersect the lines $L_1:\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+1}{-2}$ at $M(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $L_2:\frac{x+2}{-3}=\frac{y-2}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{4}$ at $N(a,b,c)$. Then the value of $\frac{(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2}{(a+b+c)^2}$ equals ________.
questions.key_idea: $P,M,N$ are collinear, so $\overrightarrow{PM}\parallel\overrightarrow{PN}$; the proportionality of components fixes both parameters.
solution: Let $P=(-1,2,3)$. A general point of $L_1$ is $M(3\lambda+1,\,2\lambda+2,\,-2\lambda-1)$ and of $L_2$ is $N(-3\mu-2,\,-2\mu+2,\,4\mu+1)$.
$P,M,N$ are collinear, so the components are proportional: $\frac{3\lambda+2}{-3\mu-1}=\frac{2\lambda}{-2\mu}=\frac{-2\lambda-4}{4\mu-2}$.
Let the common ratio be $t$: $\overrightarrow{PM}=t\,\overrightarrow{PN}$. The second component gives $2\lambda=-2\mu t$, i.e. $\lambda=-\mu t$.
The first component gives $3\lambda+2=-3\mu t-t$. Substituting $\lambda=-\mu t$: $-3\mu t+2=-3\mu t-t$, so $t=-2$ and $\lambda=2\mu$.
The third component: $-2\lambda-4=-2(4\mu-2)$, i.e. $-4\mu-4=-8\mu+4$, so $\mu=2$ and $\lambda=4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The required line is the intersection of two planes: the plane through $P$ and $L_1$, and the plane through $P$ and $L_2$; so $M$ and $N$ come from plane sections.
solution: Plane through $P$ and $L_2$ (point $B(-2,2,1)$, direction $(-3,-2,4)$): normal $=(-3,-2,4)\times(1,0,2)=(-4,10,2)\parallel(-2,5,1)$; equation $-2x+5y+z=15$.
Intersect $L_1$, $M(3\lambda+1,2\lambda+2,-2\lambda-1)$, with it: $-6\lambda-2+10\lambda+10-2\lambda-1=15$, i.e. $2\lambda+7=15$, so $\lambda=4$ and $M=(13,10,-9)$.
Sums of coordinates: $14$ and $-1$, so the ratio is $196$.

useful_results: A line through a point $P$ meeting two skew lines $L_1,L_2$ is the intersection of plane$(P,L_1)$ and plane$(P,L_2)$; it exists uniquely when neither plane is parallel to the other line.
Three points are collinear iff $\overrightarrow{PM}\times\overrightarrow{PN}=\vec 0$; with parametrised points this gives two independent equations for two unknown parameters.
The coordinate sum is linear along a line: on $L_1$, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3\lambda+2$ (=14 at $\lambda=4$); on $L_2$, $a+b+c=1-\mu$ (=$-1$ at $\mu=2$).
Plane through a point $P$ and a line (point $A$, direction $\vec d$) has normal $\vec d\times\overrightarrow{AP}$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular on a line in 3D
Perpendicular vectors (dot product)
questions.question: Let $Q$ and $R$ be the feet of perpendiculars from the point $(a,a,a)$ on the lines $x=y,\ z=1$ and $x=-y,\ z=-1$ respectively. If $\angle QPR$ is a right angle, where $P=(a,a,a)$, then $12a^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Each foot is found by $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec d=0$; then the right angle at $P$ is $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=0$.
solution: $L_1:\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{1}=\frac{z-1}{0}=\lambda$ and $L_2:\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{-1}=\frac{z+1}{0}=\mu$. So $Q=(\lambda,\lambda,1)$ and $R=(\mu,-\mu,-1)$, with directions $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,-1,0)$.
Direction ratios of $PR$ (from $R$ to $P$): $(a,a,a+1)$; of $PQ$ (from $Q$ to $P$): $(0,0,a-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A right angle at $P$ means $QR^2=PQ^2+PR^2$ (Pythagoras on side lengths) once the feet are known.
solution: Both lines are horizontal, so the foot of the perpendicular keeps the line's $z$ and equals the foot of $(a,a)$ on the line in the $xy$-plane: $Q=(a,a,1)$ (foot of $(a,a)$ on $y=x$) and $R=(0,0,-1)$ (foot of $(a,a)$ on $y=-x$).

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $A+\lambda\vec d$: $\lambda=\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$.
If a line is perpendicular to the $z$-axis (direction has $0$ in the $z$-slot), the foot from any point has the line's own $z$-value, and the $xy$-part is the planar foot of the perpendicular.
$\angle QPR=90^\circ\iff\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=0\iff QR^2=PQ^2+PR^2$ (needs $P\ne Q,R$).
Degenerate check: $a=1$ gives $P=Q$ (angle undefined) while $a=-1$ is valid; either way $12a^2=12$.

concepts: Point on a line at a given distance (distance formula in 3D)
questions.question: A line passes through $A(4,-6,-2)$ and $B(16,-2,4)$. Then the point $P(a,b,c)$, where $a,b,c$ are non-negative integers, on the line $AB$ lies at a distance of $21$ units from the point $A$. The distance between the points $P(a,b,c)$ and $Q(4,-12,3)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Move $21$ units from $A$ along the unit direction of $AB$, $\frac{(6,2,3)}{7}$; non-negativity picks the side.
solution: $|(6,2,3)|=\sqrt{36+4+9}=7$, so dividing by $7$ gives direction cosines $\left(\frac67,\frac27,\frac37\right)$.
A point at distance $21$ from $A$ satisfies $\frac{x-4}{6/7}=\frac{y+6}{2/7}=\frac{z+2}{3/7}=\pm21$.
The $+$ sign gives $x-4=18$, $y+6=6$, $z+2=9$: $P=(22,0,7)$. The $-$ sign gives $(-14,-12,-11)$, rejected since coordinates must be non-negative.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the parameter $t$ in $P=A+t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$, where $|AB|=14$, and then the cosine rule for $PQ$ without computing $P-Q$ coordinates separately.

useful_results: Points on the line through $A$ with direction cosines $(l,m,n)$ at distance $s$: $A\pm s(l,m,n)$.
If $\vec d=(p,q,r)$ has integer entries with gcd 1, the integer points on the line are $A+k\vec d$ and the distance from $A$ is $|k||\vec d|$; here $|\vec d|=7$ and $k=\pm3$.
$|PQ|^2=|AP|^2+|AQ|^2-2\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AQ}$ (cosine rule in vector form).
Whenever a sign ambiguity appears (the $\pm$ of distance), use the extra condition in the problem (here non-negativity) to discard one point.

concepts: Unit vector with given angles (dot product)
questions.question: Let a unit vector which makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with $2\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$ and an angle of $45^\circ$ with $\hat i-\hat k$ be $\vec C$. Then $\vec C+\left(-\frac12\hat i+\frac1{3\sqrt2}\hat j-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat k\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Two angle conditions are two linear equations in the components; with $|\vec C|=1$ a quadratic leaves two candidates, and the given extra vector picks one.
solution: Let $\vec C=a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ with $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ (3).

Upper sign: $\vec C=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)\hat i-\frac1{3\sqrt2}\hat j+\left(-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)\hat k$. Adding the given vector gives $\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat i-\frac12\hat k$, option (C).

Lower sign: the sum is $-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat i+\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat j-\left(\frac12+\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right)\hat k$, which matches no option (D has the opposite sign of $\hat k$), so (C) is the answer.
questions.correction_note: PDF's working for $b$ is inconsistent: it writes $b=\frac{1\pm\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}-1}{4}=-\pm\frac1{3\sqrt2}$, but with $a=\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$ one has $1-2a=\mp\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, so $b=\mp\frac1{3\sqrt2}$ (sign opposite to that of the $\sqrt2$ in $a$). The PDF also adds the given vector for one root only and never checks the other root, which gives a vector matching no option. Final answer (C) agrees with the key.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options: condition (2) is linear, so subtract the given vector and check $a-c=1$, then the norm, on the survivors.
solution: Write the given vector as $\vec w=\left(-\frac12,\frac1{3\sqrt2},-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)$. If an option is $\vec S$, then $\vec C=\vec S-\vec w$.

(B) and (C) both give $\frac{\sqrt2}{3}+\frac12$, so test $|\vec C|=1$. For (B): $\vec C=\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{3}+\frac12,0,\frac{\sqrt2}{3}-\frac12\right)$ and $|\vec C|^2=2\left(\frac29+\frac14\right)=\frac{17}{18}\ne1$, fails.

useful_results: A unit vector at angle $\alpha$ to a fixed vector $\vec p$ satisfies $\vec C\cdot\vec p=|\vec p|\cos\alpha$: each angle condition is one linear equation.

Two angle conditions plus $|\vec C|=1$ give two solutions in general; they are mirror images in the plane of the two given vectors, so their sum lies in that plane. Here the two roots sum to $(1,0,-1)$.
Reduce to one variable by solving the two linear equations, then use $|\vec C|=1$ for a quadratic.
With options present, test the linear condition first (cheap) and the norm last.

concepts: Dot product and perpendicular vectors
questions.question: For $\lambda>0$, let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\vec a=\hat i+\lambda\hat j-3\hat k$ and $\vec b=3\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$. If the vectors $\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec a-\vec b$ are mutually perpendicular, then the value of $(14\cos\theta)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot(\vec a-\vec b)=|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2=0$ gives $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$, which fixes $\lambda$.
solution: $(\vec a-\vec b)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)=0$ gives $|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2=0$, i.e. $|\vec a|^2=|\vec b|^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=\sqrt{14}$ we have $14=|\vec a||\vec b|$, so $14\cos\theta=\vec a\cdot\vec b$ directly (no need for $\cos\theta$).
solution: Perpendicular diagonals $\vec a+\vec b$, $\vec a-\vec b$ of a parallelogram mean it is a rhombus, so $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$.
$|\vec a|^2=10+\lambda^2$ and $|\vec b|^2=14$, so $\lambda=2$ and $|\vec a||\vec b|=14$.

useful_results: $(\vec a+\vec b)\perp(\vec a-\vec b)\iff|\vec a|=|\vec b|$ (diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular).
If $|\vec a||\vec b|=k$ then $k\cos\theta=\vec a\cdot\vec b$; expressions like $(k\cos\theta)^2$ need no square roots.
For equal magnitudes, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a|^2\cos\theta$; here $14\cos\theta=-5$.
Always use the sign condition (here $\lambda>0$) to reject extra roots of $\lambda^2=$ constant.

concepts: Scalar triple product
Unit vector and dot product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec c=x\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, $x\in\mathbb R$. If $\vec d$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\vec b+\vec c$ such that $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$, then $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $|\vec d|=1$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ together, after squaring, make the $x^2$ terms cancel and leave a linear equation for $x$.
solution: $\vec d=\lambda\left((2+x)\hat i+6\hat j-2\hat k\right)$, a scalar multiple of $\vec b+\vec c$.
Divide (2) by the square of (1): $(x+2)^2+40=(x+6)^2$, i.e. $x^2+4x+44=x^2+12x+36$, so $8x=8$ and $x=1$ (consistent: $x+6>0$ so $\lambda>0$).
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&1&1\\2&4&-5\end{matrix}\right|=-9\hat i+7\hat j+2\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the triple product as a determinant that is linear in $x$, and use $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=[\vec a\,\vec b\,(\vec b+\vec c)]$ to link it to $\vec d$.
solution: $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ with $\vec d=\frac{\vec b+\vec c}{|\vec b+\vec c|}$ means $\vec a\cdot(\vec b+\vec c)=|\vec b+\vec c|$, i.e. $x+6=\sqrt{(x+2)^2+40}$.

useful_results: $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c=\det$ of the component matrix; it is unchanged when a multiple of $\vec b$ is added to $\vec c$.
For a unit vector $\vec d\parallel\vec v$ with $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$: $\vec a\cdot\vec v=|\vec v|$ (so $\vec a\cdot\vec v>0$), which when squared often kills the quadratic term.
Squaring can introduce roots with the wrong sign; check $\vec a\cdot\vec v>0$ ($x+6>0$ here).
$\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ with $|\vec a|=\sqrt3$ means $\vec d$ makes $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)$ with $\vec a$.

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral using the cross product of diagonals
questions.question: If $A(1,-1,2)$, $B(5,7,-6)$, $C(3,4,-10)$ and $D(-1,-4,-2)$ are the vertices of quadrilateral $ABCD$, then its area is:
questions.key_idea: Area of a (planar) quadrilateral $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$.
solution: The diagonals are $\overrightarrow{AC}=2\hat i+5\hat j-12\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}=-6\hat i-11\hat j+4\hat k$.
$\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&5&-12\\-6&-11&4\end{matrix}\right|=(20-132)\hat i-(8-72)\hat j+(-22+30)\hat k=-112\hat i+64\hat j+8\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the quadrilateral along diagonal $AC$ into triangles $ABC$ and $ACD$ and add their areas.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=(-20-36,\;24+8,\;-6+10)=(-56,32,4)$ as well: the two triangles have equal area, and $B$, $D$ lie on opposite sides of $AC$.

useful_results: For any planar quadrilateral $ABCD$ (convex or not), area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$.

The same expression is the magnitude of the vector area $\frac12\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}$ of a skew quadrilateral too; coplanarity here: $[\overrightarrow{AB},\overrightarrow{AC},\overrightarrow{AD}]=0$.
Parallelogram: area $=|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}|=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$.
Quick simplification: pull out common factors from the cross product before taking the norm ($8(-14,8,1)$, norm $8\sqrt{261}$).

concepts: Cross product of vectors
Minimum value of a function over an interval
questions.question: Consider three vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$. Let $|\vec a|=2$, $|\vec b|=3$ and $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$. If $\alpha\in\left[0,\frac\pi3\right]$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, then the minimum value of $27|\vec c-\vec a|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\perp\vec c$ gives $|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+4$, and $|\vec a|=|\vec b||\vec c|\sin\alpha$ ties $|\vec c|$ to $\alpha$.
solution: $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ is perpendicular to both $\vec b$ and $\vec c$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec c\cdot\vec a=|\vec c|^2+4$.
$|\vec a|=|\vec b\times\vec c|=|\vec b||\vec c|\sin\alpha$, so $3|\vec c|\sin\alpha=2$, i.e. $|\vec c|\sin\alpha=\frac23$.
On $\left(0,\frac\pi3\right]$ this is smallest when $\sin\alpha$ is largest, i.e. $\sin\alpha=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ at $\alpha=\frac\pi3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The component of $\vec c$ perpendicular to $\vec b$ has fixed length $\frac23$, so $|\vec c|^2=\frac49+(|\vec c|\cos\alpha)^2$, which is minimised at the extreme angle.
solution: $\vec a\perp\vec c$, so $|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+4$.
$|\vec a|=|\vec b|\cdot(|\vec c|\sin\alpha)$ with $|\vec c|\sin\alpha$ the length of the part of $\vec c$ perpendicular to $\vec b$, so that length is $\frac23$.
Split $\vec c$ along and across $\vec b$: $|\vec c|^2=\left(\frac23\right)^2+(|\vec c|\cos\alpha)^2$, and $|\vec c|\cos\alpha=\frac23\cot\alpha$.
$\cot\alpha$ is decreasing on $\left(0,\frac\pi3\right]$, so the least value is at $\alpha=\frac\pi3$: $\frac23\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}$, whose square is $\frac4{27}$.

useful_results: If $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ then $\vec a\perp\vec b$ and $\vec a\perp\vec c$, so $|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2$ and $|\vec b-\vec a|^2=|\vec b|^2+|\vec a|^2$.
$|\vec b\times\vec c|=|\vec b||\vec c|\sin\alpha$: with $|\vec b|,|\vec a|$ fixed, the tip of $\vec c$ stays at a fixed perpendicular distance $\frac{|\vec a|}{|\vec b|}$ from the line of $\vec b$.
$|\vec c|\ge\frac{|\vec a|}{|\vec b|}$ always (equality at $\alpha=90^\circ$); restricting $\alpha\le\alpha_0<90^\circ$ moves the minimum to the endpoint $\alpha_0$.
Here the unrestricted minimum would be $\frac49$, but the range $\alpha\le\frac\pi3$ gives $\frac{16}{27}$.

concepts: Vector equation with cross products (parallel vectors)
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+5\hat j-\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be three vectors such that $(\vec c+\hat i)\times(\vec a+\vec b+\hat i)=\vec a\times(\vec c+\hat i)$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-29$, then $\vec c\cdot(-2\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Move everything to one side: $(\vec c+\hat i)\times(2\vec a+\vec b+\hat i)=\vec 0$, so $\vec c+\hat i$ is parallel to a known vector in the $xy$-plane.
solution: $(\vec c+\hat i)\times(\vec a+\vec b+\hat i)-\vec a\times(\vec c+\hat i)=\vec 0$. Since $-\vec a\times(\vec c+\hat i)=(\vec c+\hat i)\times\vec a$, this is $(\vec c+\hat i)\times(\vec a+\vec b+\hat i+\vec a)=\vec 0$.
$2\vec a+\vec b+\hat i=(4+2+1)\hat i+(10-2)\hat j+(-2+2)\hat k=7\hat i+8\hat j$.
So $\vec c+\hat i=\lambda(7\hat i+8\hat j)$ (parallel vectors; $\vec c+\hat i=\vec 0$ would give $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-2\ne-29$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parallelism means $\vec c+\hat i=(p+1,q,r)$ has no $\hat k$ component and $y:x=8:7$; solve with $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-29$ as two linear equations in $p,q$.
solution: As before, $(\vec c+\hat i)\times(7\hat i+8\hat j)=\vec 0$.
A vector parallel to $7\hat i+8\hat j$ has zero $\hat k$-component and $\hat i,\hat j$ components in ratio $7:8$. So $\vec c=p\hat i+q\hat j$ with $\frac{q}{p+1}=\frac87$, i.e. $q=\frac{8(p+1)}{7}$.

useful_results: $\vec u\times\vec p=\vec q\times\vec u\Rightarrow\vec u\times(\vec p+\vec q)=\vec 0\Rightarrow\vec u\parallel(\vec p+\vec q)$ (when both nonzero). Here $\vec u=\vec c+\hat i$.
$\vec u\times\vec v=\vec 0\iff\vec u=\lambda\vec v$ for some scalar (if $\vec v\ne\vec 0$); this reduces a vector equation to one scalar unknown.
A vector parallel to a vector with zero $\hat k$-component also has zero $\hat k$-component.
Do not forget the degenerate case $\vec u=\vec 0$; check it against the other given condition.

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral using the cross product of diagonals
questions.question: If $A(3,1,-1)$, $B\left(\frac53,\frac73,\frac13\right)$, $C(2,2,1)$ and $D\left(\frac{10}3,\frac23,-\frac13\right)$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral $ABCD$, then its area is:
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$, the diagonal formula.
solution: For quadrilateral $ABCD$ the diagonals are $AC$ and $BD$, and area $=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{BD}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes $\overrightarrow{AC}=\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k$, which is the reverse of $C-A=(-1,1,2)$ (sign error; it does not change the magnitude of the cross product), and it stops after listing $\overrightarrow{BD}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ without computing the cross product. The cross product and the final area $\frac{4\sqrt2}{3}$ (option D, matches the key) are filled in here.

alternate_solutions.idea: Opposite sides are equal and parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram and its area is $|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}|$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\left(-\frac43,\frac43,\frac43\right)$ and $\overrightarrow{DC}=C-D=\left(-\frac43,\frac43,\frac43\right)$, so $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}$ and $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

useful_results: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a parallelogram iff $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}$ (equivalently the diagonals bisect each other); then area $=|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}|=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$.
Diagonal formula $\frac12|\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}|$ is valid for any planar quadrilateral.
Reversing a vector in a cross product changes only the sign, so the area is unaffected by direction errors.
Midpoints of $AC$ and $BD$ coincide here: $\left(\frac52,\frac32,0\right)$ and $\left(\frac52,\frac32,0\right)$, confirming the parallelogram.

concepts: Cross product and angle between vectors
Vector triple product magnitude
questions.question: Let $\vec a=6\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$. If $\vec c$ is a vector such that $|\vec c|\ge6$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$, $|\vec c-\vec a|=2\sqrt2$ and the angle between $\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $60^\circ$, then $\left|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|=|\vec a\times\vec b||\vec c|\sin60^\circ$; $|\vec c|$ comes from $|\vec c-\vec a|^2=8$ with $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$, a quadratic in $|\vec c|$.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\6&1&-1\\1&1&0\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i-\hat j+5\hat k$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{27}$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=8$ gives $|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec c=8$, i.e. $|\vec c|^2+38-12|\vec c|=8$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes $|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|-2\vec c\cdot\vec a=8$ (missing the square on $|\vec a|$) but then correctly uses $|\vec a|^2=38$ (giving $|\vec c|^2-12|\vec c|+30=0$); corrected here. Question itself is inconsistent: since $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$ the angle between $\vec c$ and $\vec a$ has $\cos=6/\sqrt{38}$, and $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec a$, so the angle between $\vec c$ and $\vec a\times\vec b$ must be at least $90^\circ-\cos^{-1}(6/\sqrt{38})\approx76.7^\circ$ and cannot be $60^\circ$; no such $\vec c$ exists. The intended answer (key B, $\frac92(6+\sqrt6)$) is what the formulas give.

alternate_solutions.idea: The answer equals $\frac92|\vec c|$, so the options give $|\vec c|$ directly, and only one option satisfies $|\vec c|\ge6$.
solution: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{27}$ and $\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so $|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|=\sqrt{27}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|\vec c|=\frac92|\vec c|$.
Dividing each option by $\frac92$ gives $|\vec c|$: (A) $6-\sqrt6$, (B) $6+\sqrt6$, (C) $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$, (D) $\frac{\sqrt6}{3}$.

useful_results: $|(\vec p\times\vec q)\times\vec r|=|\vec p\times\vec q||\vec r|\sin\theta$, $\theta$ = angle between $\vec p\times\vec q$ and $\vec r$; also $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times\vec r=\vec q(\vec p\cdot\vec r)-\vec p(\vec q\cdot\vec r)$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec c$ turns $\vec a\cdot\vec c=k|\vec c|$ into a quadratic in $|\vec c|$.
Consistency check: $\vec c$ cannot make an angle with $\vec a\times\vec b$ smaller than $90^\circ-\angle(\vec c,\vec a)$, because $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec a$.
When the stated constraints are an inequality ($|\vec c|\ge6$), use it to pick the root of the quadratic.

concepts: Vector triple product
Projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec b=\left(\left(\vec a\times(\hat i+\hat j)\right)\times\hat i\right)\times\hat i$. Then the square of the projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$ is:
questions.key_idea: Evaluate the three nested cross products step by step; the projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$ is $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}$.
solution: $\vec a\times(\hat i+\hat j)=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&1&-1\\1&1&0\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$.
$(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)\times\hat i=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-1&1\\1&0&0\end{matrix}\right|=\hat j+\hat k$.
$(\hat j+\hat k)\times\hat i=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\0&1&1\\1&0&0\end{matrix}\right|=\hat j-\hat k$, so $\vec b=\hat j-\hat k$ and $|\vec b|=\sqrt2$.
Projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}=\frac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For any $\vec p$: $(\vec p\times\hat i)\times\hat i=(\vec p\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec p$, which deletes the $\hat i$-component and flips the sign of the rest.
solution: Triple-product identity $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times\vec r=\vec q(\vec p\cdot\vec r)-\vec p(\vec q\cdot\vec r)$ with $\vec q=\vec r=\hat i$: $(\vec p\times\hat i)\times\hat i=(\vec p\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec p$.
Take $\vec p=\vec a\times(\hat i+\hat j)=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ (from the determinant).
$\vec b=(\vec p\cdot\hat i)\hat i-\vec p=\hat i-(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)=\hat j-\hat k$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$, $|\vec b|^2=2$, so (projection)$^2=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}{|\vec b|^2}=\frac42=2$.

useful_results: $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times\vec r=\vec q(\vec p\cdot\vec r)-\vec p(\vec q\cdot\vec r)$ (vector triple product expansion).
$(\vec p\times\hat i)\times\hat i=-\left(p_y\hat j+p_z\hat k\right)$: it deletes the $\hat i$-component of $\vec p$ and reverses the rest.
Projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$: $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}$ (scalar); its square $\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}{|\vec b|^2}$ avoids a square root.
Check: $\vec p=(1,-1,1)\to-(-\hat j+\hat k)=\hat j-\hat k$.

concepts: Distance of a point from an axis (direction cosines in 3D)
questions.question: Let $P(x,y,z)$ be a point in the first octant, whose projection in the $xy$-plane is the point $Q$. Let $OP=\gamma$; the angle between $OQ$ and the positive $x$-axis be $\theta$; and the angle between $OP$ and the positive $z$-axis be $\phi$, where $O$ is the origin. Then the distance of $P$ from the $x$-axis is:
questions.key_idea: Distance from the $x$-axis is $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{\gamma^2-x^2}$, and $x=OQ\cos\theta=\gamma\sin\phi\cos\theta$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{OP}=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}=x\hat i+y\hat j$, with $\gamma=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance from the $x$-axis is $\gamma\sin\psi$, where $\psi$ is the angle between $OP$ and the $x$-axis, and $\cos\psi=\sin\phi\cos\theta$.
solution: The distance of $P$ from the $x$-axis is $OP\sin\psi=\gamma\sin\psi$, with $\psi$ the angle between $OP$ and the $x$-axis.
$OQ=\gamma\sin\phi$ (the projection of $OP$ on the $xy$-plane, since $OP$ makes $\phi$ with the $z$-axis).
$\sin\psi=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta}$ (all angles acute in the first octant).

useful_results: Spherical coordinates: $x=\gamma\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y=\gamma\sin\phi\sin\theta$, $z=\gamma\cos\phi$ ($\phi$ from the $z$-axis, $\theta$ the azimuth).
Distance of $(x,y,z)$ from the $x$-, $y$-, $z$-axis: $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2+z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ respectively; equals $\gamma\sin\psi$ with $\psi$ the angle with that axis.
Direction cosines of $OP$: $(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\ \sin\phi\sin\theta,\ \cos\phi)$, with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
Quick numeric check: $\gamma=2$, $\phi=0.7$, $\theta=0.4$ gives $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}=1.6099=2\sqrt{1-\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta}$.

concepts: Dot product and angle between vectors
Quadratic inequality for all real values
questions.question: The set of all $\alpha$, for which the vectors $\vec{a}=\alpha t\hat{i}+6\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=t\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\alpha t\hat{k}$ are inclined at an obtuse angle for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, is:
questions.key_idea: Obtuse for every $t$ means $\vec a\cdot\vec b<0$ for all $t$, a quadratic in $t$ that must stay negative.
solution: Obtuse angle means $\vec a\cdot\vec b<0$ for every real $t$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b=\alpha t\cdot t+6(-2)+(-3)(-2\alpha t)=\alpha t^2+6\alpha t-12$.
We need $\alpha t^2+6\alpha t-12<0$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
If $\alpha\neq0$ this is a quadratic that is negative for all $t$ exactly when $\alpha<0$ and discriminant $D<0$.
If $\alpha=0$ then $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-12<0$ for all $t$, so $\alpha=0$ also works.

alternate_solutions.idea: Separate $\alpha$: write the condition as $\alpha(t^2+6t)<12$ and use the range of $t^2+6t=(t+3)^2-9\ge-9$.
solution: The condition is $\alpha\,(t^2+6t)<12$ for all real $t$.
Complete the square: $t^2+6t=(t+3)^2-9$, which takes every value in $[-9,\infty)$.
If $\alpha>0$, then $\alpha(t^2+6t)\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, so the inequality fails.
If $\alpha=0$ the left side is $0<12$, true for all $t$.
If $\alpha<0$, the largest value of $\alpha(t^2+6t)$ occurs at the smallest $t^2+6t=-9$ and equals $-9\alpha$.

useful_results: $\alpha t^2+\beta t+\gamma<0$ for all real $t$ iff ($\alpha<0$ and $D<0$), or the degenerate case $\alpha=\beta=0,\ \gamma<0$; never forget the linear case.
The angle between two non-zero vectors is obtuse iff $\vec a\cdot\vec b<0$ (acute iff $>0$); also confirm neither vector is $\vec 0$ (here $\vec a\ne\vec 0$ since its $\hat j$ component is $6$).
Isolating the parameter ($\alpha\,g(t)<c$) and using the range of $g$ is often faster than a discriminant check.
Check: $\alpha=-1$ gives $-t^2-6t-12=-(t+3)^2-3<0$ for all $t$ (inside the interval); $\alpha=-2$ gives $-2(t+3)^2+6>0$ at $t=-3$ (outside).

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $L_1:\vec r=(2+\lambda)\hat i+(1-3\lambda)\hat j+(3+4\lambda)\hat k,\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $L_2:\vec r=2(1+\mu)\hat i+3(1+\mu)\hat j+(5+\mu)\hat k,\ \mu\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\frac{m}{\sqrt n}$, where $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then the value of $m+n$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance between skew lines $=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$.
solution: $L_1$: point $\vec a_1=2\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k$, direction $\vec b_1=\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$.
$L_2$: point $\vec a_2=2\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k$, direction $\vec b_2=2\hat i+3\hat j+\hat k$.
$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-3&4\\2&3&1\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i(-3-12)-\hat j(1-8)+\hat k(3+6)=-15\hat i+7\hat j+9\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the plane through $L_1$ parallel to $L_2$ (normal $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$) and find the distance of a point of $L_2$ from it.
solution: Normal to the plane containing $L_1$ and parallel to $L_2$ is $\vec n=\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=(-15,7,9)$.
Since $L_2$ is parallel to this plane, every point of $L_2$ is at the same distance; take $(2,3,5)$.

useful_results: Skew lines $\vec a_1+\lambda\vec b_1$, $\vec a_2+\mu\vec b_2$: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$; $d=0$ iff the lines are coplanar (intersecting or parallel-case excluded since $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\neq0$).
The numerator is the scalar triple product $[\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\ \vec b_1,\ \vec b_2]$, the volume of the parallelepiped; the denominator is the area of its base.
If the lines are parallel ($\vec b_1\parallel\vec b_2$) use $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\times\vec b|}{|\vec b|}$ instead.
Check: x-axis and the line through $(0,1,0)$ along $z$ have $d=\frac{|(0,1,0)\cdot(\hat i\times\hat k)|}{1}=\frac{|(0,1,0)\cdot(0,-1,0)|}{1}=1$, as expected.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and parallel vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=4\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=11\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be a vector such that $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec c\times(-2\vec a+3\vec b)$. If $(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot\vec c=1670$, then $|\vec c|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Bring both terms to one side: $\vec c\times(\vec a-4\vec b)=\vec 0$, so $\vec c$ is parallel to $\vec a-4\vec b$.
solution: $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec c\times(-2\vec a+3\vec b)$ gives $\vec c\times(-\vec a-\vec b)+\vec c\times(2\vec a-3\vec b)=\vec 0$.
Hence $\vec c\times(\vec a-4\vec b)=\vec 0$, so $\vec c=\lambda(\vec a-4\vec b)$.
Use $(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot\vec c=1670$: $\lambda\,(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot(\vec a-4\vec b)=1670$.
$\vec c=-(\vec a-4\vec b)=4\vec b-\vec a=40\hat i-3\hat j+3\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with components: $\vec a-4\vec b=(-40,3,-3)$ and $2\vec a+3\vec b=(41,-5,5)$, so $\vec c=s(-40,3,-3)$ and the dot product fixes $s$ at once.
solution: The cross-product condition reduces to $\vec c\times(\vec a-4\vec b)=\vec 0$, so $\vec c\parallel\vec d$ where $\vec d=\vec a-4\vec b=(4-44,\,-1+4,\,1-4)=(-40,3,-3)$.
Remark: since $(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot\vec d=-1670$ equals minus the given value, $|s|=1$ and $|\vec c|=|\vec d|$ immediately.

useful_results: $\vec c\times\vec u=\vec 0$ with $\vec u\neq\vec 0$ means $\vec c=\lambda\vec u$; combine all cross-product terms on one side to see this.
If $\vec c=\lambda\vec u$ and $\vec e\cdot\vec c=k$ then $\lambda=\frac{k}{\vec e\cdot\vec u}$ and $|\vec c|=\frac{|k|\,|\vec u|}{|\vec e\cdot\vec u|}$ (needs $\vec e\cdot\vec u\ne0$).
$(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec p$ is equivalent to $(\vec a+\vec b+\vec p)\times\vec c=\vec 0$ because $\vec c\times\vec p=-\vec p\times\vec c$.
Expansion $|x\vec a+y\vec b|^2=x^2|\vec a|^2+2xy\,\vec a\cdot\vec b+y^2|\vec b|^2$ used above: $(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot(\vec a-4\vec b)=2\cdot18-5\cdot46-12\cdot123=-1670$.

concepts: Unit vector along a given vector and dot product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+3\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec c=3\hat i-\hat j+\lambda\hat k$ be three vectors. Let $\vec r$ be a unit vector along $\vec b+\vec c$. If $\vec r\cdot\vec a=3$, then $3\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A unit vector along $\vec b+\vec c$ satisfies $\vec r\cdot\vec a=\frac{(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec b+\vec c|}$; equate it to 3 and square.
solution: $\vec b+\vec c=5\hat i+2\hat j+(\lambda-5)\hat k$. Write $\vec r=k(\vec b+\vec c)$ with $k>0$.
$\vec r\cdot\vec a=k\left(\vec b\cdot\vec a+\vec c\cdot\vec a\right)$, with $\vec b\cdot\vec a=2+6-15=-7$ and $\vec c\cdot\vec a=3-2+3\lambda=1+3\lambda$.
questions.correction_note: Step '3 = k(-3+3 lambda)' in the PDF is a slip: b.a + c.a = -7 + (1+3 lambda) = -6+3 lambda (the PDF's own next lines use -6+3 lambda). Also the PDF writes r = k(5i - 2j - (5-lambda)k) but b+c = 5i + 2j + (lambda-5)k (sign of the j and k components); the magnitude is unaffected. Final answer 25 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options: put $\lambda=\frac{25}{3}$ and check that $\frac{(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec b+\vec c|}=3$, while the other options fail.
solution: The condition is $\frac{(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec b+\vec c|}=3$ with $(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot\vec a=3\lambda-6$ and $\vec b+\vec c=(5,2,\lambda-5)$.
Option (C): $3\lambda=25$, $\lambda=\frac{25}{3}$, so $\vec b+\vec c=\left(5,2,\frac{10}{3}\right)$, $|\vec b+\vec c|^2=25+4+\frac{100}{9}=\frac{361}{9}$, $|\vec b+\vec c|=\frac{19}{3}$.
$(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot\vec a=5+4+10=19$, and $\frac{19}{19/3}=3$. It works.
Option (A): $\lambda=10$ gives numerator $24$ and $|\vec b+\vec c|=\sqrt{54}$; $\frac{24}{\sqrt{54}}\ne3$.
Option (B): $\lambda=7$ gives $15$ and $|\vec b+\vec c|=\sqrt{33}$, ratio $\ne3$; option (D): $\lambda=9$ gives $21$ and $\sqrt{45}$, ratio $\ne3$.

useful_results: The component of $\vec a$ along the unit vector $\hat u$ is $\vec a\cdot\hat u$; for a unit vector along $\vec p$, $\hat u=\frac{\vec p}{|\vec p|}$.
$\vec p\cdot\vec a=3|\vec p|$ forces $(\vec p\cdot\vec a)\ge0$ before squaring; squaring can add a spurious root, so check the sign (here $\lambda-2>0$).
The projection of $\vec a$ on any direction is at most $|\vec a|=\sqrt{14}\approx3.74$, so a value of $3$ is feasible; this gives a quick sanity check.
