Check: with $\lambda=\frac{25}{3}$ we get $\vec r=\frac{3}{19}\left(5,2,\frac{10}{3}\right)$, $|\vec r|=1$.

concepts: Area of a triangle using the cross product
questions.question: Let three vectors $\vec a=\alpha\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec b=5\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$, $\vec c=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ form a triangle such that $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b$ and the area of the triangle is $5\sqrt6$. If $\alpha$ is a positive real number, then $|\vec c|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$ fixes $\alpha$; then $|\vec c|^2=|\vec a-\vec b|^2$.
solution: $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b=(\alpha-5)\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$.
Area of the triangle $=\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|=5\sqrt6$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=10\sqrt6$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&4&2\\5&3&4\end{matrix}\right|=10\hat i-(4\alpha-10)\hat j+(3\alpha-20)\hat k$.
$\vec c=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$, so $|\vec c|^2=9+1+4=14$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Lagrange's identity $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ and avoid the determinant.
solution: $\alpha=8$ (positive). Then $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b=(3,1,-2)$ and $|\vec c|^2=14$.

useful_results: Area of the triangle with sides $\vec a,\vec b$ from a common vertex is $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$; for a triangle with sides $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c=\vec a-\vec b$ the area is the same.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ - useful when a parameter sits in $\vec a$ because it gives a quadratic with simple coefficients.
Always read side conditions (like $\alpha>0$) to discard roots: here $\alpha=0$ also satisfies the area equation.
Check: $\alpha=0$ gives $\vec a\times\vec b=(10,10,-20)$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{600}=10\sqrt6$, confirming $\alpha=0$ is a valid root that the condition rejects.

concepts: Area of a parallelogram and quadrilateral using the cross product
questions.question: Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\vec a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=6\vec a+5\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=3\vec b$, where $O$ is the origin. If the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}$ is $15$ sq. units, then the area (in sq. units) of the quadrilateral $OABC$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area of a quadrilateral is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ with diagonals $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$, and everything reduces to $|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
solution: Area of quadrilateral $OABC=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$, with diagonals $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$.
Expand: $(3\vec b-2\vec a)\times(6\vec a+5\vec b)=18\,\vec b\times\vec a+15\,\vec b\times\vec b-12\,\vec a\times\vec a-10\,\vec a\times\vec b=-28\,\vec a\times\vec b$.
So Area $=\frac12\cdot28\,|\vec a\times\vec b|=14|\vec a\times\vec b|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split $OABC$ into triangles $OAB$ and $OBC$ and use $\frac12|\vec p\times\vec q|$ for each; both are multiples of $\vec a\times\vec b$.
solution: Area of $\triangle OAB=\frac12|\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}|=\frac12|2\vec a\times(6\vec a+5\vec b)|=\frac12\cdot10|\vec a\times\vec b|=5|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
$\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{OC}=(6\vec a+5\vec b)\times3\vec b=18\,\vec a\times\vec b$, so area of $\triangle OBC=9|\vec a\times\vec b|$.

$\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}=10\,\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{OC}=18\,\vec a\times\vec b$ have the same direction, so $OB$ is a diagonal inside the quadrilateral and the areas add.
From $|2\vec a\times3\vec b|=15$ we get $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\frac52$, hence area $=35$.

useful_results: Area of a quadrilateral (convex, or any simple quadrilateral) with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$.
Properties used: $\vec x\times\vec x=\vec 0$ and $\vec x\times\vec y=-\vec y\times\vec x$; any cross product of vectors in the span of $\vec a,\vec b$ is a multiple of $\vec a\times\vec b$.
Area of the parallelogram on $\vec p,\vec q$ is $|\vec p\times\vec q|$; of the triangle, $\frac12|\vec p\times\vec q|$.
Check with a square $O(0,0),A(1,0),B(1,1),C(0,1)$: $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-1,1)$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=(1,1)$, cross $=-2$, area $=\frac12\cdot2=1$.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and Lagrange's identity
Trigonometric identities in a triangle
questions.question:
Between the following two statements:
Statement I: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$. Then the vector $\vec r$ satisfying $\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$ is of magnitude $\sqrt{10}$.
Statement II: In a triangle $ABC$, $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C\ge-\frac32$.
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
questions.answer: (B) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
questions.key_idea: Lagrange's identity gives $|\vec r|^2$ from $|\vec a\times\vec r|=|\vec a\times\vec b|$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$; and $\sum\vec{OA}=\vec 0$-type square gives the triangle inequality.
solution: For any $\vec c,\vec d$: $|\vec c\times\vec d|^2=|\vec c|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec c\cdot\vec d)^2$. Put $\vec c=\vec a$, $\vec d=\vec r$.
$|\vec a\times\vec r|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec r|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec r)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec r|^2$ since $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$.
But $\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec r|^2$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\hat i(-2+3)-\hat j(-1+6)+\hat k(1-4)=\hat i-5\hat j-3\hat k$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=35$; $|\vec a|^2=14$.
$35=14|\vec r|^2$, so $|\vec r|=\sqrt{\frac{35}{14}}=\sqrt{\frac52}\neq\sqrt{10}$. Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: let $O$ be the circumcentre, radius $R$. Then $\left|\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}\right|^2\ge0$.
The angle between $\overrightarrow{OA},\overrightarrow{OB}$ is $2C$ (central angle), etc., so $3R^2+2R^2(\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C)\ge0$.
Hence $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C\ge-\frac32$. Statement II is correct. Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Statement I by direct solution: $\vec a\times(\vec r-\vec b)=\vec 0$ gives $\vec r=\vec b+t\vec a$. Statement II by $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C$ with $\cos A\cos B\cos C\le\frac18$.
solution: Statement I: $\vec a\times(\vec r-\vec b)=\vec 0$ means $\vec r-\vec b=t\vec a$, so $\vec r=\vec b+t\vec a$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b+t|\vec a|^2=0$ with $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2+2+3=7$ and $|\vec a|^2=14$, so $t=-\frac12$.
$\vec r=\vec b-\frac12\vec a=\left(\frac32,0,\frac12\right)$, $|\vec r|^2=\frac94+\frac14=\frac52$, so $|\vec r|=\sqrt{\frac52}\ne\sqrt{10}$: Statement I is false.
Statement II: in any triangle $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C$.
$\cos A\cos B\cos C\le\frac18$ (equality for the equilateral triangle; it is negative for an obtuse triangle).
So $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C\ge-1-\frac12=-\frac32$: Statement II is true. Answer (B).

useful_results: $|\vec c\times\vec d|^2+(\vec c\cdot\vec d)^2=|\vec c|^2|\vec d|^2$ (Lagrange's identity). Whenever $\vec a\cdot\vec r$ and $\vec a\times\vec r$ are both given, $|\vec r|^2=\frac{|\vec a\times\vec r|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec r)^2}{|\vec a|^2}$.
$\vec a\times\vec x=\vec a\times\vec y\iff\vec x=\vec y+t\vec a$ for some scalar $t$; together with $\vec a\cdot\vec x=k$ this fixes $\vec x$ uniquely.
In any triangle: $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C\ge-\frac32$, and $\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C\ge\frac34$.

If $O$ is the circumcentre, $\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{OH}$ (H orthocentre), so $|OH|^2=R^2(3+2\sum\cos2A)\ge0$; $H=O$ only for the equilateral triangle.

concepts: Area of a parallelogram from its diagonals (cross product)
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+\alpha\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=-\hat i+\hat k$, $\vec c=\beta\hat j-\hat k$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are integers and $\alpha\beta=-6$. Let the values of the ordered pair $(\alpha,\beta)$, for which the area of the parallelogram of diagonals $\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec b+\vec c$ is $\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$, be $(\alpha_1,\beta_1)$ and $(\alpha_2,\beta_2)$. Then $\alpha_1^2+\beta_1^2-\alpha_2\beta_2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area of a parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$; combine with $\alpha\beta=-6$ and integrality.
solution: Area of a parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=\frac{\sqrt{21}}2$, so $|(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec b+\vec c)|=\sqrt{21}$.
$\vec a+\vec b=\hat i+\alpha\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec b+\vec c=-\hat i+\beta\hat j$.
$(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec b+\vec c)=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&\alpha&2\\-1&\beta&0\end{matrix}\right|=-2\beta\,\hat i-2\hat j+(\alpha+\beta)\hat k$.
Integers with $\alpha\beta=-6$ and $\alpha^2+5\beta^2=29$: $\beta^2=4,\ \alpha^2=9$ (the other divisor pairs give $41,\ 49,\ 181,\dots$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand the cross product by distributivity ($\vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0$) and solve the integer condition from a biquadratic in $\beta$ instead of trial.
solution: $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec b+\vec c)=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c$ because $\vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=(\alpha,-3,\alpha)$, $\vec a\times\vec c=(-\alpha-\beta,\,2,\,2\beta)$, $\vec b\times\vec c=(-\beta,-1,-\beta)$.
Sum $=(-2\beta,\,-2,\,\alpha+\beta)$; its squared length is $21$, giving $\alpha^2+5\beta^2=29$ (using $\alpha\beta=-6$).
Factor: $(5\beta^2-9)(\beta^2-4)=0$, so $\beta^2=4$ or $\frac95$; only $\beta^2=4$ gives an integer, so $\beta=\pm2$, $\alpha=\mp3$.

useful_results: A parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ has sides $\frac{\vec d_1\pm\vec d_2}{2}$ and area $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ (half the cross product of the diagonals).
Cross product is distributive and anti-commutative: $(\vec p+\vec q)\times(\vec q+\vec r)=\vec p\times\vec q+\vec p\times\vec r+\vec q\times\vec r$.
A constraint like $\alpha\beta=-6$ with integer unknowns means check the finite divisor pairs; or eliminate to a biquadratic in one variable.

concepts: Area of a triangle using the cross product
questions.question: Let $ABC$ be a triangle of area $15\sqrt2$ and the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}=\hat i+2\hat j-7\hat k$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=6\hat i+d\hat j-2\hat k$, $d>0$. Then the square of the length of the largest side of the triangle $ABC$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$ gives a quadratic for $d$; then compare the three squared sides.
solution: The largest side is $AB$; its square is $54$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|^2=|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2-(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC})^2$ to avoid the determinant.

useful_results: $|\vec p\times\vec q|^2=|\vec p|^2|\vec q|^2-(\vec p\cdot\vec q)^2$ avoids the $3\times3$ determinant when the dot product is easy.
Triangle area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$; the third side is $\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}-\overrightarrow{AB}$.
Cosine rule in vector form: $BC^2=AB^2+AC^2-2\,\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}$; here $54+44-2\cdot24=50$.
Always apply the stated restriction (here $d>0$) to discard the second root $d=-\frac25$.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and parallel vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i-3\hat j+7\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be a vector such that $(\vec a+2\vec b)\times\vec c=3(\vec c\times\vec a)$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec c=130$, then $\vec b\cdot\vec c$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Moving everything to one side gives $(\vec b+2\vec a)\times\vec c=\vec 0$, so $\vec c\parallel\vec b+2\vec a$.
solution: $(\vec a+2\vec b)\times\vec c=3(\vec c\times\vec a)=-3(\vec a\times\vec c)$, so $\vec a\times\vec c+2\,\vec b\times\vec c+3\,\vec a\times\vec c=\vec 0$.
That is $4\,\vec a\times\vec c+2\,\vec b\times\vec c=\vec 0$, i.e. $\vec b\times\vec c+2(\vec a\times\vec c)=\vec 0$.
Hence $(\vec b+2\vec a)\times\vec c=\vec 0$, so $\vec c=\lambda(\vec b+2\vec a)$.
$\vec b+2\vec a=(2+2)\hat i+(-1-6)\hat j+(1+14)\hat k=4\hat i-7\hat j+15\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\vec c=\lambda\vec u$, $\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec c}{\vec a\cdot\vec c}=\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec u}{\vec a\cdot\vec u}$ with $\vec u=\vec b+2\vec a$, so $\vec c$ itself is not needed.
solution: As above $\vec c\parallel\vec u=\vec b+2\vec a$.
Then $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\lambda\,\vec b\cdot\vec u$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=\lambda\,\vec a\cdot\vec u$, so $\vec b\cdot\vec c=130\cdot\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec u}{\vec a\cdot\vec u}$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec u=|\vec b|^2+2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=6+24=30$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec u=\vec a\cdot\vec b+2|\vec a|^2=12+118=130$.

useful_results: Reduce the vector equation to the form $\vec p\times\vec c=\vec 0$ (using $\vec c\times\vec a=-\vec a\times\vec c$); then $\vec c=\lambda\vec p$ and every dot product with $\vec c$ is $\lambda$ times that with $\vec p$.
If $\vec c\parallel\vec u$, then $\frac{\vec x\cdot\vec c}{\vec y\cdot\vec c}=\frac{\vec x\cdot\vec u}{\vec y\cdot\vec u}$ whenever $\vec y\cdot\vec u\ne0$.
$\vec x\times\vec c=k(\vec y\times\vec c)\iff(\vec x-k\vec y)\times\vec c=\vec 0$ (the cross product is linear in the first factor).
Check: with $\vec c=(4,-7,15)$ both $(\vec a+2\vec b)\times\vec c$ and $3(\vec c\times\vec a)$ equal $(-12,-39,-15)$.

concepts: Vector triple product and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k$ and a vector $\vec c$ be such that $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)+\vec b\times\vec c=\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$, then $\left(24-\vec b\cdot\vec c\right)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Cross the whole equation with $\vec a$, expand the triple products, and dot with $\vec b$ so that only $\vec b\cdot\vec c$ remains.
solution: The condition is $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec v$, where $\vec v=\hat i+8\hat j+13\hat k$.
Take $\vec a\times$ on both sides: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)+\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec c)+\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec a\times\vec v$.

Expand each with $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z$: $(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a-|\vec a|^2\vec b+(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a-|\vec a|^2\vec c+(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.
Substituting: $-26\vec a-29\vec b+13\vec a-29\vec c+13\vec b+26\vec c=-13\vec a-16\vec b-3\vec c$.
So $-13\vec a-16\vec b-3\vec c=\vec a\times\vec v$.
Dot with $\vec b$: $-13\,\vec a\cdot\vec b-16|\vec b|^2-3\,\vec b\cdot\vec c=(\vec a\times\vec v)\cdot\vec b$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c=(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c$, solve $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ for $\vec c$ explicitly and use $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$ to fix the free multiple.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b+(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec v$. Compute $\vec a\times\vec b=(-1,22,17)$ and $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b=(5,1,-1)$.
So $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ with $\vec w=\vec v-\vec a\times\vec b=(2,-14,-4)$. Check $\vec s\cdot\vec w=10-14+4=0$, as required for a solution.
General solution: $\vec c=\frac{\vec w\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}+t\vec s$. Here $\vec w\times\vec s=(18,-18,72)$ and $|\vec s|^2=27$, so $\vec c=\left(\frac23,-\frac23,\frac83\right)+t(5,1,-1)$.

useful_results: Group terms: $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b+(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c$, turning the condition into the standard form $\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$.

$\vec s\times\vec c=\vec w$ is solvable iff $\vec s\cdot\vec w=0$; then $\vec c=\frac{\vec w\times\vec s}{|\vec s|^2}+t\vec s$ (the free $t$ is fixed by one more condition such as $\vec a\cdot\vec c=13$).

Vector triple product: $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z$; and $(\vec x\times\vec y)\cdot\vec z=[\vec x\,\vec y\,\vec z]$, the determinant of the three vectors.
Taking $\vec a\times$ of an equation then dotting with a suitable vector isolates the scalar you want when the unknown vector enters through dot products with known vectors.
Check: $\vec c=(-1,-1,3)$ gives $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-2+3+12=13$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-22$.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and dot product with a parameter
questions.question: Let $\vec a=9\hat i-13\hat j+25\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i+7\hat j-13\hat k$ and $\vec c=17\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k$ be three given vectors. If $\vec r$ is a vector such that $\vec r\times\vec a=(\vec b+\vec c)\times\vec a$ and $\vec r\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0$, then $\frac{\left|593\vec r+67\vec a\right|^2}{(593)^2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $(\vec r-(\vec b+\vec c))\times\vec a=\vec 0$ gives $\vec r=(\vec b+\vec c)+\lambda\vec a$; the second condition gives $\lambda=-\frac{67}{593}$, so $593\vec r+67\vec a=593(\vec b+\vec c)$.
solution: $\vec r\times\vec a=(\vec b+\vec c)\times\vec a$ gives $\left(\vec r-(\vec b+\vec c)\right)\times\vec a=\vec 0$, so $\vec r=(\vec b+\vec c)+\lambda\vec a$.
$\vec b+\vec c=20\hat i+5\hat j-12\hat k$, so $\vec r=(20+9\lambda)\hat i+(5-13\lambda)\hat j+(25\lambda-12)\hat k$.
$\vec b-\vec c=-14\hat i+9\hat j-14\hat k$, and $\vec r\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0$.
Then $593\vec r+67\vec a=593(\vec b+\vec c)$ and the required ratio is $|\vec b+\vec c|^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\lambda$ without components: $(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=|\vec b|^2-|\vec c|^2$, so only $\vec a\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)$ is needed.
solution: As before $\vec r=(\vec b+\vec c)+\lambda\vec a$.
$\vec r\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)+\lambda\,\vec a\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=0$.
Then $593\vec r+67\vec a=593(\vec b+\vec c)$ and the ratio $=|\vec b+\vec c|^2=569$.

useful_results: $\vec r\times\vec a=\vec p\times\vec a\iff\vec r=\vec p+\lambda\vec a$ for a scalar $\lambda$ (they differ by a multiple of $\vec a$, when $\vec a\ne\vec 0$).
$(\vec b+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=|\vec b|^2-|\vec c|^2$: the difference-of-squares identity saves a component computation.

If $\vec r=\vec p+\lambda\vec a$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec q=0$ then $\lambda=-\frac{\vec p\cdot\vec q}{\vec a\cdot\vec q}$ (need $\vec a\cdot\vec q\ne0$); this is the intersection of a line with a plane through the origin.
The expression $593\vec r+67\vec a$ is designed to cancel $\lambda$: always look at what the target expression is built from before computing $\vec r$.

concepts: Straight line in 3D: parametric points at a given distance
questions.question: Let the point, on the line passing through the points $P(1,-2,3)$ and $Q(5,-4,7)$, farther from the origin and at a distance of $9$ units from the point $P$, be $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Points at distance $9$ from $P$ along the line are $P\pm9\hat u$; pick the one farther from $O$.
solution: Their squared distances from $O$ are $49+25+81=155$ and $25+1+9=35$; the farther point is $(7,-5,9)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the required points as $P\pm9\hat u$ with $\hat u$ the unit direction and expand $|OP\pm9\hat u|^2$; the sign of $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\hat u$ decides which is farther.
solution: Required points: $\overrightarrow{OP}\pm9\hat u$ with $\overrightarrow{OP}=(1,-2,3)$, $|\overrightarrow{OP}|^2=14$ and $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\hat u=\frac23+\frac23+2=\frac{10}3$.
The farther point takes the $+$ sign, giving $155$ (the other gives $35$).

useful_results: Points at distance $d$ from $P$ on the line through $P$ with unit direction $\hat u$ are $P\pm d\hat u$; in parametric form $P+t\vec b$ the condition is $t=\pm\frac{d}{|\vec b|}$.
$|\vec p+d\hat u|^2=|\vec p|^2+d^2+2d\,(\vec p\cdot\hat u)$, so the point farther from the origin is the one with the sign of $\vec p\cdot\hat u$.
Direction ratios $(l,m,n)$ come from the difference of two points; the unit vector is $\frac{(l,m,n)}{\sqrt{l^2+m^2+n^2}}$.

concepts: Intersection of lines in 3D
Distance of a point from a line in 3D
questions.question: Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-4}{5}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ and $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{2}$. Then, the shortest distance of $P$ from the line $4x=2y=z$ is:
questions.key_idea: Find $P$ by equating the parametric points, then drop the perpendicular to the line $4x=2y=z$ with direction $(1,2,4)$.
solution: Equating coordinates: $\lambda+2=2\mu+3$ and $5\lambda+4=3\mu+2$ (the third equation repeats the first).
The line $4x=2y=z$ is $\frac{x}{1/4}=\frac y{1/2}=\frac z1$ through the origin with direction $\vec B=\frac14\hat i+\frac12\hat j+\hat k$.
Let $M=\left(\frac\alpha4,\frac\alpha2,\alpha\right)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$; $\overrightarrow{PM}\cdot\vec B=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of a point from a line through the origin: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{OP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ with $\vec d=(1,2,4)$.
solution: The lines meet at $P=(1,-1,1)$ (as found from the parametric equations).
The line $4x=2y=z$ passes through $O$ with direction $\vec d=(1,2,4)$ (since $x=\frac z4,\ y=\frac z2$).

useful_results: Distance of a point $P$ from the line $A+t\vec d$: $\frac{|(\overrightarrow{AP})\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$; equivalently $\sqrt{|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2-\frac{(\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}}$.
$4x=2y=z$ means $x:y:z=\frac14:\frac12:1=1:2:4$; always convert to direction ratios by dividing by the LCM-type denominators.
Two lines meet iff the parametric equations are consistent for all three coordinates; with three equations in two unknowns, solve two and check the third.
Check via Pythagoras: $|OP|^2=3$, projection on $\vec d$ is $\frac{(P\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}=\frac{9}{21}$, distance$^2=3-\frac37=\frac{18}7$.

concepts: Angle between lines in 3D (direction ratios, perpendicularity)
questions.question: If the line $\frac{2-x}{3}=\frac{3y-2}{4\lambda+1}=4-z$ makes a right angle with the line $\frac{x+3}{3\mu}=\frac{1-2y}{6}=\frac{5-z}{7}$, then $4\lambda+9\mu$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Rewrite each line in standard form $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c}$ with unit coefficients of $x,y,z$ before reading direction ratios.
solution: Line 1: $\frac{2-x}{3}=\frac{3y-2}{4\lambda+1}=\frac{4-z}{1}$. Make each numerator of the form $x-x_1$: $\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y-\frac23}{\frac{4\lambda+1}{3}}=\frac{z-4}{-1}$.
So the direction ratios of line 1 are $\left(-3,\ \frac{4\lambda+1}{3},\ -1\right)$.
So the direction ratios of line 2 are $(3\mu,\ -3,\ -7)$.
The lines are at right angles, so $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The condition is linear in $(\lambda,\mu)$ and the asked quantity is exactly its combination, so test one convenient value, $\mu=0$.
solution: Direction vectors (up to non-zero scale): $\vec d_1=(-3,\frac{4\lambda+1}{3},-1)$ and $\vec d_2=(3\mu,-3,-7)$; perpendicularity gives $-9\mu-4\lambda+6=0$, a single linear relation.
Hence $4\lambda+9\mu$ is the same constant for every admissible pair $(\lambda,\mu)$, so it can be found from any one pair.
Take $\mu=0$: $\vec d_2=(0,-3,-7)$. Then $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=-(4\lambda+1)+7=0$ gives $4\lambda=6$.
Check with another pair: $\lambda=0$ gives $\mu=\frac23$, and then $d_1\cdot d_2=-9\cdot\frac23-1+7=0$ holds.

useful_results: Lines $\frac{x-x_1}{a_1}=\frac{y-y_1}{b_1}=\frac{z-z_1}{c_1}$ and the same with $a_2,b_2,c_2$ are perpendicular iff $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$.
Direction ratios are read only after each of $x,y,z$ has coefficient $1$ in its numerator: $\frac{2-x}{3}=\frac{x-2}{-3}$ and $\frac{3y-2}{k}=\frac{y-2/3}{k/3}$.
If the answer is a fixed combination of parameters appearing linearly in one condition, set a convenient parameter to $0$ to find it quickly.

concepts: Intersection of two lines and distance between points in 3D
questions.question: Let $d$ be the distance of the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x+6}{3}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ and $\frac{x-7}{4}=\frac{y-9}{3}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ from the point $(7,8,9)$. Then $d^2+6$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Use a different parameter for each line and match all three coordinates (two equations fix the parameters, the third checks).
solution: The $z$ equation is satisfied: $\lambda-1=2$ and $2\mu+4=2$. So the lines meet at $(3,6,2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cartesian elimination: each line is the intersection of two planes; solve the four plane equations together.
solution: Line 1: $\frac{x+6}{3}=\frac y2$ gives $2x-3y=-12$, and $\frac y2=\frac{z+1}{1}$ gives $y-2z=2$.
From $2x-3y=-12$ and $3x-4y=-15$: multiply by 4 and 3 to get $8x-12y=-48$ and $9x-12y=-45$; subtracting gives $x=3$, then $y=6$.
From $y-2z=2$: $z=2$. Check $2y-3z=12-6=6$ holds, so the point $(3,6,2)$ is common to both lines.

useful_results: Two lines meet iff a common parameter solution exists for all three coordinates; use two coordinates to solve and the third to verify (otherwise the lines are skew).
Always use distinct parameters ($\lambda,\mu$) for the two lines; reusing one letter loses solutions.
Symmetric form $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c}$ equals the planes $b(x-x_1)=a(y-y_1)$ and $c(y-y_1)=b(z-z_1)$.
Skew test: lines through $A,B$ with directions $\vec p,\vec q$ meet (or are coplanar) iff $(\vec B-\vec A)\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)=0$; here it equals $0$.

concepts: Image (reflection) of a point in a line in 3D
questions.question: Let $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the image of the point $(8,5,7)$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-2}{5}$. Then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The foot $F$ of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $P$ and its image, and $\vec{PF}$ is perpendicular to the direction $(2,3,5)$.
solution: Let $P(8,5,7)$ and let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular on the line; the image $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ satisfies $F=\frac{P+Q}{2}$. The direction vector is $\vec a=(2,3,5)$.
A general point of the line is $F=(2\lambda+1,\ 3\lambda-1,\ 5\lambda+2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflect the vector $\vec{AP}$ about the direction directly with the formula $\vec{AQ}=2\,\frac{\vec{AP}\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a-\vec{AP}$, no foot needed.
solution: Take $A(1,-1,2)$ on the line, $\vec a=(2,3,5)$, so $\vec{AP}=(7,6,5)$.
$\vec{AP}\cdot\vec a=14+18+25=57$ and $|\vec a|^2=4+9+25=38$, so the ratio is $\frac{57}{38}=\frac32$.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in the line through $A$ with direction $\vec a$: $Q=A+2\,\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a-(P-A)$ (check: $Q=(0,2,12)$ here).
The foot of the perpendicular is $A+\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a$, and the image is $2F-P$.
Reflection preserves distances from every point of the line: $QA=PA$ ($|PA|^2=110=|QA|^2=1+9+100$).

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y+15}{-7}=\frac{z-9}{5}$ and $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-9}{-3}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Use $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec d)|}{|\vec b\times\vec d|}$; the cross product here is a multiple of $(1,1,1)$.
solution: Points and directions: $\vec a_1=3\hat i-15\hat j+9\hat k$, $\vec a_2=-\hat i+\hat j+9\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-7\hat j+5\hat k$, $\vec d=2\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k$.
$\vec b\times\vec d=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&-7&5\\2&1&-3\end{matrix}\right|=16\hat i+16\hat j+16\hat k$.
Shortest distance $=\frac{|(\vec a_1-\vec a_2)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec d)|}{|\vec b\times\vec d|}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the plane through the second line parallel to the first, then the distance of a point of the first line from it.
solution: The normal to both lines is $\vec b\times\vec d\parallel(1,1,1)$.
Plane through $(-1,1,9)$ (on line 2) containing the direction of line 2: $x+y+z=-1+1+9=9$.
Line 1 is parallel to this plane (its direction $(2,-7,5)$ has $2-7+5=0$), so every point of it is at the same distance from the plane; use $(3,-15,9)$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec r=\vec a_1+s\vec b$, $\vec r=\vec a_2+t\vec d$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec d)|}{|\vec b\times\vec d|}$; it is $0$ iff the lines are coplanar.
Equivalent view: distance from a point of one line to the plane through the other line parallel to the first.
Any scalar multiple of $\vec b\times\vec d$ may be used as the normal: using $(1,1,1)$ avoids big numbers (ratio is unchanged).

concepts: Image of a point in a line
Area of a triangle using vectors
questions.question: Let $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the image of the point $Q(3,-3,1)$ in the line $\frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1}$ and $R$ be the point $(2,5,-1)$. If the area of the triangle $PQR$ is $\lambda$ and $\lambda^2=14K$, then $K$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The foot $S$ of the perpendicular from $Q$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, so area $=\frac12\,PQ\times(\text{length of the component of }QR\text{ along the line})$.
solution: Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the line; then $PQ\perp$ line and $S$ is the midpoint of $PQ$. Direction of the line: $\vec d=(1,1,-1)$.
Let $\theta$ be the angle between $RQ$ and the line: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec{RQ}\cdot\vec d|}{|\vec{RQ}||\vec d|}=\frac{|1-8-2|}{\sqrt{69}\sqrt3}=\frac{9}{3\sqrt{23}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{23}}$.
The distance from $R$ to the foot $S$ measured along the line: $RS=QR\cos\theta=\sqrt{69}\cdot\frac{3}{\sqrt{23}}=3\sqrt3$ (since $QS\perp$ line, $RS$ is the projection of $RQ$ on the line).
Triangle $PQR$ has base $PQ$ and $RS\perp PQ$ (as $RS$ lies on the line, which is perpendicular to $PQ$), so area $=\frac12(PQ)(RS)=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt{42}\cdot3\sqrt3=3\sqrt{126}=9\sqrt{14}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's figure labels the foot of the perpendicular T while the working calls it S, and it writes cos(theta)=-3/sqrt23 in one line and +3/sqrt23 in the next (the angle with the line is taken acute, so the modulus is needed). Values, area 9 sqrt14 and K=81 are correct; the labels and modulus are fixed and the missing sin(theta) step supplied.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute $P$ explicitly (image $=2S-Q$) and take half the magnitude of $\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}$.

useful_results: Area of triangle with vertices $P,Q,R$ is $\frac12|\vec{PQ}\times\vec{PR}|$; with $\vec{PQ}=\vec a,\ \vec{PR}=\vec b$: area $=\frac12\sqrt{|a|^2|b|^2-(a\cdot b)^2}$.
If $P$ is the image of $Q$ in a line $\ell$ and $R\in$ any point, then triangle $PQR$ has $PQ\perp\ell$ and area $=\frac12PQ\times(\text{distance along }\ell\text{ from the foot to the foot of }R)$.
Image of $Q$ in a line: $2S-Q$ with $S$ the foot; $PQ=2\,d(Q,\ell)$.

concepts: Distance between parallel lines in 3D
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{2}=\frac{y-4}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ and $\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z-7}{8}$ is $\frac{13}{\sqrt{29}}$, then a value of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: The direction vectors $(2,3,4)$ and $(4,6,8)$ are parallel, so use the parallel-lines formula $\frac{|(\vec b-\vec a)\times\vec p|}{|\vec p|}$ (not the skew formula).
solution: Directions $(2,3,4)$ and $(4,6,8)$ are proportional, so the lines are parallel.
For parallel lines $d=\frac{|(\vec b-\vec a)\times\vec p|}{|\vec p|}$, with $\vec a=(\lambda,4,3)$, $\vec b=(2,4,7)$, $\vec p=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$.
$(\vec b-\vec a)\times\vec p=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2-\lambda&0&4\\2&3&4\end{matrix}\right|=-12\hat i+4\lambda\hat j+3(2-\lambda)\hat k$.
So $\lambda=\frac{11}{25}$ or $\lambda=1$; only $\lambda=1$ is among the options, i.e. (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes b - a = (2 - lambda)i + j + 4k (printed 'gamma' for lambda and a j-component 1); the j-component is 0 since both lines pass through y=4. The cross product printed afterwards, -12i + 4 lambda j + 3(2-lambda)k, is the correct one for b-a=(2-lambda,0,4), so the answer is unaffected. Corrected the line. Also note lambda=11/25 is a second valid value but not an option (option A is 13/25, not 11/25).

alternate_solutions.idea: Pythagoras: $d^2=|\vec{AB}|^2-(\text{component of }\vec{AB}\text{ along the direction})^2$.
solution: Take $A(\lambda,4,3)$ and $B(2,4,7)$, so $\vec{AB}=(2-\lambda,0,4)$ and $\vec p=(2,3,4)$, $|\vec p|^2=29$.

useful_results: Parallel lines: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\times\vec p|}{|\vec p|}$; the skew formula gives $\frac00$ because $\vec b\times\vec d=\vec0$.
Equivalent: $d^2=|\vec{AB}|^2-\left(\frac{\vec{AB}\cdot\vec p}{|\vec p|}\right)^2$ (Lagrange identity $|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-(u\cdot v)^2$).
Always compare direction ratios first: proportional ones mean parallel lines and the quadratic in the parameter may give two valid values.

concepts: Line intersecting two given lines and parallel to a third line
questions.question: Let the line $L$ intersect the lines $x-2=-y=z-1$ and $2(x+1)=2(y-1)=z+1$ and be parallel to the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{2}$. Then which of the following points lies on $L$?
questions.key_idea: A point on each given line is parametrised; the join of the two points must be parallel to $(3,1,2)$.
solution: $L$ joins these two points and is parallel to $(3,1,2)$, so $(s-k-3,\ s+k+1,\ 2s-k-2)$ is proportional to $(3,1,2)$: $\frac{s-k-3}{3}=\frac{s+k+1}{1}=\frac{2s-k-2}{2}$.
Test $\left(-\frac13,1,-1\right)$: $\frac{-\frac13-\frac23}{3}=-\frac13$, $\ \frac{1-\frac43}{1}=-\frac13$, $\ \frac{-1+\frac13}{2}=-\frac13$. All equal, so it lies on $L$ (option C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Describe $L$ as the intersection of two planes, each through one given line and parallel to $(3,1,2)$; then test options.
solution: Plane 1 contains line 1 (point $(2,0,1)$, direction $(1,-1,1)$) and is parallel to $(3,1,2)$: normal $=(1,-1,1)\times(3,1,2)=(-3,1,4)$.
Plane 2 contains line 2 (point $(-1,1,-1)$, direction $(1,1,2)$) and is parallel to $(3,1,2)$: normal $=(1,1,2)\times(3,1,2)=(0,4,-2)\parallel(0,2,-1)$.
$L$ is the line common to both planes, so the correct point satisfies both equations.
(C) $(-\frac13,1,-1)$: $2+1=3$ and $1+1-4+2=0$. Both hold, so the answer is (C).

useful_results: A line meeting two lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and parallel to a given direction $\vec v$ is the intersection of the planes (line $\ell_1$, direction $\vec v$) and (line $\ell_2$, direction $\vec v$).
A plane containing a line with direction $\vec u$ and parallel to $\vec v$ has normal $\vec u\times\vec v$.
For 'which option lies on it' questions, find two plane equations and test options: faster than parameter solving.
Divide fractional denominators out first: $\frac{x+1}{1/2}=\frac{y-1}{1/2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ has direction $(1,1,2)$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y+7}{-11}=\frac{z-1}{5}$ and $\frac{x-5}{3}=\frac{y-9}{-6}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Apply $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$ directly.
solution: Line 1: $\vec r=(3\hat i-7\hat j+\hat k)+\lambda(4\hat i-11\hat j+5\hat k)$; line 2: $\vec r=(5\hat i+9\hat j-2\hat k)+\mu(3\hat i-6\hat j+\hat k)$.
Shortest distance $=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$.
$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\4&-11&5\\3&-6&1\end{matrix}\right|=19\hat i+11\hat j+9\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Equation of the plane containing line 1 and parallel to line 2, then the distance of a point of line 2 from it.
solution: Line 2 is parallel to the plane, so all its points are equidistant; take $(5,9,-2)$.

useful_results: Skew lines: $d=\frac{|[\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\ \vec b_1,\ \vec b_2]|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$ (scalar triple product in the numerator).
The numerator is a determinant: here $\left|\begin{matrix}2&16&-3\\4&-11&5\\3&-6&1\end{matrix}\right|=187$ (checkable with sympy).
Direction vector $(a,b,c)$ must be read after normalising each ratio to unit coefficients; the sign of the numerator does not matter because of the modulus.

concepts: Distance of a point from a line measured along a given direction
questions.question: Consider the line $L$ passing through the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,3,5)$. The distance of the point $\left(\frac{11}{3},\frac{11}{3},\frac{19}{3}\right)$ from the line $L$ along the line $\frac{3x-11}{2}=\frac{3y-11}{1}=\frac{3z-19}{2}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The required distance is the length of the segment from the given point $A$ to the point $B$ where its line (direction $(2,1,2)$) meets $L$.
solution: $L$ passes through $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,3,5)$, so its direction is $(1,1,2)$: $L:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-3}{2}$.
A general point of this line is $B\left(\frac{11}{3}+2\lambda,\ \frac{11}{3}+\lambda,\ \frac{19}{3}+2\lambda\right)$.
The first equality: $\frac83+2\lambda=\frac53+\lambda$, so $\lambda=-1$. (Check the third: $\frac{\frac{10}{3}-2}{2}=\frac23=\frac53-1$. It holds.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Direct vector approach: $\vec{AB}\parallel(2,1,2)$ and $B\in L$; eliminate the parameter of $L$ by subtracting coordinates.
solution: Let $B=(1+s,\ 2+s,\ 3+2s)$ on $L$. Then $\vec{AB}=\left(s-\frac83,\ s-\frac53,\ 2s-\frac{10}{3}\right)$ must equal $k(2,1,2)$.
Subtract the first two components: $\left(s-\frac83\right)-\left(s-\frac53\right)=-1=2k-k=k$, so $k=-1$.
The first component gives $s-\frac83=-2$, so $s=\frac23$; the third gives $2s-\frac{10}{3}=-2$, so $s=\frac23$. Consistent.

useful_results: Distance of $A$ from a line measured along direction $\vec u$: find $B$ on the line with $\vec{AB}=k\vec u$; the distance is $|k||\vec u|$. It differs from the perpendicular distance unless $\vec u\perp$ line.
The two lines are guaranteed to meet only if coplanar: here $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$ was satisfied.
Subtracting components that share the same coefficient in both direction vectors eliminates the unknown parameter.

concepts: Image (mirror image) of a point in a line in 3D
questions.question: Consider a line $L$ passing through the points $P(1,2,1)$ and $Q(2,1,-1)$. If the mirror image of the point $A(2,2,2)$ in the line $L$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha+\beta+6\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $L$ has direction $\vec B=(1,-1,-2)$; the foot $M$ of the perpendicular from $A$ is the midpoint of $A$ and its image.
solution: Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$: $M=(\lambda+1,\ -\lambda+2,\ -2\lambda+1)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the perpendicularity condition as 'PM . B = 0' but evaluates (lambda-1, -lambda, -2lambda-1), which is AM (A is (2,2,2)), not PM, so the label is wrong (PM would be (lambda, -lambda, -2lambda)). The numbers and the answer 6 are correct; corrected to AM.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflect the vector $\vec{PA}=(1,0,1)$ about the direction of $L$ and add to $P$.
solution: Reflection of $\vec u$ about $\vec B$: $2\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec B}{|\vec B|^2}\vec B-\vec u=-\frac13(1,-1,-2)-(1,0,1)=\left(-\frac43,\frac13,-\frac13\right)$.

useful_results: Mirror image of a point in a line: $A'=2M-A$ where $M$ is the foot.
Equivalent formula with $P$ on the line: $A'=P+2\frac{(A-P)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d-(A-P)$.
Check: $PA'=PA$; both have squared length $2$, since $\frac{16+1+1}{9}=2$ and $1+0+1=2$.

concepts: Common perpendicular (line of shortest distance) of two skew lines
questions.question: Let the point $(-1,\alpha,\beta)$ lie on the line of the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+2}{-3}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-5}{2}$ and $\frac{x+2}{-1}=\frac{y+6}{2}=\frac{z-1}{0}$. Then $(\alpha-\beta)^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The common perpendicular joins feet $P,Q$ with $\vec{PQ}\parallel\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; its equation is the line through $P$ and $Q$.
solution: $PQ$ is perpendicular to both lines, so it is parallel to $\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\-1&2&0\\-3&4&2\end{matrix}\right|=4\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\parallel(2,1,1)$.
From the last two: $2\mu-4\lambda-8=-2\lambda-4$ gives $\mu=\lambda+2$. From the first and third: $3\lambda-\mu=-4\lambda-8$ gives $7\lambda=\mu-8$.
$P=(1,-2,3)$ and $Q=(-3,-4,1)$, so the line of shortest distance is $\frac{x+3}{2}=\frac{y+4}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Describe the common perpendicular as the intersection of two planes, each through one line and containing the common normal direction $(2,1,1)$.
solution: Direction of the common perpendicular: $\vec n=\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(-4,-2,-2)\parallel(2,1,1)$ with $\vec d_1=(-3,4,2)$, $\vec d_2=(-1,2,0)$.
Plane 1 contains line 1 and $\vec n$: normal $=\vec d_1\times(2,1,1)=(2,7,-11)$; through $(-2,2,5)$: $2x+7y-11z+45=0$.
Plane 2 contains line 2 and $\vec n$: normal $=\vec d_2\times(2,1,1)=(2,1,-5)$; through $(-2,-6,1)$: $2x+y-5z+15=0$.
The common perpendicular is the intersection of these planes. Put $x=-1$: $7\alpha-11\beta=-43$ and $\alpha-5\beta=-13$.
From the second, $\alpha=5\beta-13$; then $35\beta-91-11\beta=-43$ gives $24\beta=48$, so $\beta=2$, $\alpha=-3$.

useful_results: The line of shortest distance between skew lines is perpendicular to both; its direction is $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
Plane method: the plane through line 1 containing $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ and the corresponding plane for line 2 intersect in the common perpendicular.
Its length equals $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$ (here $|PQ|=\sqrt{16+4+4}=\sqrt{24}$, since $\vec{PQ}=(-4,-2,-2)$).
The feet $P,Q$ are the points with $\vec{PQ}\perp\vec d_1,\vec d_2$; this gives two linear equations in the parameters.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line in 3D
Distance between two points
questions.question: Let $P$ be the point $(10,-2,-1)$ and $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $R(1,7,6)$ on the line passing through the points $(2,-5,11)$ and $(-6,7,-5)$. Then the length of the line segment $PQ$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Parametrise the line, impose $\vec{RQ}\perp$ direction, then find $Q$ and its distance from $P$.
solution: Let $Q=(-2\lambda+2,\ 3\lambda-5,\ -4\lambda+11)$. The direction ratios of $QR$ are $(-2\lambda+2-1,\ 3\lambda-5-7,\ -4\lambda+11-6)=(-2\lambda+1,\ 3\lambda-12,\ -4\lambda+5)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the perpendicular component: $R-Q=\vec{AR}-\text{(projection on the line)}$, so $\vec{QP}$ follows without the coordinates of $Q$.
solution: $\vec{AR}\cdot\vec d=2+36+20=58$, so the projection is $\frac{58}{29}\vec d=2\vec d=(-4,6,-8)$.
$R-Q=\vec{AR}-2\vec d=(-1,12,-5)-(-4,6,-8)=(3,6,3)$ (the component of $\vec{AR}$ perpendicular to the line).

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line $A+t\vec d$: $t=\frac{(R-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$.
The vector from the foot to $R$ is the part of $\vec{AR}$ perpendicular to $\vec d$: $\vec{AR}-\frac{\vec{AR}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$.
Reduce direction ratios by common factors ($(-8,12,-16)\to(-2,3,-4)$) to keep arithmetic small.
Distance from $R$ to the line: $\sqrt{9+36+9}=\sqrt{54}$ here.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $\frac{x+2}{-3}=\frac{y+5}{2}=\frac{z-4}{4}$ is $\frac{44}{\sqrt{30}}$, then the largest possible value of $|\lambda|$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The distance is a modulus, so $|6\lambda+126|=132$ has two roots; the larger $|\lambda|$ comes from the negative one.
solution: $L_1:\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ passes through $(\lambda,2,1)$ with direction $\vec n_1=(3,-1,1)$; $L_2$ passes through $(-2,-5,4)$ with direction $\vec n_2=(-3,2,4)$.
$\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&-1&1\\-3&2&4\end{matrix}\right|=-6\hat i-15\hat j+3\hat k$, with magnitude $\sqrt{36+225+9}=\sqrt{270}$.
$(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)=(-2-\lambda)\hat i-7\hat j+3\hat k$; using $\vec a_1-\vec a_2=(\lambda+2)\hat i+7\hat j-3\hat k$ only changes the sign inside the modulus.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes only 'lambda + 21 = +22' and then states |lambda|max = 43; that is inconsistent, since lambda=1 gives |lambda|=1. The modulus gives lambda+21=+-22, so lambda=1 or -43, and the maximum of |lambda| is 43 (from the negative root). Fixed. Answer 43 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Plane method: plane through line 2 parallel to line 1 has normal $(2,5,-1)$; distance of $(\lambda,2,1)$ from it.
solution: Every point of $L_1$ is at the same distance from this plane; take $(\lambda,2,1)$: $2\lambda+10-1+33=2\lambda+42$.

useful_results: If the shortest distance equals a given value $D$, the signed numerator $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot\vec n=\pm D|\vec n|$ gives two parameter values (two lines at distance $D$ on either side).
Cancel common factors in normals: $(-6,-15,3)\to(2,5,-1)$ and in magnitudes, e.g. $\sqrt{270}=3\sqrt{30}$.
The skew-line distance as a function of a parameter in one line's position is $\frac{|k\lambda+c|}{|\vec n|}$, linear in the parameter.

concepts: Image (reflection) of a point in a line in 3D
questions.question: Let $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be the image of the point $Q(1,6,4)$ in the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{3}$. Then $2\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The foot $R$ of the perpendicular from $Q$ is the midpoint of $QP$; find $R$ from $\vec{QR}\perp(1,2,3)$.
solution: Let $\frac x1=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{3}=t$, so $R=(t,\ 2t+1,\ 3t+2)$ is a point on the line.

alternate_solutions.idea: Vector reflection formula about the direction $(1,2,3)$ from the point $A(0,1,2)$ on the line.

useful_results: Image of $Q$ in the line through $A$ with direction $\vec d$: $P=A+2\frac{(Q-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d-(Q-A)$.
Any linear combination of the image's coordinates is twice that of the foot minus that of $Q$: $2\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2(2R_x+R_y+R_z)-(2+6+4)=2\cdot\frac{34+48+79}{14}-12=11$.
The foot is unique: $t=\frac{(Q-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}=\frac{17}{14}$.

concepts: Image (reflection) of a point in a line in 3D
questions.question: The square of the distance of the image of the point $(6,1,5)$ in the line $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z-2}{4}$ from the origin is ________.
questions.key_idea: Find the foot $A$ of the perpendicular from $P$ using the direction $(3,2,4)$; the image is $2A-P$.
solution: Let $P(6,1,5)$ and let $A=(3\lambda+1,\ 2\lambda,\ 4\lambda+2)$ be the foot of the perpendicular on the line.
The image $P'$ is such that $A$ is the midpoint of $PP'$: $P'=2A-P=(8-6,\ 4-1,\ 12-5)=(2,3,7)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Vector reflection: $\vec{AP'}=2\,\frac{\vec{A_0P}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d-\vec{A_0P}$; here the projection equals $\vec d$ exactly.
solution: Take $A_0(1,0,2)$ on the line and $\vec d=(3,2,4)$, $\vec{A_0P}=(5,1,3)$.
$\vec{A_0P}\cdot\vec d=15+2+12=29=|\vec d|^2$, so the projection of $\vec{A_0P}$ on the line is exactly $\vec d$.

useful_results: Reflection formula: $P'=A_0+2\,\mathrm{proj}_{\vec d}(P-A_0)-(P-A_0)$; the foot is $A_0+\mathrm{proj}_{\vec d}(P-A_0)$.
Distance of the image from any point $X$ of the line equals the distance of $P$ from $X$: $|P'A_0|=|PA_0|$ ($\sqrt{35}=\sqrt{1+9+25}$ here).
Image of a point in a line preserves distance from the line, $d(P',\ell)=d(P,\ell)$ ($=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$ here).
